children.translated_text: <s>Yuktidīpikā</s> (Lamp of Reasoning).
The doctrines of the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> elephant — whose tusks are the existent and the non-existent, who frequents the forests of schools of thought —
are fragile like the breaking of <s>sallakī</s> (frankincense) groves [before that elephant]. (1)
To the <s>Ṛṣi</s> (sage) of supreme austerity, equal in brilliance to the rays of the sun,
to the Guru who is the sun dispelling the darkness within the dense forest of <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence) — homage! (2)
To the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> named <s>Āsuri</s>, who desired to know the truth, the sage
taught that great doctrine (<s>tantra</s>) for the cessation of the three kinds of suffering. (3)
Its comprehension cannot be achieved even in hundreds of years,
due to its vastness — so thinking, by sages of subtle intellect, (4)
having condensed that teaching of the <s>Ṛṣi</s> into a small text,
it was composed by those of stainless wisdom, out of desire for the welfare of students. (5)
The opponents of that [teaching] are: the proponents of [individual] selves (<s>puruṣa</s>), God (<s>īśvara</s>), and atoms (<s>aṇu</s>);
the annihilationists (<s>vaināśikas</s>), the naturalists (<s>prākṛtikas</s>), and those [who posit] transformation and <s>puruṣa</s> [as separate principles]. (6)
For the purpose of defeating their doctrines, by teachers of subtle intellect,
difficult passages of reasoning were composed in their respective treatises. (7)
Those are unfathomable by students whose understanding is confused about the meaning of the categories;
therefore, by <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, this [work] was made in condensed form. (8)
The treatise called the 'Seventy' [<s>Saptati</s>] — or the entire <s>śāstra</s> itself —
since herein the explanation of all categories will be made. (9)
The existence of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter), its oneness, its purposefulness, and its otherness [from <s>Puruṣa</s>],

children.text: pārārthyañca tathānaikyaṃ viyogo yoga eva ca // 10 //
children.translated_text: its subservience to another (<s>pārārthya</s>), and likewise the plurality [of <s>Puruṣas</s>], separation, and also conjunction — (10)
residual activity (<s>śeṣavṛtti</s>) and the non-agency [of <s>Puruṣa</s>] — these are remembered as the ten supplementary topics (<s>cūlikārtha</s>).
Misapprehension (<s>viparyaya</s>) is fivefold, and the satisfactions (<s>tuṣṭi</s>) are stated as nine. (11)
The incapacity of the instruments (<s>karaṇa</s>) is considered to be of twenty-eight kinds.
Thus [there are] sixty categories together with the eight accomplishments (<s>siddhi</s>). (12)
These will be fully described here in order and by definition.
Therefore, this <s>śāstra</s> is sufficient for establishing the manifold [categories]. (13)
Of small text but not small in meaning, endowed with all the merits of a treatise —
like the image in a mirror of the doctrine of the <s>Ṛṣi</s>. (14)
I shall compose a commentary (<s>vyākhyā</s>) on it, for the establishment of proper reasoning.
May the learned accept it with compassion, even if it be imperfect. (15)

children.text: āha, kariṣyati bhavān vyākhyām / idaṃ tvādāvupanyastaṃ sarvaistantraguṇairyutamidaṃ tantramiti / ke tantraguṇāḥ, kiyanto veti ?

children.translated_text: It is replied:
<s>Sūtras</s> (aphorisms), <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), <s>avayavas</s> (components), and their establishment;
non-deficiency, the statement resolving doubt, enumeration, specification, sequential order, and instruction in terminology — these constitute the excellence of a treatise (<s>tantrasampat</s>).
[Objection:] 'You propose to compose a commentary. But this has been stated at the outset: "endowed with all the merits of a treatise." What are the merits of a treatise, and how many are there?'

children.text:
sūtrāṇi ca pramāṇāni ca avayavāśca, sūtrapramāṇāvayavāḥ / teṣām upapattiḥ sūtrapramāṇāvayavopapattiḥ / upapattiḥ sambhava ityanarthāntaram / ananyo 'rtho 'narthāntaram / upapattiśabdaḥ pratyekaṃ parisamāpyate sūtropapattirityādi /
  āha, lakṣaṇopetasūtropapattiriti vaktavyam /
  itarathā hi alakṣaṇopetasyāpi sūtrasya tantrāṅgabhāvaḥ syāditi /
  ucyate na, nāntarīyakatvāt / na hyantareṇa lakṣaṇopetatvaṃ sūtratvam / ato na vaktavyametaditi /
  āha, atha sūtramiti kasmāt ?
  ucyate- sūcanāt sūtram / sūcayati tāṃstānarthaviśeṣāniti sūtram / tadyathā- kāraṇamastyavyaktam (

children.translated_text: <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 16
), 'Because of the finitude of the differentiated' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 15

children.text: ) / atra pratijñāhetū kaṇṭhoktau / tayorupayogi dṛṣṭāntaṃ sādhyasiddhaye samarthamiti kṛtvā mūlaśakalādayo 'trāntaranabhihitā apyetasmādavasīyante / athavā bhikṣorupasaṃhṛtabahiṣkaraṇāntaḥkaraṇasya teṣu teṣvatīndriyeṣu api pradhānādiṣvartheṣu buddhiṃ sūcayatīti sūtram / athavā, saukṣmyāttadanupalabdhiriti (
children.translated_text: ). Here the thesis and the reason are stated explicitly. Since an example (<s>dṛṣṭānta</s>) useful for those [thesis and reason], capable of establishing the conclusion, [is implied] — therefore the root, the fragments (<s>mūlaśakala</s>), etc., though not explicitly stated herein, are understood from this. Or alternatively: for a <s>bhikṣu</s> (monk) who has withdrawn his external and internal organs, in those various supersensory objects such as <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) and the rest, [the <s>sūtra</s>] indicates (<s>sūcayati</s>) the understanding — hence '<s>sūtra</s>.' Or alternatively, 'Because of its subtlety, it is not perceived' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 8
) is a <s>sūtra</s>. Namely:
'Of few syllables, unambiguous, having essence, facing all directions,
without filler, and faultless — this the knowers of <s>sūtras</s> know as a <s>sūtra</s>.'

<s>Sūtras</s>, <s>pramāṇas</s>, and <s>avayavas</s> — these are '<s>sūtra-pramāṇa-avayavas</s>.' Their establishment (<s>upapatti</s>) is the 'establishment of <s>sūtras</s>, <s>pramāṇas</s>, and components.' '<s>Upapatti</s>' means 'possibility' — that is not a different meaning. The word '<s>upapatti</s>' is individually completed [as]: 'the establishment of <s>sūtras</s>,' etc.
  [Objection:] It should be said: 'the establishment of <s>sūtras</s> possessing proper characteristics.' Otherwise, even a <s>sūtra</s> not possessing characteristics would be a limb of the treatise.
  [Reply:] No, because it is inseparable [from characteristics]. For without possessing characteristics, there is no <s>sūtra</s>-nature. Therefore, this need not be stated.
  [Objection:] Then, why [is it called] a '<s>sūtra</s>'?
  [Reply:] Because it indicates (<s>sūcanāt</s>). It indicates those various particular meanings — hence '<s>sūtra</s>.' For example: 'The cause exists; it is unmanifest' (
'Short, indicating their meaning, of few syllables and words,
essential in every respect — the wise call these <s>sūtras</s>.'
'Without filler' means 'without repetition.' And also:

children.text: pramāṇāni ca pratyakṣādīni, tānyuttaratra vakṣyati 'dṛṣṭamanumānamāptavacanaṃ ca'; (

children.translated_text: <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 4
); 'The ascertainment of each sense-object is perception,' etc. (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 5

) /
  avayavāḥ punarjijñāsādayaḥ, pratijñādayaśca / tatra jijñāsādayo vyākhyāṅgam / pratijñādayaḥ parapratyāyanāṅgam /tānuttaratra vakṣyāmaḥ /
  āha, avayavānabhidhānamupadeśāt / na hi tathā pratyakṣādīni pramāṇānyupadiṣṭāni tathā avayavā upadiṣṭāḥ / tasmādavayavopapattirityetadasat /
  bhāṣyakāraprāmāṇyādadoṣa iti cet syānmatam / yadyapi sūtrakāreṇāvayavopadeśo na kṛtastathāpi bhāṣyakārāḥ kecideṣāṃ saṃgrahaṃ cakruḥ / te ca naḥ pramāṇam / tasmādyukatamavayavopapattiriti / etaccāyuktam / kasmāt ?
  utsūtratvāt / nahyutsūtraṃ vyācakṣāṇā bhāṣyakārāḥ pramāṇaṃ bhavanti / tathā caitadutsūtritamiti /
  ucyate, na / liṅgāt / naitadyuktamanupadeśānna santi jijñāsādayaḥ / kintarhyanupadiṣṭamapyeṣāmastitvaṃ liṅgāt pratipadyāmahe yadayamācāryo duḥkhatrayābhighātājjijñāsā tadapaghātake hetāviti (
children.translated_text:
).
  The <s>avayavas</s> (components) are inquiry (<s>jijñāsā</s>) and the rest, and thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>) and the rest. Among these, inquiry and the rest are limbs of the commentary. Thesis and the rest are limbs of convincing others. These we shall state later.
  [Objection:] The mention of <s>avayavas</s> is based on teaching. For the <s>pramāṇas</s> such as perception and the rest were not taught in the same way as the <s>avayavas</s> were taught. Therefore, 'the establishment of components' — this is incorrect.
  [Possible reply:] If one says 'there is no fault because of the authority of the <s>bhāṣyakāras</s> (commentators)' — that may be the view. Although the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the aphorisms) did not teach the components, some <s>bhāṣyakāras</s> did compile them. And they are authoritative for us. Therefore, 'the establishment of components' is correct. But this too is incorrect. Why?
  Because it goes beyond the <s>sūtras</s>. For <s>bhāṣyakāras</s> commenting beyond the <s>sūtras</s> are not authoritative. And this indeed goes beyond the <s>sūtras</s>.
  [Reply:] No. Because of indication (<s>liṅga</s>). It is not correct [to say] that because of non-instruction, inquiry and the rest do not exist. Rather, even though not explicitly taught, we understand their existence from indication. For this teacher states the inquiry and its purpose [in]: 'From the affliction of the threefold suffering [arises] the inquiry into the means of removing it' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 1
); he makes the thesis [in]: 'The cause exists; it is unmanifest' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 16
); he teaches the reason [in]: 'Because of the finitude of the differentiated' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 15
); he illuminates the example [in]: 'Like an actor, the <s>liṅga</s> (subtle body) operates' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 42

children.text: ) dṛṣṭāntaṃ dyotayati / kṣīrasya yathā tathā pravṛttiḥ pradhānastyetyupasaṃharati (
children.translated_text: ); he makes the application [in]: 'Just as with milk, so is the activity of <s>Pradhāna</s>' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 57
); he concludes [in]: 'Therefore the threefold instrument is the doorway' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 35

) nigamayati / na cānabhipretairācāryāṇāṃ śāstre vyavahāro lakṣyate / tena vayaṃ liṅgātpratipadyāmahe santi jijñāsādayo 'vayavāḥ śāstra iti /
  āha, satāmanupadeśe prayojanavacanam / evaṃ cenmanyase- santi jijñāsādayo 'vayavāḥ, śāstre teṣāmanupadeśe prayojanaṃ vaktavyam- amuṣmāddhetorācāryeṇa nopadiśyante, santi ca te iti /
  ucyate, pramāṇāntarbhāvāt / pramāṇeṣvantarbhāva eṣāmityayamupadiṣṭo heturasmābhiḥ / anumānāṅgaṃ hi jijñāsādayaḥ, tasmāttadantarbhūtāste iti na pṛthagupadiśyante / kiñca, tantrāntarokteḥ / tantrāntareṣu hi vindhyavāsiprabhṛtirācāryairupadiṣṭāḥ / pramāṇaṃ ca naste ācāryā ityataścānupadeśo jijñāsādīnāmiti /
  āha na, pramāṇānupadeśaprasaṃgāt / yadi ca tantrāntaropadeśādevāvayavānāmanupadeśaḥ, pratyakṣādīnyapi ca tantrāntareṣūpadiśyante / śrotrādivṛttiḥ pratyakṣam / sambandhādekasmāccheṣasiddhiranumānam / yo yatrābhiyuktaḥ karmaṇi cāduṣṭassa tatrāptastasyopadeśa āptavacanamiti teṣāmapyanupadeśaprasaṅgaḥ / atha sati tantrāntaropadeśe pramāṇānyupadiśyante nāvayavā iti, nanvetadicchāmātramiti /
  ucyate, pūrva eva tarhi parihāro 'stu / athavā punarastu tantrāntarokterityayamapi parihāraḥ / yattūktaṃ pramāṇānupadeśaprasaṅga iti atra brūmaḥ- ayuktametat / kasmāt ? prayojanavatāmupadeśasyādoṣatvāt / anupadeśo hi prayojanavataścodyata iti yuktametat / upadeśameva tu sadoṣa iti kṛtvā kaḥ pratyācakṣīta ? tasmānna kiñcidetat / kiñcānyat, pradhānopadeśe guṇabhūtāntarbhāvasiddheḥ / tadyathā, takṣṇuhi caitra ityukte yāvadbhissādhanaviśeṣairvinā takṣaṇaṃ nopapadyate sarvāstāṃścaitra upādatte / tathā pratyakṣādiṣu pramāṇeṣūpadiṣṭeṣu yaireṣāmavinābhāvaḥ sarvāṇi tānyupādāsyāmahe / kiñcānyāt, anyatrāpi tadanuṣṭhānāt / na kevalamiha, anyatrāpyayamācāryaḥ pradhānāmevopadeśaṃ karoti / tadaṅgabhūtāstu tadupadeśādeva pratīyante / tadyathā, kāraṇamastyavyaktam (
children.translated_text:
). And one does not observe the teachers employing [terms] in the <s>śāstra</s> that are not intended [by them]. Therefore, we understand from indication that inquiry and the rest are components in the <s>śāstra</s>.
  [Objection:] When things exist but are not explicitly taught, a reason [for that non-teaching] must be stated. If you think thus — 'inquiry and the rest are components that exist' — then the reason for their non-teaching in the <s>śāstra</s> must be stated: 'For such-and-such a reason the teacher does not teach them, yet they exist.'
  [Reply:] Because they are subsumed under the <s>pramāṇas</s>. Their subsumption within the <s>pramāṇas</s> — this is the reason stated by us. For inquiry and the rest are limbs of inference; therefore, being subsumed within that, they are not separately taught. Moreover, because they are stated in other treatises. For in other treatises, they have been taught by teachers such as <s>Vindhyavāsin</s> and others. And those teachers are authoritative for us — therefore too, the non-teaching of inquiry and the rest [here is justified].
  [Objection:] No — because it would entail the non-teaching of the <s>pramāṇas</s> [as well]. If the non-teaching of components is [justified] simply because they are taught in other treatises, then perception and the rest are also taught in other treatises: 'The function of the ear and other [senses] is perception'; 'From connection, from one thing, the establishment of the rest is inference'; 'One who is competent in a field of action and is not defective — he is reliable there, and his instruction is reliable testimony' — of these too there would be the consequence of non-teaching. If [you say] that though taught in other treatises, the <s>pramāṇas</s> are taught [here] but not the components — well, is this not merely arbitrary wish?
  [Reply:] Then let the earlier refutation stand. Or alternatively, let this refutation — 'because of statement in other treatises' — also stand. As for what was said — 'there would be the consequence of non-teaching of the <s>pramāṇas</s>' — to this we say: that is incorrect. Why? Because there is no fault in teaching what is purposeful. For non-teaching is objected to in the case of what is purposeful — that is correct. But who would reject the teaching itself as faulty? Therefore, this [objection] amounts to nothing. Moreover, because when the principal is taught, the subsidiary is established as subsumed. Just as, when told 'Caitra, do carpentry,' <s>Caitra</s> takes up all those particular tools without which carpentry is not possible — so too, when the <s>pramāṇas</s> of perception and the rest are taught, we shall take up all those [components] without which they cannot function. Furthermore, because it is practiced elsewhere too. Not only here — elsewhere too this teacher teaches only the principal [topics]; the subsidiary limbs are understood from that very teaching. For example: 'The cause exists; it is unmanifest' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 16
), 'Because of the finitude of the differentiated' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 15

children.text: ) / itarathā hi dṛṣṭāntābhāvādasādhanametatsyāt / paśyati tvācāryo nādṛṣṭāntaṃ sādhanaṃ sādhyamāpnotīti kṛtvā pratipādakāḥ pratipādanakāle tantrāntaropadiṣṭānapi mūlaśakalādīnākṣepsyanti iti / kiñcānyat, anumāne bhūtavadupadeśāt / ataścaitadevaṃ yadayamācāryastrividhamanumānamākhyātamiti (
children.translated_text: ). Otherwise, in the absence of an example, this would be an unestablished proof. But the teacher sees: 'A proof without an example does not reach the conclusion' — and therefore the exponents, at the time of demonstration, will invoke the root, fragments, etc., taught in other treatises, as well. Furthermore, because of the teaching in the past tense regarding inference. And this is so because the teacher says: 'Inference, which is threefold, has been stated (<s>ākhyāta</s>)' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 5

) bravīti / kathaṃ kṛtvā jñāpakam? ākhyātasya hi pratyāmnāye bhūtavācinā śabdenopadeśo bhavati / na cānena pūrvaṃ trividhamanumānamākhyātam / ākhyātamiti cet, na tadākhyātaṃ kvaciditi śakyaṃ pratipādayitum / so 'yamanākhyāyāpi yadbhūtavācinaṃ śabdamupādatte tajjñāpayatyācāryastantrāntaraklṛptānāmapīha sanniveśo 'ṅgīkriyate / kimetasya jñāpane prayojanam ? tantrāntaropadiṣṭo 'pi karmayonīnām prāṇabhedādīnāṃ ca lakṣaṇopadeśassaṃgṛhīto bhavatīti siddhaṃ tantrāntaropadeśādavayavānupadeśaḥ / tasmātsūktamevāvayavopapattiriti /

  aṣṭāviṃśatibhedā tuṣṭirnavadhāṣṭadhā siddhiḥ // (

children.translated_text: <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 47

satisfaction (<s>tuṣṭi</s>) is ninefold, accomplishment (<s>siddhi</s>) is eightfold, [and misapprehension] of twenty-eight kinds.' Thus [there are] fifty dispositions. This makes sixty categories. Their establishment is non-deficiency.
  The statement resolving doubt (<s>saṃśaya-nirṇaya-ukti</s>). Doubt and resolution — these are 'doubt-and-resolution'; their statement is 'the statement of doubt and resolution.' A general statement produces doubt. For example: when it is said 'the great (<s>mahat</s>) and the rest — that is the effect — is dissimilar to <s>Prakṛti</s> and similar [to it]' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 8

children.text: ) saṃśayo bhavati kena dharmeṇa kāryaṃ prakṛtivirūpaṃ kena vā sarūpamiti / viśeṣābhidhānaṃ nirṇayaḥ / sa ca dvividhaḥ, śabdato 'rthataśca / śabdastāvat yathā hetumadādibhiḥ kāryaṃ prakṛtivirūpam, traiguṇyādibhiḥ prakṛtisarūpamiti / arthatastat yathā tebhyo bhūtāni pañca pañcabhyaḥ, ete smṛtā viśeṣāḥ (
children.translated_text: ), doubt arises: 'By which property is the effect dissimilar to <s>Prakṛti</s>, and by which is it similar?' A specific statement is resolution. And that is twofold: by word and by meaning. By word, for instance: 'By [properties such as] having a cause (<s>hetumad</s>), etc., the effect is dissimilar to <s>Prakṛti</s>; by [properties such as] having the three <s>guṇas</s>, etc., it is similar to <s>Prakṛti</s>.' By meaning, for instance: 'From those [tanmātras arise] the five elements; from [those] five, these are known as the specific [objects]' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 38

children.text: ) / kiṃ kāraṇam ? yasmāt śāntā ghorāśca mūḍhāśca (
children.translated_text: ). What is the reason? 'Because they are tranquil, turbulent, and dull' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 38

children.text:
) / aśāntaghoramūḍhatvāttanmātrāṇyaviśeṣāḥ /
  uddeśanirdeśam / uddeśaśca nirdeśaśca uddeśanirdeśam / sarvo dvandvo vibhāṣayaikavadbhavati iti dvandvaikavadbhāvaḥ / saṅkṣepavacanamuddeśaḥ / tadyathā, eṣa pratyayasargo viparyayāśaktituṣṭisiddhyākhyaḥ (
children.translated_text:
). Because the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) are not tranquil, turbulent, or dull — they are non-specific (<s>aviśeṣa</s>).
  Enumeration and specification (<s>uddeśa-nirdeśa</s>). Enumeration and specification — these are 'enumeration-and-specification.' Every <s>dvandva</s> compound optionally becomes singular — hence the singular form of the compound. A brief statement is 'enumeration.' For example: 'This is the creation of dispositions (<s>pratyaya-sarga</s>), called misapprehension, incapacity, satisfaction, and accomplishment' (

children.translated_text: ) thus ends [the section]. <s>Saṃjñā</s> (technical designation) and <s>upadeśa</s> (instruction): A word whose purpose is to convey knowledge to the one designated is called <s>saṃjñā</s>. It is of two kinds: based on meaning (<s>arthanibandhanā</s>) and based on form (<s>svarūpanibandhanā</s>). Of these, the meaning-based designation, by virtue of the meaning, depends on purposeful action and, containing within itself the true nature of the referent such as universal class etc., conveys the designated object just as it truly is. For example, 'cook' (<s>pācaka</s>), 'reaper' (<s>lāvaka</s>). The form-based designation, on the other hand, is merely a means of conveying the designated object; being useful only through its form, without the meaning of its components, it conveys the designated object by convention even though it does not truly correspond. For example, '<s>Gajakarṇa</s>' (Elephant-ear), '<s>Aśvakarṇa</s>' (Horse-ear). Since the blessed supreme <s>ṛṣi</s> (seer), having apprehended through his extraordinary knowledge the true nature of all realities, established the designations, there is no word that is merely form-based. For example, '<s>Pradhāna</s>' (the Primal) means 'that in which the modifications are contained'; '<s>Puruṣa</s>' (the Person) means 'that which lies in the city.' Following his doctrine, even for the later teachers, since they operate with those very designations, there is no need for establishing novel designations. <s>Upadeśa</s> (instruction): Instruction is the statement of procedure and result. For example: 'Thus from the knowledge of truth, through non-attachment, "I am not, nothing is mine, there is no I" — without remainder, through non-error, pure, absolute knowledge arises.' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 64

) These — <s>sūtra</s> (aphorism), <s>upapatti</s> (demonstration), and the rest — are the excellences of a treatise (<s>tantraguṇa</s>). Thus 'by means of' (<s>karaṇa</s>) indicates the manner. Other such [excellences] of similar nature should also be recognized. For example: <s>utsarga</s> (general rule), <s>apavāda</s> (exception), <s>atideśa</s> (extended application), and so forth. Among these, the general rule is: 'the manifest is unlike the source' (
<s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 8
); 'and it is of the same form' (
<s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 8
) — this is the exception. Similarly, 'and the reverse of that' (
<s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 11
) is the general rule; 'and <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Person)' (
<s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 11

children.translated_text: ) — this is the extended application. In this way, other treatise-techniques too can be demonstrated here, but since excessive elaboration would obscure the main subject, we desist. It is established that this is a treatise because of the connection with treatise-techniques. Furthermore, because it does not contradict other treatises: even if this were a subsidiary work (<s>prakaraṇa</s>), it would be a supplement to one among other treatises — the <s>Pātañjala</s>, the <s>Pañcādhikaraṇa</s>, the <s>Vārṣagaṇa</s>, and others. And we shall explain that there is no contradiction with those in their respective places. If one objects that it is a supplement to an earlier treatise, the same applies: those too are supplements to earlier treatises, so the same objection of being mere subsidiary works would apply to them. If the view is held that those are independent treatises because they comprehend all categories, then here too, since all categories are comprehended, the status of being an independent treatise must be accepted. Therefore, it is proper that this is a treatise. Thus ends the <s>upodghāta</s> (introduction).

children.translated_text: One asks: to a student possessing what qualifications should this treatise be explained? It is said: the treatise should be explained to a student who is inquisitive, intelligent, an examiner of doctrine, who has a purpose and who has presented himself. Why? Because of the authority of the supreme <s>ṛṣi</s> (seer). Since the blessed <s>Viśvāgraja</s> (Foremost of the Universe), the supreme seer, having perceived the inquisitiveness of the blessed <s>Āsuri</s> and his endowment with superior distinctive qualities, taught him. '<s>Rajas</s> (passion/activity) itself is suffering; the discrimination that seeks to remove it — that arises from <s>sattva</s> (goodness/being); and <s>sattva</s> does not arise from this' — such and similar statements propound this meaning, and it has been stated by the great authorities. Therefore, this treatise has been set forth for the cessation of the threefold suffering, for one who, afflicted by the suffering caused by <s>rajas</s>, is inquisitive, and who, through <s>sattva</s>, seeks to bring to fruition the roots of merit such as <s>dharma</s> and the rest. For his benefit the student is transformed. 'How may the student's supreme good be attained?' — with this purpose is this exposition undertaken. One asks: it has been said that the exposition should be given to one who is inquisitive; then whence does this inquisitiveness arise, and regarding what subject? It is replied: as to the question 'whence does this inquisitiveness arise?' — we say:
'From the affliction of the threefold suffering arises the desire to know.'

children.translated_text: Suffering is <s>rajas</s> — this is not a different thing. 'It causes suffering, therefore it is suffering.' 'Three' is a numeral word applicable to all substances, and it is qualified by the word 'suffering.' And because of predominance, being apprehended by discriminating cognition, by virtue of being a relation, it takes the sixth case (genitive) as indicating the substratum of differentiation — 'three of sufferings,' i.e., the threefold suffering. 'That by which one is struck' is <s>abhighāta</s> (affliction). What then is this 'affliction'? It is said: the connection of the power of consciousness with the inner organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) through the aforementioned threefold suffering. Therefore, from the affliction of the threefold suffering arises the desire to know. As to the question 'regarding what subject does it arise?' — to that the text says:
'Regarding the cause that removes that [suffering].'

children.translated_text: 'Just as the function of the individual faculties, each established in its own domain, each falling upon its own object,
is not obtained apart from the body,

'That which removes' is <s>apaghātaka</s> (remover); 'the remover of that' is <s>tadapaghātaka</s> (remover of that [suffering]). One objects: the compound 'tadapaghātake' is grammatically impossible, because of the prohibition — the sixth case (genitive) cannot be compounded with agent nouns formed with the suffixes <s>tṛc</s> and <s>aka</s>. Therefore one should say 'tasyāpaghātaka.' It is replied: no, because it is seen in authoritative texts. The usage is found in the <s>śāstra</s>: 'tatprayojako hetuśca' ('and the cause that impels that'). And the <s>Padakāra</s> (word-commentator) says: 'because it denotes a class.' Moreover, 'sometimes a quality becomes a specific quality, sometimes a quality is specified by the possessor of the quality' — such is the usage of the <s>cūrṇikāra</s> (prose commentator). Therefore this is blameless. The summary meaning is this: a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, afflicted by the threefold suffering, desires to know the cause that would remove it — 'what indeed would be that cause which would strike down the threefold suffering?' One objects: the word 'suffering' should not be uttered at the beginning [of a treatise] because it has an inauspicious meaning. For treatises that begin with auspicious words flourish and become heroic, and students whose mental impressions are touched by auspiciousness easily grasp the meaning of the treatise. And this word 'suffering' has an inauspicious meaning; therefore it should not be commenced with at the beginning of a treatise. It is replied: no, because the word is employed for the meaning of the sentence, and because an individual word by itself is purposeless, the charge of inauspiciousness does not hold. A sentence is employed for conveying meaning, because it denotes a qualified meaning — not an individual word. For indeed, apart from the meanings of individual words, the qualified sentence-meaning alone is understood; but an individual word, not having departed from its general meaning, is incapable of denoting a qualified meaning. For this very reason it is not employed as being capable of conveying the intended meaning. For example, the word '<s>Devadatta</s>' is taken as denoting the agent, but because it applies to all actions, without the words for object and action, no qualified meaning is understood. Similarly, 'cow' denotes the object, because it can serve as the ground for denoting all actions and agents. Similarly, 'drives' is the action, because it applies to all objects and agents. But when one says '<s>Devadatta</s> drives the cow, the white one,' then by means of <s>Devadatta</s>, the cow-word is separated from other objects and established in itself; the action and the cow-word establish <s>Devadatta</s> as the agent separated from all other agents; agent and object are determined as the means of accomplishment of the action of driving; the words 'white' and 'cow' separate the cow-word, which applies to all qualities, from other possible predicates, fix it as the substratum of themselves, and convey their applicability to it — in this manner the qualified sentence-meaning is established. But individual words, not having departed from their general meaning, because they do not denote particulars, are purposeless. And it is said:
so too, for all words, each denoting its own individual meaning,
separated from sentences, meaningfulness is not obtained.'

children.translated_text:
) from the statement yet to be made. Moreover, because another <s>tattva</s> (reality-principle) is not established — there is no <s>tattva</s> other than the <s>guṇas</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> in reality, the inquiry into which could be conceived as being conceived. Therefore, inquiry is not established.
  [Reply:] It is said: As to what was stated — that from affliction (<s>abhighāta</s>), there would be an over-extension regarding inquiry, since it arises in all beings — to this we say: No, because affliction is not apprehended as such [by all]. Even though the affliction is undifferentiated, not all beings apprehend it as affliction. For even when the three kinds of suffering — <s>ādhyātmika</s> (pertaining to the self), etc. — are present, and even in acquisition, preservation, diminution, attachment, and injury, because of pleasure and passionate attachment [to objects], they have neither revulsion nor aversion toward objects. Nor does abandonment of objects occur. Therefore, the affliction is not undifferentiated. [Objection:] Should one state the cause for the differentiation of the apprehension of affliction? [Reply:] Or it may be that this apprehension of the three kinds of suffering that exists in the revered <s>Āsuri</s> alone but not in others, even in the absence of differentiation among all living beings — the cause of this should be stated. For without a cause, that differentiation cannot be established. But this too is incorrect. Why? Because it is irrelevant to the question. The question was first posed by the questioner: 'From what does inquiry arise?' And affliction is its direct cause; since other causes are not stated, only this has been indicated. Now, the further question about the cause of the cause — that is not answered, from fear of an infinite regress. But if insistence is made, then [we say:] we do not deny that the accumulation of merit from a previous birth and the maturation of the cultivation of wholesome roots is the cause of the cause — so why is this very thing not accepted? By this, the earlier over-extension is answered. As to what was stated — 'If there is that affliction, there would be no liberation, because it is not complete' — this too is incorrect. Why? Because the meaning of the <s>śāstra</s> (teaching) has not been understood. The eightfold divine realm and the fivefold animal realm and the single human realm (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 53

children.text: ) ityetāvānasmākaṃ saṃsāraḥ / na tu tadvyatiriktāḥ kāmarūpārūpyadhātavaḥ kvacidapi siddhāḥ / caturdaśavidhe ca saṃsāre yā sukhamātrā sā duḥkhabhūyastvāttacchabdavācyā bhavatīti / tathā coktam-
children.translated_text: ) — this much is our <s>saṃsāra</s> (cycle of transmigration). But the realms of desire, form, and formlessness beyond that are nowhere established. And in the fourteen-fold <s>saṃsāra</s>, whatever modicum of pleasure exists, because of the preponderance of suffering, it is designated by that term [i.e., 'suffering']. And thus it has been said —

children.text: atra janmajarāmaraṇakṛtaṃ duḥkhaṃ prāpnoti cetanaḥ puruṣaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here the conscious <s>puruṣa</s> (person) obtains suffering caused by birth, old age, and death;
because the <s>liṅga</s> (subtle body) has not ceased, therefore, in brief, all is suffering. //

This being so, whence comes the certainty that this word 'suffering' has an inauspicious meaning, inasmuch as it is doubtful whether it is employed for conveying its own meaning or for indicating what is to be abandoned? But the sentence has an auspicious meaning, because it is employed for the purpose of the removal of suffering. For a sentence that is employed for the purpose of removing suffering is seen to have an auspicious meaning. For example, 'may the disease depart, may misfortune not occur.' This sentence is employed for the purpose of removing suffering; therefore it has an auspicious meaning. Hence what was said — 'the word suffering should not be uttered at the beginning because of its inauspicious meaning' — that is incorrect. One objects: the word 'three' is purposeless, because the quality (<s>guṇa</s>) is one. You have accepted that suffering is <s>rajas</s>, and that is a single thing as taught in the treatise. Therefore the use of 'three' is purposeless. If you say that from the difference of causes there is a figurative attribution of difference, this might be the view. Although suffering is one, still, because of the difference of causes — characterized as <s>ādhyātmika</s> (pertaining to the self), <s>ādhibhautika</s> (pertaining to beings), and <s>ādhidaivika</s> (pertaining to fate) — a figurative attribution of difference would be made. But this is not so. Why? Because the infinity of causes would lead to an infinity of qualities. For the <s>ādhyātmika</s> is of two kinds: bodily and mental. The bodily is caused by the disequilibrium of <s>vāta</s> (wind), <s>pitta</s> (bile), and <s>śleṣma</s> (phlegm). The mental is caused by desire, anger, greed, delusion, dejection, fear, jealousy, envy, discontent, and non-discrimination. The <s>ādhibhautika</s> is caused by humans, domestic animals, wild animals, birds, reptiles, and plants. The <s>ādhidaivika</s> is caused by cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning, frost, and possession. Since the threefold division is based on the difference of causes, an infinity of qualities would follow — and that is undesirable; therefore the threefold division is not based on the difference of causes. It is replied: what was said — that the threefold division is untenable because <s>rajas</s> is one, and that the figurative attribution of threefold division is from the difference of causes — is true. But what was said — that the infinity of causes leads to an infinity of qualities — that is incorrect. Why? Because even when there is difference, a fixed enumeration is tenable, just as with classes (<s>varṇa</s>). For example, in the case of the enumeration 'there are four classes,' even when there is differentiation into <s>Paippalāda</s> and others, since they do not differ from being <s>brāhmaṇa</s>s etc., they do not constitute grounds for a different enumeration; nor, because there is no difference from being classes, does unity result. Similarly, in the case of the enumeration 'there are three sufferings,' even when there is differentiation into bodily etc., since they cannot differ from being <s>ādhyātmika</s> etc., they do not constitute grounds for a different enumeration; nor, because there is no difference from being sufferings, should unity result. Moreover, you yourself have accepted that there is a figurative attribution of difference from the difference of causes. And a figurative attribution is not the ultimate reality — so enough with effort in the wrong place. One objects: from affliction, the desire to know would follow for everyone, since it exists for all. Just as it is held that the desire to know arises for <s>Āsuri</s> from the affliction of the threefold suffering, so since all are afflicted, the desire to know would follow for all. If the view is that affliction by suffering sometimes produces the desire to know in some and not in others — well, this is mere whim, and because of a prior objection: even before, <s>Āsuri</s> was afflicted by the threefold suffering, yet the desire to know did not arise in him regarding the ultimate cause. Then what follows? What is to be stated is that from which it subsequently arose in him. Just as elsewhere the desire to know arises for a <s>brāhmaṇa</s> from the destruction of demerit through the habit of meditation, and from the grace of prior merit, so for others it arises from the maturation of the habit of roots of merit. This has not been stated explicitly, hence it is stated briefly. Moreover, from the removal of that [threefold suffering] there would be no complete liberation, because it is only partial. For liberation is sought from the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, or from the three modes of existence — divine, human, and animal. The threefold suffering is only a part of <s>saṃsāra</s> (cyclic existence). Therefore the purpose stated is also incorrect. Furthermore, because of the existence of other motives, the desire to know can arise even for one who is not concerned with divine enjoyment, desire, or meditative happiness — not only for one who is distressed by suffering. Therefore the motive stated is also incorrect. Moreover, because it is impossible in both ways: this desire to know, even when hypothetically posited, would belong either to <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Person/Self) or to the <s>guṇa</s>s (qualities/constituents). What of it? First, it cannot belong to <s>Puruṣa</s>. Why? Because of the accepted doctrine that it has no qualities. Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, <s>dharma</s>, <s>adharma</s>, knowledge, and mental impressions are not accepted by you as qualities of the self. Nor can it belong to the <s>guṇa</s>s, because they are non-conscious. For non-conscious things like pots are not seen desiring to know the attainment and avoidance of the beneficial and harmful. And the <s>guṇa</s>s are not conscious according to you, since '<s>Pradhāna</s> (the Primal) is shared, non-conscious, and productive' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 55

And in the world, designation is seen based on the majority [quality]. Just as [one says] 'a mango grove' [even when other trees are present]. Therefore, this is a denial of the view that the designation is total. Now, as to what was said — that the reason is invalid because inquiry would arise even in one indifferent to divine pleasures and <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation) pleasures — that too is unfounded. Why? Because of the subsequent denial. This very point has been included [in the system]. And thus the teacher will subsequently deny it with the later <s>sūtra</s>: 'That which is heard of [i.e., scriptural remedies] is like the visible [i.e., worldly remedies], for it is connected with impurity, decay, and excess' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 2

  āha, na brūmo 'vidyamānasambandho 'sambandhaḥ kintarhyayuktasambandho yaḥ sa khalvasambandhaḥ / tadyathā anācāro māṇavaka iti dravyeṇa kriyāśaktitvānna śakyaṃ kiñcidanācāravatā kṣaṇamapyavasthātum / ayuktaṃ tvācarannanācāra ityucyate / tathā cāsya tacchabdasya pratipadaṃ sambandho na yuktastasmādanarthakastacchabdaḥ /
  ānantaryājjijñāsāśabdasyeti cet, syānmatam / anantarasya vidhirvā bhavati pratiṣedho vetyanayā yuktyā jijñāsāśabdasya tacchabdenābhisambandhaḥ śakya iti / tacca naivam / kasmāt ? tadapaghāte prayojanāsadbhāvāt / na hi jijñāsāpaghāte kiñcit prayojanamastīti satyapi sambandhe na tacchabdenārthaḥ /
  abhighātasyeti cet ? athāpi syādyadi jijñāsāpaghātena kiṃcitprayojanamastīti / atastatsambandho neṣyate / tena tarhyabhighātaśabdenāsyābhisambandhaḥ kariṣyate / tathā cāpi tacchabdorthavān bhaviṣyatīti / etadanupapannam / kasmāt ? nimittāvasthāne punaḥ punarutpatteḥ / naimittiko 'yamabhighātastasya nimittavattvādātyantiko 'paghāto na syāt / itarathā jvaranimittako dāha iva śītadravyasaṃsparśātpraśānto 'pi nimittāvasthānātpunaḥ punaḥ pravartate ityaphalatvamasya vyāyāmasya /
  trayaśabdasyeti cet na, pāratantryāt / āśrayaparatantrā hi saṃkhyā, tasyā nāntareṇāśrayeṇopaghātamapaghātaḥ śakyaḥ kartum / ānarthakyañca samānamiti sutarāṃ tacchabdena nārthaḥ /
  duḥkhaśabdasyeti cetsāmānyam - yadyeteṣāmpadānāmabhisambandhe yathoktadoṣopapattiḥ, duḥkhaśabdaṃ tarhi tat-śabdenābhisaṃbhantsyāmaḥ / tasminneṣa niṣedho viśatīti / tacca naivam / kasmāt ? anekapadavyavadhānāt / kathamanantaravṛttinā sarvanāmnānekapadavyavahitasya duḥkhaśabdasyābhisambandhaḥ śakyet pratipādayitum ? tasmānna kiñcidetat / kiñcānyat / upasarjanatvāt / ayaṃ khalvapi duḥkhaśabdaḥ samāsa upasarjanībhūtaḥ / na caikasminkāle śabdasya pradhānatvamupasarjanatvaṃ ca yuktitaḥ sambhavati / pradhānasya ca padāntareṇābhisambandhaḥ / tasmādvivādāspadamevaitatsūtram / kiñcānyat / nityānāmapaghātānupapatteḥ / iha nityānāmapaghātaḥ kartuṃ na śakyate / tadyathā puruṣāṇām / anityānāñcāpaghāto dṛṣṭaḥ / tadyathā, jvarādīnām / nityañca duḥkham / tasmāttadapaghāte 'bhyutthānānarthakyam / vṛttyapaghāte tadapaghāta iti cet, syātpunareṣā buddhiḥ / satyaṃ nityānāmapaghāto na yuktitaḥ sambhavati / na tu vayaṃ guṇalakṣaṇasya duḥkhasyāpaghātaṃ brūmaḥ, kintarhi vṛttirasyābhibhūyata iti / tacca naivam / kasmāt ? uktottaratvāt / uktamatrottaraṃ nimittāvasthāne punaḥ punarutpatteriti / tasmādayamapyamārgaḥ / kiñcānyat / aviśeṣātkalpayitvāpi vṛttyapaghātaṃ vṛttivṛttimatorananyatvād vṛttyapaghāte vṛttimadapaghātaḥ prāpta iti nāsti kaścidviśeṣaḥ / tasmāt kṛśo 'yaṃ parihāra iti nārthastacchabdena /
  ucyate- yaduktaṃ tacchabdānarthakyam, pratipadamasambandhādityastu duḥkhaśabdenābhisambandhaḥ / tatsambandhe yathoktadoṣopapattiriti cet syānmatam / yadi tarhi tacchabdasya duḥkhaśabdenaivābhisambandho 'bhyupagamyate tena ye 'smābhiḥ pūrvamabhihitā doṣāste prasajyante / tasmāt pratiṣiddhasya pakṣasya parigrahe sāhasamātramiti / etacca naivaṃ, kasmāt ? pratividhānāt / satyamasati pratividhāne sāhasamātraṃ syāt / pratividhīyate tu, tasmādadoṣo 'yamiti /
  kintaditi cet syānmatam / ucyatāntarhi kintat pratividhānaṃ yasyāvaṣṭambhenānekadoṣavyāhato 'pyayaṃ pakṣa āśrīyate / na hyanuktamasmābhirākāramātreṇa śakyaṃ pratipattumiti /
  ucyate- bāḍham / yattāvaduktamanekapadavyavadhānānna duḥkhaśabdasya tacchabdenābhisambandha ityatra brūmaḥ na, anabhyupagamāt / yo hyanantarakṛtaṃ śabdasya śabdāntareṇa saha sambandhamācaṣṭe tampratyayamupālambhaḥ syāt / vayantvarthakṛtaṃ sambandhamācakṣmahe / tathā coktam-
children.translated_text:
). Therefore, inquiry is appropriate even for one indifferent to divine pleasures. <s>Dhyāna</s>-pleasure too does not escape decay and excess. That too is included here. Therefore, since this position must be denied, nothing [further] need be said. As to what was also said — that inquiry is not established because it is impossible in either way — let there be inquiry into the <s>guṇas</s>. As to what was said — that it is impossible because [the guṇas] are unconscious — though they are indeed unconscious, we shall demonstrate in what follows that the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>) possesses desire and the like.
  Therefore, inquiry is established.
  [Objection:] The word 'tat' (that) is meaningless, because it lacks connection with each word. This word 'tat' which the teacher has placed in the <s>sūtra</s> — we do not find even the slightest meaning in it, since it lacks connection with each word [in the compound]. Therefore, we shall not study this text of insufficient meaning.
  [Reply:] How indeed could a word, being dependent on the speaker, not have connection with another word?
  [Objection:] We do not say the connection is non-existent, but rather an inappropriate connection is [effectively] a non-connection. Just as [one says] 'the ill-conducted youth' — since a substance has the capacity for action, nothing can remain even for a moment without conduct. But conducting himself inappropriately, he is called 'ill-conducted.' Similarly, the word 'tat' does not have an appropriate connection with each word; therefore the word 'tat' is meaningless.
  [Counter:] If it could be connected with the word 'jijñāsā' (inquiry) by proximity — one might think: by the principle that what is proximate is either an injunction or a prohibition, the word 'tat' can be connected with the word 'jijñāsā.' But that is not so. Why? Because when that [suffering] is removed, there is no purpose. For when inquiry is removed, there is no purpose at all; therefore, even though a connection exists, there is no meaning with the word 'tat.'
  [Counter:] If [connected] with 'abhighāta' (affliction)? One might think: if there is some purpose in the removal of inquiry, and therefore the connection is not desired, then the connection should be made with the word 'abhighāta.' And thus the word 'tat' would be meaningful. This is unfounded. Why? Because, when the cause persists, it arises again and again. This affliction is caused [by conditions]; because it has causes, its complete removal would not be possible. Otherwise, like fever-caused burning which, though pacified by contact with cool substances, arises again and again when the cause persists — thus the effort would be fruitless.
  [Counter:] If [connected] with the word 'traya' (three)? No, because of dependence. Number is dependent on its substrate; without the removal of the substrate, its removal cannot be accomplished. And the meaninglessness is the same — therefore there is even less meaning with the word 'tat.'
  [Counter:] If [connected] with the word 'duḥkha' (suffering) — that would be general. If there is the stated fault in connecting with these words, then we shall connect the word 'tat' with the word 'duḥkha.' The denial would apply to that. But that is not so. Why? Because of the separation by many intervening words. How could one demonstrate the connection of the pronoun, which functions with what is proximate, with the word 'duḥkha' separated by many words? Therefore this amounts to nothing. Moreover, because it is subordinate — this word 'duḥkha' has become subordinate in the compound. And it is not logically possible for a word to be both principal and subordinate at the same time. And the principal [element] has connection with another word. Therefore, this very <s>sūtra</s> is a matter of dispute. Moreover, because the removal of permanent things is impossible. Here, permanent things cannot be removed — such as <s>puruṣas</s>. And the removal of impermanent things is seen — such as fevers and the like. And suffering is permanent. Therefore, exertion toward its removal is futile. [Counter:] If [one says] the removal of its manifestation is its removal — one might think: true, the removal of permanent things is not logically possible. But we do not speak of the destruction of suffering which is a property of the <s>guṇas</s>; rather, its manifestation is suppressed. But this is not so. Why? Because the answer has already been given — it was said above that because of repeated arising when the cause persists. Therefore this path too is untenable. Moreover, because there is no difference — even if one posits the removal of its manifestation, since the manifestation and the possessor of manifestation are not different, the removal of manifestation entails the removal of what possesses manifestation, so there is no difference. Therefore this defense is thin, and there is no meaning with the word 'tat.'
  [Final Reply:] It is said: As to what was stated — that the word 'tat' is meaningless, because it lacks connection with each word — let it be connected with the word 'duḥkha.' [Objection:] If the stated faults arise in that connection — one might think: if the connection of the word 'tat' with the word 'duḥkha' alone is accepted, then the faults we previously stated would follow. Therefore, the acceptance of a denied position is mere rashness. But this is not so. Why? Because of the countermeasure. True, without a countermeasure, it would be mere rashness. But a countermeasure is provided; therefore there is no fault.
  What is that countermeasure? One might ask: Then state what that countermeasure is, relying on which this position is adhered to even though struck by many faults. For we cannot understand [it] from a mere indication without its being stated.
  [Reply:] Very well. As to what was first stated — that the word 'tat' cannot be connected with the word 'duḥkha' because of separation by many intervening words — to this we say: No, because we do not accept [proximity as the sole basis of connection]. For the objection would apply to one who declares that the connection of a word with another word is based on proximity. But we declare that the connection is based on meaning. And thus it has been said —
The connection of that [word] with which [another word] is connected exists even when they are far apart;
but where the meanings are dissimilar, even proximity does not yield connection. //

children.text: kiñcānyat- śāstre darśanāt / śāstre ca vyavahitānāmapi sarvanāmnāmabhisambandho dṛśyate "yasya guṇasya hi bhāvāddravye śabdaniveśastadabhidhāne tvatalā"vityatrārthakṛtaśca sambandhaḥ śabdānāmabhyupagataḥ / ṅyāpprātipadikāt, bahuṣu bahuvacanam, supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ, aluguttarapade ityevamādīnāṃ sambandhābhyupagamaḥ / tathā "anaḍvāhamudahāriṇi bhagini vahasi yā tvaṃ śirasi kumbhamavācīnamabhidhāvantamadrākṣīriti" vārtike dṛṣṭāntaḥ / na hyatra satyānantarye śirasānaḍuho vahanaṃ kumbhasya vā saraṇamupapadyate / yathā cātra vyavahitānāmabhisambandhastathehāpi draṣṭavyaḥ / yatpunaretaduktamupasarjanatvātpadāntareṇānabhisambandha iti etadanupapannam / kasmāt ? samāsādapoddhāre buddhayā vyavasthitasya svātantryopapatteḥ / satyamupasarjanasya padāntareṇābhisambandho nopapadyate / na tu vayaṃ samāsavṛttereva tacchabdenābhisambandha iti pratipadyāmahe, kintarhi samāsādapoddhṛtasya buddhivyavasthitasyopajanitasvātantryasya śabdāntareṇa sambandhamicchāma iti / athaitadaniṣṭam "yogapramāṇe ca tadabhāve darśanaṃ syāt" "atha śabdānuśāsanaṃ, keṣāṃ śabdānām" iti caivamādīnāmprayogāṇāṃ virodhaḥ prāpnoti / aniṣṭañcaitat / yatpunaretaduktam- nityānāmapaghātānupapattervṛttyapaghāte ca tadapaghātaprasaṅgāditi, etadapyanupapannam / kasmāt ? guṇaśakteḥ prayojanoparame satyātmakalpena vyavasthānābhyupagamāt / naitadabhyupagamyate guṇasyocchittirbhavati, vṛttirvāsyābhibhūyate / kintarhi puruṣārthanibandhanā caritārtha śaktirasya puruṣārthapravṛttau prayojanāsadbhāvādātmakalpena vyavatiṣṭhata ityetadvivakṣitam / tasmādyuktametattadapaghātake hetau jijñāsā pravartata iti /
children.translated_text: Moreover — because it is seen in the <s>śāstra</s> (grammatical science). In the <s>śāstra</s>, the connection of pronouns even with separated [words] is seen. As in [<s>Pāṇini</s>'s rule:] 'A word-form receives application to that substance whose quality-presence determines its linguistic imposition — the suffixes <s>-ta</s> and <s>-la</s> [apply] to that designation' — here a meaning-based connection of words is accepted. [Similarly,] 'Case-endings [apply] to nominal stems,' 'plural number for many,' '<s>sup</s>-endings apply to both verbal roots and nominal stems,' '<s>aluk</s> in a subsequent member' — the connection is accepted in such [rules]. Likewise, in the <s>Vārttika</s>, the example is given: 'O sister, who carry an ox on your head in a water-bearing vessel, I saw [him] running inverted' — here, despite proximity, neither the carrying of an ox by the head nor the running of a pot is established [as the intended meaning]. Just as there the connection of separated [words] is [understood], so should it be seen here too. Now, as to what was stated — that because of being subordinate, there is no connection with another word — this is unfounded. Why? Because when extracted from the compound, what is established in the mind has the possibility of independence. True, a subordinate [element] does not have connection with another word. But we do not understand that the connection of the word 'tat' is with the compound-form alone; rather, we desire the connection with [the word] that has been extracted from the compound and established in the mind, having acquired independence, with another word. And if this is not accepted, then the usages such as 'in <s>yoga</s> and authority and in its absence, seeing would occur,' and 'now the teaching of words — of which words?' — contradiction would follow with such usages. And this is not acceptable. Now, as to what was stated — that because of the impossibility of removing permanent things, and because in the removal of manifestation there would be the removal of that [permanent thing] itself — this too is unfounded. Why? Because when the purpose of the <s>guṇa</s>'s power is fulfilled, we accept that it abides as if in its own nature. It is not accepted that the <s>guṇa</s> is destroyed, nor that its manifestation is suppressed. Rather, what is meant is this: the power that is oriented toward the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s>, having fulfilled its purpose, in the absence of purpose for further activity, abides as if in its own nature. Therefore, it is appropriate that inquiry arises toward the cause of the removal of that [suffering].
[Objection:] If the purpose is served by perceived [means] (<s>dṛṣṭe sāpārthā cet</s>)

children.text: syādetat pratyakṣo duḥkapratīkāraheturasti / tasya samatikrame kiṃ prayojanam ? tadyathā śārīrasya tāvadayamapagamaheturanekadravyarasāyanopabhogaḥ / mānasasyāpi manojñastrīpānavilepanabhojanavastrālaṅkārādiviṣayasamprāptiḥ / ādhibhautikasya nītiśāstrābhyāsaḥ, śastrāstrakuśalatā, viṣamasthānānadhyāsanaṃ ca / ādhidaivikasyāpi yathākālaṃ vividhanivasanāstaraṇagarbhagṛhaprāsādajālāntaracandanavyajanamaṇihārādisevā vividhauṣadhamaṃgalastutimantraprayogānuṣṭhānamiti dṛṣṭe hetau sā jijñāsāpārtheti cet -
children.translated_text: [One might say:] there is a perceived cause for counteracting suffering. What is the use of going beyond it? For example: for bodily [suffering], the cause of removal is the enjoyment of various substances and elixirs (<s>rasāyana</s>). For mental [suffering] too, the attainment of desirable objects such as beautiful women, drinks, ointments, food, clothing, ornaments, and the like. For suffering caused by other beings (<s>ādhibhautika</s>), the study of the science of statecraft (<s>nītiśāstra</s>), skill in weapons and missiles, and not dwelling in dangerous places. And for suffering caused by divine agencies (<s>ādhidaivika</s>), the seasonal use of various garments, cushions, inner chambers, palace lattice-windows, sandalwood, fans, jewel-necklaces and the like, and the performance of various medicines, auspicious rites, prayers, and <s>mantra</s>-practices. If, since the cause is perceived, that inquiry is purposeless —
[Reply:] No, because there is no absolute and permanent absence [of suffering from these means]. // <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 1 //

children.text:
etacca naivam / kasmāt ? ekāntātyantato 'bhāvāt / ekānto nāma niyamena bhāvaḥ / atyantaṃ bhūtasyāvināśaḥ / ekāntaśca atyantaṃ ca te ekāntātyante tayorabhāva ekāntātyantato 'bhāvaḥ tasmāt / ṣaṣṭhīsthāne pañcamī / ṣaṣṭhyā eva vā tasiḥ ṣaṣṭhyā vyāśraya iti yogavibhāgāt / asamāsakaraṇaṃ vṛttapūraṇārtham, mānasasya ca duḥkhasya pratīkāre doṣāntaropasaṃgrahārtham / tathā hi, stryādīnāṃ satyetasmin doṣadvaye 'śakyamarjjanaṃ kartumasvābhāvikatvāt / satyarjane rakṣaṇamaśakyaṃ, sādhāraṇatvāt / sati ca rakṣaṇe kṣayaḥ, kṛtakatvāt / saṅgāccānupaśamo bhūtopaghātamantareṇa cāsambhava ityete doṣāḥ /
  āha, kathametadavagamyate yaddṛṣṭasya hetoranaikāntikatvamanātyantikatvaṃ ceti ?
  ucyate- pratyakṣa evaitadupalabhyate / yadāyurvedavihitasya kriyākramasyābhiyuktamātmavantaṃ bheṣajabhiṣakparicārakasampannaṃ pratyānarthakyam / āha ca -

children.translated_text: Of all forms of disease, the cause is declared to be threefold:
diet, activity, and <s>karma</s> (action previously performed).

And this is not so. Why? Because of the absence of certainty and permanence (<s>ekāntātyantato 'bhāva</s>). '<s>Ekānta</s>' means existence with certainty; '<s>atyanta</s>' means the non-destruction of what has come into being. '<s>Ekānta</s>' and '<s>atyanta</s>' — their absence is '<s>ekāntātyantato 'bhāva</s>'; therefore (the compound is thus). The fifth case ending is used in place of the sixth. Or alternatively, the <s>tasi</s> suffix is used with the sixth case itself, by the division of the grammatical rule 'with the sixth case there is dependence.' The non-compounding is for the purpose of completing the meter, and for the purpose of including other defects regarding the remedy for mental suffering. For thus: given these two defects, it is impossible for women and the like to accomplish purification, because they are not intrinsic to their nature. Even if acquisition occurs, protection is impossible, because they are shared by all. And even if there is protection, there is destruction, because they are produced. From attachment there is no cessation of suffering, and without injury to living beings there is no possibility of obtaining them — these are the defects. He asks: How is this known — that the empirical remedy is non-definitive and non-permanent? It is replied: This is perceived by direct experience itself. For the procedure prescribed by <s>Āyurveda</s> is sometimes ineffective even for one who is diligent, self-controlled, and well-equipped with medicine, physician, and attendant. And it is said:
Of these, medicine removes diseases arising from diet and activity;
but the disease produced by <s>karma</s> ceases only at death.
Again it is said:
A disease that is accompanied by complications, that is of every kind, that destroys strength, flesh, and the senses,
and that is accompanied by fatal signs — the physician should abandon such a patient.

children.text:
ityevamanaikāntikatvam / anātyantikatvaṃ tu nivṛttānāmapi vyādhīnāmpunarutpattidarśanāt / mahatā khalvapi prayatnena nivartitā vyādhayaḥ punarutpadyante / tathā coktam -
  punarjvare samutpanne kriyā pūrvajvarānugā / iti
  tasmādyathaivāsyāyurvedādeḥ pratīkārahetutvaṃ pratyakṣasiddhamevamekāntātyantato 'bhāvo 'pi / tathā mānasasya ca / yathā ca śārīraduḥkhapratīkārahetavo 'naikāntikāḥ tathā stryādayo 'pi / kasmāt ? tatsannidhāne viṣayāntarābhilāṣadarśanāt / yadi hi stryādayo viṣayāḥ sarvadā duḥkhapratīkārasamarthā bhaveyuḥ, kimati teṣu sannihiteṣu viṣayiṇo viṣayāntarajighṛkṣā syāt ? evamanaikāntikatvam / anātyantikatvamapi / nivṛttecchānāmapi bhūyaḥ prārthanāsambhavāt / yadi hi viṣayopabhogo 'tyantameva mānasaṃ duḥkhamapahanyāt kiṃ prāptaṃ yena bhūyastaṃ prati viṣayiṇo 'bhilāṣaḥ syāt ? kiṃ kāraṇam ? yasmānna hyavidyamāne tamasi devadattasya pradīpaṃ pratyapekṣā bhavati / dṛśyate ca nivṛttecchānāmapi viṣayopabhogādviṣayiṇāṃ bhūyo viṣayābhilāṣaḥ / tena manyāmahe nāyaṃ dṛṣṭo heturduḥkhamahapanti / kintarhi sutarāṃ vṛddhiṃ karoti / āha ca -

children.translated_text: Desire is never pacified by the enjoyment of desires;
like fire with clarified butter, it only increases further.

Thus non-definitiveness is established. As for non-permanence, it is from the observation that even diseases that have been cured arise again. Even diseases removed with great effort arise again. And thus it is said: 'When fever arises again, the treatment follows that of the previous fever.' Therefore, just as the efficacy of <s>Āyurveda</s> and the like as remedial causes is established by direct perception, so too is the absence of certainty and permanence. Similarly also for mental suffering. And just as the remedial causes for bodily suffering are non-definitive, so too are women and the like. Why? Because desire for other objects is observed even in their presence. For if women and other sense-objects were always capable of counteracting suffering, why would a person, even when they are present, have a desire for other objects? Thus non-definitiveness. And also non-permanence — because even those whose desires have ceased may again experience longing. For if sense-enjoyment permanently removed mental suffering, what would have been achieved such that there would be further desire toward those objects? For what reason? Because <s>Devadatta</s> has no need for a lamp when there is no darkness. And yet it is seen that even after their desires have ceased through sense-enjoyment, sense-enjoyers again have desire for objects. Therefore we hold that this empirical remedy does not remove suffering; rather, it increases it all the more. And it is said:
Another says:
Because of being witnessed, because of being burdensome, because of being censured by the good,
and because of non-availability everywhere — the empirical remedy is not accepted.

children.text: saṃvedyatvāt / bhogasādhanavikalānāmarthināṃ madhye viṣayiṇopayujyamānāstaissaṃvedyante / teṣāmapradāyopayujyamānaṃ nairghṛṇyamāviṣkuryāt / viṣayiṇā pradīyamāno vārthibhyaḥ parimitatvādavacchidyetetyanupāyo 'yaṃ duḥkhāpaghāte buddhimatām / kiṃ ca gurutvāt / bhogānāṃ vividhanivasanastrīpānabhojanavilepanālaṃkārādīnāṃ samagrye sukhamutpadyate / nānyataravaikalye / sāmagryaṃ caiṣāṃ svābhāvikatvādanupapannam / āha ca -
nābhijātiṃ na vijñānaṃ na ca śauryamapekṣate /
children.translated_text: <s>Lakṣmī</s> (prosperity) does not regard birth, learning, or valor;
through a combination of favorable circumstances, she resides somewhere or other.

'Because of being witnessed': among those who seek the means of enjoyment and who are destitute, when objects are enjoyed by the enjoyer, they are witnessed by them. If one enjoys without giving to them, one would display cruelty. But if the enjoyer gives to the needy, since enjoyable objects are limited, they would be diminished — so this is not a means for removing suffering for the wise. Moreover, 'because of being burdensome': happiness arises only when all means of enjoyment are complete — various dwellings, women, drinks, foods, unguents, ornaments, and the like — not when any one is lacking. And completeness of all these is impossible because they are not naturally obtainable. And it is said:

children.text: ityevamanekārthāśrayatvād gururviṣayopabhogaḥ / kiṃ ca ninditatvācca sādhubhiḥ / ninditaḥ khalvapi sādhubhirviṣayopabhogaḥ / yasmādāha-

children.translated_text: Toils, frustrations, deceptions, fears,
and whatever else is inauspicious in the world — all that proceeds from desires.
Thus, because it depends on many things, sense-enjoyment is burdensome. Moreover, 'because of being censured by the good': sense-enjoyment is indeed censured by the good. Because it is said:
Again it is said:
This is a disease that has its field of action, this is a perpetual fever,
this is the seat of calamities, this is the womb of sins.
This is a fathomless abyss, this is a quagmire difficult to cross,
filled with afflictions, diseases, and fears — this is a terrifying pit.
This is the great abode of various toils and sorrows,
this is the open field of dejection, fatigue, and despair.
Since from sense-enjoyment — like a bird from a cage —

children.text: gato vaneṣu ramate sa sukhāni samaśnute //
children.translated_text: one who has gone and delights in the forests, that one enjoys true pleasures.

children.text: tasmāt sādhubhirapākṛtatvādasādhurviṣayopabhogaḥ / kiṃ ca sarvatrāsannidhānāt / na hi supratiniviṣṭasyāpi kāminaḥ sarvatra viṣayasannidhānena bhavitavyam / no khalvapi ekasmin deśe 'vasthānaṃ sambhavati, viṣayābhāvaprasaṅgāt / tasmādavaśyaṃ viyogena bhavitavyam / viyoge ca sati dhruvo 'niṣṭānubandha iti ko 'rtho viṣayaparigraheṇa ? tatra yaduktaṃ dṛṣṭasya hetoḥ sadbhāvādapārthakā jijñāseti etadayuktam // 1 //
children.translated_text: Therefore, since it has been rejected by the good, sense-enjoyment is unwholesome. Moreover, 'because of non-availability everywhere': for even the most firmly established pleasure-seeker cannot have sense-objects present everywhere. And indeed, staying in one place is not possible, because of the consequent absence of other objects. Therefore separation is inevitable. And when there is separation, an undesirable sequel is certain — so what is the use of clinging to sense-objects? Therefore, what was said — that because of the existence of an empirical remedy, inquiry into the unseen is pointless — that is not valid.
<s>Kārikā</s> 2.

children.text:
āha- yadyekāntātyantato 'bhāvāddṛṣṭe hetāvaparitoṣastena tarhyastyayamanyo heturubhayadoṣavarjitaḥ sa kasmānna parigṛhyate ? ko 'sāviti cet ucyate, śāstroktaḥ karmavidhiḥ / sa hyaikāntikaḥ / katham ? evaṃ hyāha - paśubandhena sarvāṃllokān jayati / na tūktaṃ kadācijjayati, kadācinneti / phalasya pratyakṣānupalabdheranaikāntikatvamiti cet, syānmatam pratyakṣata evedaṃ vihitasya karmaṇaḥ phalaṃ nopalabhyate / tathā hi putrakāma iṣṭiṃ nirūpya duhitaramapi na prāpnoti / arthakāmaśca karma kṛtvā māṣakamapi na labhate / tasmānnāyamanaikāntika iti / etacca naivam / kasmāt ? sādhanavaikalyāttadanupapatteḥ / anekasādhanasādhyo hi karmavidhiḥ / yatra phalaṃ nopalabhyate tatra sādhanavaikalyamanumātavyam / kasmāt ? na hyetadiṣṭaṃ, sati kāraṇe kāryaṃ na bhavati / kiṃ cānyat, saṃsārābhāvaprasaṅgāt / yadi khalvapi karmaṇaḥ phalavattvaṃ neṣyate tena tannimittasya saṃsāsarasyābhāvaprasaṅgaḥ / aniṣṭaṃ caitat / tasmātsiddhamasyaikāntikatvam /
  ātyantikatvamapi siddhameva / yasmādāha apāma somamamṛtā abhūmeti / atra somapānādamṛtatvāvāptiḥ śrūyate / tasmāttadevānuṣṭhātavyam / kimanyena hetunā parikalpiteneti jijñāsāpārthaiveti /
  ucyate
children.translated_text: He says: If, because of the absence of certainty and permanence in the empirical remedy, there is dissatisfaction with it, then is there some other remedy free from both defects? Why is that not accepted? What is it? It is replied: the ritual procedure prescribed by scripture. For that is definitive. How? For it says thus: 'By means of animal sacrifice one conquers all worlds.' It does not say 'sometimes he conquers, sometimes not.' If one objects that non-definitiveness follows from the non-perception of the result by direct experience — the objection may be: the fruit of prescribed ritual action is indeed not perceived through direct experience. For thus: one who desires a son, having performed the <s>iṣṭi</s> (sacrifice), does not even obtain a daughter. And one who desires wealth, having performed the ritual, does not obtain even a small coin. Therefore this is not non-definitive. This is not so. Why? Because its non-accomplishment is due to deficiency in the means of accomplishment. For the ritual procedure requires many means. Where the result is not perceived, deficiency in the means should be inferred. Why? Because it is not accepted that, when the cause exists, the effect does not arise. Moreover, because there would be the consequence of the non-existence of <s>saṃsāra</s>. For if the productiveness of <s>karma</s> is not accepted, then there would follow the non-existence of <s>saṃsāra</s>, which is caused by it. And this is undesirable. Therefore its definitiveness is established. Its permanence too is established. Because it says: 'We have drunk <s>Soma</s>, we have become immortal.' Here, the attainment of immortality through drinking <s>Soma</s> is heard in scripture. Therefore that alone should be practiced. Why should one resort to some other imagined remedy? — thus the inquiry would be pointless. It is replied:
'The scriptural remedy is like the empirical one' (<s>dṛṣṭavad ānuśravikaḥ</s>).

children.text:
anuśrūyate ityanuśravaḥ / anuśrave bhava ānuśravikaḥ / dṛṣṭena tulyaṃ vartate dṛṣṭavat / kimasāvanabhipreta iti vākyaśeṣaḥ /
  āha kaḥ punarayamanuśravaḥ ?
  ucyate- mantrabrāhmaṇaṃ yāvadvā purātanamanuśrūyamāṇaṃ prāmāṇyenābhyupagamyate tatrabhavadbhiḥ / yathāśrutinibandhanāḥ smṛtayaḥ / aṅgāni vedāstarkā vā / yathāha
  vedavedāṅgatarkeṣu vedasaṃjñā nirucyate / iti /
  āha, kiṃ pūrvasmādeva hetorayamānuśraviko heturanabhipreta iti ?
  netyucyate / kintarhi
children.translated_text: 'That which is heard' (<s>anuśrūyate</s>) is <s>anuśrava</s>. 'That which exists in <s>anuśrava</s>' is <s>ānuśravika</s>. 'It functions like the empirical' is '<s>dṛṣṭavat</s>.' 'It too is not desired' — this is the completion of the sentence. He asks: What then is this <s>anuśrava</s> (scriptural tradition)? It is replied: whatever ancient tradition from the <s>mantra</s> and <s>brāhmaṇa</s> portions of the <s>Veda</s> is accepted as authoritative by those persons. As also the <s>smṛtis</s> based on <s>śruti</s>. The <s>Vedāṅgas</s> or the systems of reasoning (<s>tarka</s>). As it says: 'In the <s>Vedas</s>, <s>Vedāṅgas</s>, and systems of reasoning, the designation "<s>Veda</s>" is employed.' He asks: Is this scriptural remedy not desired for the same reason as the previous empirical one? No, it is said. Then for what reason?
For it is associated with impurity, destruction, and gradation (<s>aviśuddhi-kṣaya-atiśaya-yuktaḥ</s>).

children.text:
iti / sa ityānuśravikasya hetoḥ pratinirdeśaḥ / hiśabdo yasmādarthe / aviśuddhiśca kṣayaścātiśayaśca tairyuktaḥ / etaduktaṃ bhavati / yasmādayamānuśraviko heturaviśuddho 'nityastāratamyavāṃścāto dṛṣṭa ivānabhipretaḥ /
  tatrāviśuddhiyuktastāvat hiṃsāvidhānāt / yadāha brāhmaṇe- brāhmaṇamālabhetetyādi / tathā-

children.translated_text: Five hundred and ninety-seven animals are enjoined on the middle day
of the <s>Aśvamedha</s> (horse sacrifice), as prescribed, diminished by three animals.

'<s>Sa</s>' refers back to the scriptural remedy. The word '<s>hi</s>' has the meaning of 'because.' '<s>Aviśuddhi</s>' (impurity), '<s>kṣaya</s>' (destruction), and '<s>atiśaya</s>' (gradation) — associated with these. This means: because this scriptural remedy is impure, impermanent, and involves gradation, therefore it is not desired, just like the empirical one. Of these, it is first associated with impurity, because of the prescription of violence (<s>hiṃsā</s>). As it says in the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>: 'One should sacrifice a <s>brāhmaṇa</s>-type animal' and so forth. And also:

children.text:
iti hiṃsā cāviśuddhiḥ / prāṇināmiṣṭaśarīravyāpādanāt /
  āha, tadanupapattiḥ / śāstracoditatvāt / yadi śāstreṇa coditeyaṃ hiṃsā na syāt muktasaṃśayamaviśuddhitvamasyāḥ pratipadyāmahe, śāsracoditā tu / tasmānneyamaviśuddhiḥ /
  tatprāmāṇyānabhyupagamādaviśuddhiriti cet syānmatam, vedaprāmāṇyamabhyupagacchatāmasaṃśayametadevaṃ syāt / hetuvādakuśalāstu vayam / tasmādadhīyatāṃ yadi kaścidastyubhayapakṣaprasiddho hetuḥ yato nissaṃśayaḥ pratyayaḥ syāditi / etaccāyuktam / kasmāt ? abhyupagamavirodhāt / dṛṣṭamanumānamāptavacanaṃ ceti prāmāṇyatrayamabhyupagataṃ bhavadbhiḥ / idānīṃ vedasyāptavacanatve satyaprāmāṇyaṃ bruvataḥ svamatavyāghātaḥ / tasmādayuktametat /

  ucyate - na, abhiprāyānavabodhāt / citramapi bahvetadabhidhīyamāno nābhiprāyaṃ veda bhavān / kiṃ kāraṇam ? yasmānna vayaṃ vedasya prāmāṇyaṃ pratyācakṣmahe / no khalvapi brūmaḥ śāstracoditāyāṃ hiṃsāyāṃ pravartamānasyāniṣṭaphalasambandho bhavati / kintarhi sati svargaprāptinimittatve vedavihitasya karmaṇaḥ samanuṣṭhānaṃ prāṇijamupaghātamantareṇa na sambhavati iti hitakāmairabhyupekṣyate / yasmāt na hyetaduktaṃ yadanyeṣāmupaghātenātmānugrahaḥ kārya iti / āha -

children.translated_text: 'One should not inflict upon another what is adverse to oneself;
this, in brief, is <s>dharma</s> (righteousness); anything else proceeds from desire.'

Thus, <s>hiṃsā</s> (violence) is impurity, because it destroys the desired body of living beings. One objects: that is untenable, because it is enjoined by scripture. If this violence were not enjoined by scripture, we would accept without doubt that it is impurity; but it is enjoined by scripture. Therefore it is not impurity. If you say it is impurity because we do not accept the authority [of the Veda] — this might be the view: for those who accept the authority of the <s>Veda</s>, this would undoubtedly be so. But we are skilled in reasoning. Therefore let it be examined whether there is any argument established in both positions from which a certain conviction may arise. But this too is incorrect. Why? Because it contradicts your own position. You have accepted three means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>): perception (<s>dṛṣṭa</s>), inference (<s>anumāna</s>), and authoritative testimony (<s>āptavacana</s>). Now, while accepting the <s>Veda</s> as authoritative testimony and yet denying its authority, you contradict your own doctrine. Therefore this is incorrect. If you say there is no fault because the <s>Veda</s>'s status as authoritative testimony is untenable — this might be the view: this reproach would be proper to make after first establishing the <s>Veda</s> as authoritative testimony. But it has been established as true. Therefore this is no reproach. But this too is untenable. Why? Because if a verbal statement has its origin in human intelligence, then due to its connection with passion etc., the word would be worthy of examination — whether it is authoritative testimony or not. But the sacred tradition (<s>āmnāya</s>), not having its origin in human intelligence, is self-sufficient and operates for the supreme good of persons. Therefore it does not merit this kind of unwelcome examination. Moreover, because the charge of impurity would be untenable: if you too were to apply yourself to this matter — how is it determined that violence is impurity because it destroys the desired body of living beings? — it would necessarily have to be said 'from scripture.' And that very scripture prescribes violence in sacrifice. Therefore what reason is there that the same authority is valid elsewhere but should be invalid here regarding 'dharma arises from violence'? If you say that the beneficial and harmful nature of non-violence and violence is established by perception, because they are characterized by benefiting and harming — the view might be: from non-violence comes benefit characterized by preservation of the desired body, and from violence comes harm characterized by destruction of the desired body. And since it is proper to infer a result corresponding to the action, their causation of desirable and undesirable results is established by perception. Therefore what role has scripture here? But this too is untenable. Why? Because undesirable consequences would follow. For if this were posited thus, then even in the case of going to another's wife, there would be a connection with desirable results due to the capacity to benefit another being. And for one who, having brought a student into discipleship, engages him in vows, injunctions, purity, celibacy (<s>brahmacarya</s>), study, begging of alms, tending of the sacred fire, service to the teacher, and the like — there would be a connection with undesirable results. Therefore unsound reasoning that contradicts both worldly convention and scripture is not accepted. If one says that there is the consequence of scriptural contradiction because scripture prescribes both — the view might be: that very scripture teaches non-violence, and that very same scripture teaches violence. This being so, since two mutually contradictory meanings are enjoined, and since both cannot be upheld, there is the consequence of scriptural contradiction. But this is not so. Why? Because the general rule (<s>utsarga</s>) and exception (<s>apavāda</s>) have different domains. For scripture, having laid down non-violence as a general rule in the general case, teaches an exception in the specific case characterized by sacrifice. And what is prescribed generally is overridden by what is prescribed specifically. For example: 'Let curds be given to <s>brāhmaṇa</s>s; buttermilk to <s>Kauṇḍinya</s>.' Therefore, because the general rule and exception have different domains, there is no scriptural contradiction. Moreover, as in the case of approaching a maiden, because there is no fault in a re-prescription: just as approaching a maiden is prohibited in scripture, but one who, having properly accepted a maiden, approaches her does not incur <s>adharma</s>, because of the existence of another scriptural injunction: 'A householder should marry a suitable wife, one not previously married to another.' Similarly, violence is prohibited in scripture, but one who engages in violence in a sacrifice does not partake of undesirable results, because of the existence of the same scriptural injunction mentioned above. Therefore what was said — that violence is impurity because it destroys the desired body of living beings — that is incorrect. It is replied: no, because you do not understand the intention. Despite all this elaborate discourse, you do not know the intention. Why? Because we do not deny the authority of the <s>Veda</s>. Nor do we say that one who engages in violence enjoined by scripture incurs undesirable results. Rather, the point is this: given that Vedically-enjoined action is a means to the attainment of heaven, its performance is impossible without causing harm to living beings, and this is overlooked by those who seek the good. For it has not been said that one should benefit oneself through harm to others. One says:

āha yadyetannābhyupagamyate kathaṃ pūrvamuktaṃ prāṇināmiṣṭaśarīravyāpādanādaviśuddhirhiṃseti ?

) / samānajātīyaṃ ca pratiyoginamapekṣya prakarṣapratyaya utpadyate / yadi cānuśravikasya praśasyatā nābhipretā syāt prakarṣapratyayānupapattiprasaṅgaḥ / tasmānnotsūtrametat /
