children.translated_text: ). And a cognition of superiority arises with reference to a competitor of the same class. If the praiseworthiness of what is taught by scripture were not intended, there would be the consequence of the cognition of superiority being untenable. Therefore this is not inconsistent with the aphorism. One objects: renunciation (<s>sannyāsa</s>) is untenable, because of the scriptural teaching of non-separation [from ritual action]. For you are not master of the non-abandonment and renunciation of ritual action. Rather, whatever scripture teaches must necessarily be done. And it teaches non-separation from ritual actions until death. Why? For it says thus: 'This is a lifelong sacrificial session — namely the <s>Agnihotra</s> (fire-offering), the <s>Darśapaurṇamāsa</s> (new and full moon sacrifices); one is released from this session only by old age and by death.' And again it says: 'One who desires to live a hundred years should perform actions here.' Therefore there is non-abandonment of actions until death. This being so, other actions motivated by different reasons would be purposeless. It is replied: no, because the means of accomplishment are not inherent. This system of ritual action is accomplished through many means such as union with a wife and the like. And since these are not inherent, it has been demonstrated that it is impossible to acquire them from the outset through practice. Therefore ritual actions are impermanent. If you say that when reasoning and scripture conflict, scripture is stronger — the view might be: where there is conflict between reasoning and scripture, since inference is more liable to error, scripture must necessarily be accepted as stronger. But this too is untenable. Why? Because the injunction is made according to capacity. Scripture, having regard to capacity, enjoins actions like <s>Agnihotra</s> and indicates their impermanence. How? For it says thus: 'One who, being qualified for <s>Agnihotra</s>, does not offer the <s>Agnihotra</s> — him that deity shuts out from this world and the next.' Therefore actions are impermanent. Moreover, from the force of the word 'old age': in your own indicative statement there is the word 'old age.' From this it is inferred that action is dependent on capacity and is impermanent. Moreover, because scripture itself would be undermined: for both are prescribed in scripture — ritual actions and renunciation. If ritual actions are held to be obligatory for all time, then the scripture teaching renunciation is undermined. Therefore this is merely your display of attachment to sense objects. One objects: no, because scripture (<s>śruti</s>) is stronger. For when two equally authoritative scriptures converge on a single topic and both cannot be upheld simultaneously, they become either alternatives or sequential. And when <s>śruti</s> (revealed scripture) and <s>smṛti</s> (remembered tradition) converge, <s>śruti</s> is stronger, and renunciation is enjoined by <s>smṛti</s>. Therefore there is no alternative between them. Nor is sequential ordering appropriate. It is replied: the same applies on the other side. Just as scripture teaches the performance of ritual actions, so too it teaches renunciation. How? For it says thus:

children.text: na karmaṇā na prajayā dhanena tyāgenaikenāmṛtatvamānaśuḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Not by action, not by progeny, not by wealth — by renunciation alone did they attain immortality.

children.text: pareṇa nākaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ vibhrājate yadyatayo viśanti //
children.translated_text: That supreme [state], deposited in the cave, shines forth beyond heaven, into which the ascetics enter.'

One asks: if this is not accepted, how was it said earlier that violence is impurity because it destroys the desired body of living beings? It is replied: because of the figurative transfer of the cause to the effect. That distress which arises in our minds out of compassion due to violence — that indeed is the impurity intended. The cause being figuratively transferred, it is said 'violence is impurity.' Just as one says 'satisfied by the beans, happy by the cows.' One asks: how is it understood that the teacher intended by 'impurity' only the distress that is the effect of violence, and not violence itself? It is replied: because a cognition of superiority is obtained. The [teacher] will say: 'from what has been taught, the opposite is better' (

children.text: na karmaṇā mṛtyumṛṣayo niṣeddhuḥ prajāvanto draviṇamicchamāṇāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'The <s>ṛṣi</s>s (seers) did not ward off death by actions, desirous of offspring and seeking wealth.
But other <s>ṛṣi</s>s, the wise ones, attained immortality beyond actions.'

brāhmaṇaṃ cātra bhavati- "tadya idaṃ viduḥ, ye ceme 'raṇyāḥ śraddhātapa ityupāsate te 'rciṣamabhisambhavanti / arciṣo harahna āpūryamāṇapakṣamāpūryamāṇapakṣādyānṣaḍudaṅḍeti māsāṃstānmāsebhyaḥ saṃvatsaraṃ saṃvatsarādādityamādityāccandramasaṃ candramaso vidyutaṃ tatpuruṣo 'māṇavaḥ sa etān brahma gamayati /" punarapyāha- "etameva viditvā munirbhavati, etameva pravrājino lokamicchantaḥ pravrajanti / etaddha sma vai pūrve vidvāṃsaḥ prajāṃ nākāmayanta, prajayā kiṃ kariṣyāmo yeṣāṃ nāyamātmā nāyaṃ loka iti te ha sma putraiṣaṇāyāśca vittaiṣaṇāyāśca lokaiṣaṇāyāśca vyutthāyātha bhikṣācaryaṃ carantīti /" tasmādete tyāgasannyāsayorubhayorliṅgam /
  āha - yadyapyevaṃ śāstraṃ tathāpi samanuṣṭhāne vidhirasti / vihitaṃ cāvaśyaṃ kartavyam / sannyāse tvarthavādamātramityanayorayaṃ viśeṣaḥ / tasmin sati samanuṣṭhānaṃ jyāyo na tyāgaḥ /
  ucyate- ko 'yaṃ vidhiḥ, ko 'yamarthavādaḥ ?
  āha- vidhistadarthatvenāpūrvopadeśaḥ / yo hi vidhyarthena liṅā loṭā kṛtyairvāpūrvopadeśaḥ kriyate sa vidhiḥ / yathā- agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāmaḥ / vāyavyaṃ śvetamajamālabheta bhūtikāma iti / stutirarthavādaḥ / tasya tu vihitasya prarocanārthaṃ yā stutiḥ so 'rthavādaḥ / tadyathā- "vāyurvai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā vāyumeva tena bhāgadheyenopadhāvati, sa evainaṃ bhūtiṃ gamayati" iti / evaṃvidhāṃ hi stutimupaśrutya phalārthine hi yajamānāya vidhiḥ prarocate / etasmin hitakāmaḥ pravartate iti /
  ucyate- na, ata eva sannyāsasiddhiḥ / evaṃ cenmanyase yamāmnāyaḥ śreyāṃsamarthaṃ manyate, taṃ prarocanāya stauti tathā sannyāsasiddhiḥ / kasmāt ? stutatvāt / bahulārthināṃ sannyāsamāmnāyaḥ stauti / sa kasmānna prarocate ? itarathā hyānarthakyam / yadi khalvapyarthavādaḥ stuvannapi na prarocayet yaduktaṃ prarocanārtho 'rthavāda iti tadbhavadbhirhāpitavyaṃ syāt / anarthako hyevaṃ satyarthavādo na prarocanārthaḥ / arthāntaravacanaṃ vā / yadi prarocanārthatvamasya neṣyate tena tarhyarthāntaraṃ vaktavyam / mā bhūdanarthakatvaṃ vedaikadeśasyeti / tasmānnānayā vibhīṣikayā vayaṃ śakyāḥ sanmārgādapanetum / kiṃcānyat / ubhayathā vikalpe 'niṣṭaprasaṅgāt / ihāyamāmnāyo vidheyatvena vā sannyāsaṃ stūyāt avidheyatvena vā / kiṃcātaḥ ? tadyadi tāvadvidheyatvena stauti kimanyadvicāryate ? siddhaḥ sannyāsaḥ / atha vidheyatvena, stutāvasya prayojanaṃ kartavyam / yaddhi kartavyatayā neṣṭaṃ tadapuruṣabuddhipūrvakaḥ svatantraḥ puruṣaniśśreyasārthaṃ pravartamāna āmnāyaḥ kimiti prarocayeta ? tasmādetāmapi kalpanāṃ kṛtvā kṛśamevaitat / athavobhathā vikalpa ityasyāyamanyo 'rthaḥ / ihāyamāmnāyo bhūtārthena vā sannyāsaṃ prarocayet / abhūtārthena vā ? kiṃ cātaḥ ? tadyadi tāvadbhūtārthena prarocayati tathā satyamṛtatvaprāpakasya sannyāsasyāparigrahe viṣayārāgādanyo heturvaktavyaḥ / athābhūtārthena, puruṣo niḥśreyasāddhīyate / kasmāt ? na hyetadyuktaṃ yadaśreyasi mārge pramāṇabhūta āmnāyo mātṛmodakanyāyenehitārthinaḥ prāṇinaḥ pratārayet / tasmādayuktametat / kiñcānyat anekāntāt / nacāyamekānto yadvihitameva kartavyam / tathā ca śābarāḥ paṭhanti grāmagamanaṃ bhavataḥ śobhanamityatrāntareṇa vidhiṃ stutireva devadattaṃ grāmagamanāya prarocayatīti / kiñcānyat, āśaṅkāprasaṅgāt / yadi khalvapi kiñcit satyaṃ kiñcidanṛtaṃ brūyādvedaḥ tathā sati pauruṣeyavākyavadvedavākye 'pi āśaṃkā prasajyeta / tathā ca sati yaduktameva prasaṃgaḥ / aniṣṭaṃ caitat / kiṃ ca vidhyanumānaṃ vā tat, evamekadeśabhūtatvāt / athavā vidhyekadeśo 'rthavāda

And here there is a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> [passage]: 'Those who know this, and those who worship in the forest with faith and austerity — they reach the flame. From the flame [they reach] the day, from the day the waxing fortnight, from the waxing fortnight the six months during which the sun moves northward, from those months the year, from the year the sun, from the sun the moon, from the moon lightning. There is a person who is non-human (<s>amānava</s>); he leads them to <s>Brahman</s>.' Again it says: 'Having known this alone, one becomes a <s>muni</s> (sage); desiring this world alone, wandering ascetics (<s>pravrājin</s>s) go forth. Indeed, the ancient wise ones did not desire offspring, [thinking]: What shall we do with offspring, we for whom there is neither this self nor this world? Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, they then practiced the life of mendicancy.' Therefore, these are the marks of both <s>tyāga</s> (renunciation) and <s>sannyāsa</s> (complete abandonment).
  [The objector] says: Even if scripture [says] thus, nevertheless there is an injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) for [ritual] performance. And what is enjoined must necessarily be performed. Regarding <s>sannyāsa</s>, however, it is mere <s>arthavāda</s> (eulogy) — this is the distinction between the two. When that [injunction] exists, performance is superior, not renunciation.
  It is replied: What is this <s>vidhi</s> (injunction)? What is this <s>arthavāda</s> (eulogy)?
  [The objector] says: A <s>vidhi</s> is an unprecedented teaching for the purpose of that [action]. That which is taught as unprecedented through the optative (<s>liṅ</s>), imperative (<s>loṭ</s>), or verbal adjective (<s>kṛtya</s>) forms for the purpose of injunction — that is <s>vidhi</s>. For example: 'One desiring heaven should offer the <s>agnihotra</s>.' 'One desiring prosperity should consecrate a white goat for <s>Vāyu</s>.' Praise constitutes <s>arthavāda</s>. The praise that serves to encourage what has been enjoined — that is <s>arthavāda</s>. For example: '<s>Vāyu</s> is indeed the swiftest deity; one approaches <s>Vāyu</s> alone with that offering; he alone leads one to prosperity.' For having heard such praise, the injunction appeals to the sacrificer who desires the fruit. One who desires benefit engages in this.
  It is replied: No, precisely from this, <s>sannyāsa</s> (renunciation) is established. If you think that the scripture praises what it considers to be the highest good for the purpose of encouragement, then renunciation is established. Why? Because it is praised. The scripture praises renunciation for the many who seek [the highest good]. Why would it not encourage [them]? Otherwise there would be purposelessness. If indeed <s>arthavāda</s>, even while praising, would not encourage, then what you said — that <s>arthavāda</s> is for the purpose of encouragement — would have to be abandoned by you. For if so, <s>arthavāda</s> would be purposeless, not serving encouragement. Or it would be a statement of something else. If its purpose of encouragement is not accepted, then something else must be stated, lest a portion of the <s>Veda</s> be purposeless. Therefore, we cannot be led away from the right path by this intimidation.
  Moreover, because in either alternative there follows an undesirable consequence. Here the scripture would praise <s>sannyāsa</s> either as something to be enjoined (<s>vidheya</s>) or as something not to be enjoined (<s>avidheya</s>). What follows from this? If it praises it as something to be enjoined, what else is there to deliberate? <s>Sannyāsa</s> is established. If [it praises it] as something not to be enjoined, the purpose of the praise must be fulfilled. For why would the scripture — which is not preceded by human intention, is autonomous, and operates for the highest good of the person — encourage what is not to be done? Therefore, even after making this supposition, this [objection] is feeble.
  Or alternatively, 'in either alternative' has another meaning. Here the scripture would encourage <s>sannyāsa</s> either with true content or with false content. What follows from this? If it encourages with true content, then — this being so — for the non-acceptance of <s>sannyāsa</s> which leads to immortality, a reason other than attachment to sense objects must be stated. If with false content, the person is deprived of the highest good. Why? Because it is not proper that the scripture, which is an authority, should deceive living beings who seek their own welfare, like [a mother deceiving a child with] a sweet — according to the maxim of the mother and the sweet (<s>mātṛmodakanyāya</s>). Therefore this is improper.
  Moreover, because of non-exclusivity (<s>anekānta</s>). It is not an absolute rule that only what is enjoined must be done. And thus the <s>Śābara</s>s [followers of <s>Śabara</s>] teach: 'Your going to the village is excellent' — here, without any injunction, praise alone encourages <s>Devadatta</s> to go to the village.
  Moreover, because of the consequence of doubt. If the <s>Veda</s> were to speak some things that are true and some things that are false, then — this being so — doubt would arise regarding Vedic statements just as it does regarding human statements. And this being so, the very consequence [you wish to avoid] would follow. And this is undesirable.
  Furthermore, is that [<s>arthavāda</s>] an inference of [the existence of] an injunction? [If so, it follows] because it is a part of the same [textual unit]. Or rather, you have conceded too much [by saying] '<s>arthavāda</s> is a part of an injunction.' In that case, upon finding <s>arthavāda</s> regarding <s>sannyāsa</s>, the existence of an injunction too should be inferred. If [you say] there is no fault because of non-apprehension [of the injunction] — that would be so if that injunction were [somewhere] apprehended. Therefore, from non-apprehension, this defect will not be averted. And this too is untenable. Why? Because of the multiplicity of divisions. Let effort be made in apprehension! For the scripture has manifold divisions in each <s>Veda</s>. Therefore, what was said — that the primacy of action [follows] from the existence of an injunction — this too is improper.
  If [you say] <s>sannyāsa</s> is untenable because there is no teaching of procedural details (<s>itikartavyatā</s>) — [the argument would be:] even if the scripture were to consider <s>sannyāsa</s> as something to be enjoined, then just as it teaches the procedural details of the householder's life — marrying a wife, etc. — along with <s>mantra</s>s, so too it should teach <s>sannyāsa</s>. But it has not taught [such details]. Therefore <s>sannyāsa</s> does not exist.
  This too is improper. Why? Because of absence [being its very nature]. <s>Sannyāsa</s> is precisely the absence of all procedural details. What would scripture teach there? Whatever procedural detail constitutes a limb of <s>sannyāsa</s>, that the scripture does teach. How? For thus it says: 'Those who dwell in the forest with austerity and faith, tranquil, learned, practicing the life of mendicancy — they, free from impurity, proceed through the gate of the sun to where that immortal, imperishable <s>Puruṣa</s> [abides].' There, 'those who dwell with austerity and faith' refers to the <s>dharma</s> characterized by <s>yama</s> (restraints) and <s>niyama</s> (observances), accompanied by faith. 'In the forest' indicates departure from the household. 'Tranquil' indicates the withdrawal of the senses and the inner organ from craving for objects. 'Learned' indicates the practice of knowledge by the <s>yogin</s> who is unwearied during the early and late watches of the night and other times. 'Practicing the life of mendicancy' indicates the regulation of limited food intake for the maintenance of the body. And the latter half declares the fruit. The elaboration based on that, regarding the procedural details of <s>sannyāsa</s>, has been stated by <s>Manu</s> and others. And the <s>smṛti</s>s (remembered traditions), which are expositions of <s>śruti</s> (revelation), are authoritative for you — this is [our] position. Therefore, what was said — that <s>sannyāsa</s> does not exist because of the absence of teaching procedural details — this is improper.
  And thus the obligatory rites (<s>nitya karmāṇi</s>). As for what he said — that the scriptural cause is non-conclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) — this is true. For the fruit of action must necessarily be accepted. Otherwise, from the non-existence of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) caused by it, an undesirable consequence would follow. Therefore this is indeed undesirable for the teacher [i.e., you].
  [The objector] asks: How is this to be inferred?
  It is replied: From the force of the word '<s>kṣaya</s>' (decay). If what was stated in the previous <s>sūtra</s> were simply continued here, the use of the word '<s>kṣaya</s>' would be purposeless. Why? Because <s>kṣaya</s> is synonymous with absolute absence. Thus the connection with impurity (<s>aviśuddhiyoga</s>) is established.
  [The objector] asks: How is the connection with decay (<s>kṣayayoga</s>) now to be inferred?
  It is replied: The connection with decay [is established] from the limited number of constituents (<s>aṅgaparimāṇa</s>). The connection with decay of this cause is to be understood from the limited number of its constituents. For the constituents of sacrifice — the sacrificial animal, the <s>puroḍāśa</s> (rice cake), and so forth — are limited in number. It is observed that limited means — threads and the like — produce a limited effect — cloth and the like. And what is limited is observed to be subject to decay. Likewise here.
  Moreover, from the observation of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration). For this <s>saṃsāra</s> is observed, caused by the variety of different actions characterized by differences in speech, intellect, nature, food, and conduct. But if action directly performed were to produce an imperishable fruit, then — owing to the absence of return — <s>saṃsāra</s> of living beings would not be observed.
  If [you say] eternality [follows] from the force of verbal testimony — [the argument would be:] 'We are those for whom verbal testimony is authoritative; what the word says, that is our authority.' And it [the word] declares immortality for this cause: 'He crosses over death, he crosses over sin,' and so forth. Therefore, even unwillingly, this must necessarily be accepted. Or if not accepted, there would be abandonment of the thesis that the <s>Veda</s> is authoritative.
  And this is not so. Why? Because of contradiction with other verbal testimony. The word permits the non-eternality of this cause. And this being so, a contradiction results. How? For thus it says: 'But those who in the village worship with sacrifices, charitable works, and gifts — they travel that very same path and return again. [They go] to space, from space to wind. They reach smoke. Having become smoke, they become cloud. Having become cloud, they rain down. They are born here as rice, barley, herbs, trees, sesame, and beans. From this, whoever eats food and whoever deposits seed — he comes into being again.' Therefore, what was said — that eternality [follows] from the force of verbal testimony — this is improper.
  If [you say] there is the consequence of contradiction of scripture from statement in both ways — [the argument would be:] the very same scripture states eternality, and the very same [states] non-eternality. This being so, since mutually contradictory meanings are enjoined and it is impossible to accommodate both, there is the consequence of scriptural contradiction.
  And this is not so. Why? Because when there is impossibility, a different meaning is postulated. For where authoritative <s>śruti</s> enjoins an impossible meaning, there a different meaning is postulated. For example: 'He dug out the <s>vapā</s> (omentum) of himself,' 'the mind is a thief,' 'speech is a liar' — in such cases. Likewise here too, there is no possibility that one and the same thing could be both eternal and non-eternal. Therefore, we shall postulate a different meaning through secondary signification (<s>bhakti</s>) for the other scripture that speaks of eternality.
  If [you say] the same [could be done] to the other side too — [the argument would be:] just as you have postulated a meaning through secondary signification for eternality due to the impossibility of both eternal and non-eternal [applying] to the same thing, so too [secondary signification] could be applied to non-eternality.
  And this is improper. Why? Because there would be the consequence of contradiction with all means of valid knowledge. For if destruction were to be postulated through secondary signification, there would be contradiction with all <s>pramāṇa</s>s (means of valid knowledge). How? First, contradiction with perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), from the observation of <s>saṃsāra</s>. Contradiction with inference (<s>anumāna</s>), because when the constituents are limited, eternality of the whole is untenable. Contradiction with verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>), from the statement 'they reach smoke.' But when eternality is postulated through secondary signification, this defect does not arise. Therefore, this [objection] is unfair.
  [The objector] asks: How then is the scripture to be interpreted through secondary signification?
  It is replied: Through the sense of eminence (<s>prakṛṣṭārtha</s>). Just as it is said: 'Immortal — or, the dead one has been fully restored to life; may your vital breaths not abandon your body' — and yet the vital breaths do not abandon living beings permanently, but rather for an extended time. Likewise, here too it is said 'he crosses over death' — he does not cross over death permanently, but rather for an extended time. For in common usage, the word 'eternal' (<s>nitya</s>) is used figuratively for 'eminence.' For example: 'eternally laughing,' 'eternally chattering.' Thus the connection with decay (<s>kṣayayoga</s>) is established.
  [The objector] asks: How is the connection with gradation (<s>atiśayayoga</s>) of this cause now to be inferred?
  It is replied: The connection with gradation [is established] from the repetition of action. For where action occurs once and where it recurs repeatedly, gradation is observed — as in agriculture and the like. And in sacrifice, there is dependence on the capacity for gathering materials. Sometimes there is a single performance; sometimes there is repeated performance. Therefore there must be gradation. Moreover, from the gradation of constituents. Here, from the gradation of constituents, gradation of the whole too — like a pot and the like — is observed. And there is this gradation of constituents such as the sacrificial fee (<s>dakṣiṇā</s>) in each sacrifice.
  Therefore, here too there must be gradation.
  If [you say] that because the deity enters the state of being a constituent, the [defects of] decay and gradation are untenable — [the argument would be:] whoever infers that in sacrifice only material substance has the status of a means, for him the defects of decay and gradation would be unavoidable. But we know that the deity inherent in the material substance enters the state of being a constituent of the rite. Therefore there is no defect.
  And this is untenable. Why? Because [the unlimited nature of deities] is what needs to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>). The unlimitedness of the deities is what needs to be proved. And the absence of defect [follows] from their entering the state of being constituents. Moreover, our established doctrine is that the self does not become a constituent of action, because of its indifference (<s>udāsīnatva</s>). Therefore this is improper.
  Or even granting [your position], there follows the consequence of the purposelessness of performing sacrificial rites. If, having found that the deity inherent in the material substance enters the state of being a constituent, and thereby an imperishable and non-gradational cause is obtained — if this is your position — then any Vedic action whatsoever, performed in any way, would suffice to obtain the goal. What need is there for rites that cause the destruction of living beings? How so? For there is no action whatsoever in which the body does not serve as a constituent. And the body is composed of all deities, as it is said: 'Therefore the wise one considers this person as <s>Brahman</s>; for all the deities are established in this body.' Therefore, what was said — that because the deity enters the state of being a constituent, decay and gradation are untenable — this is improper.
  Thus this cause [i.e., Vedic ritual] has three defects. Accordingly, it can be inferred that whatever particular fruit is produced [by it] is also of the same character [i.e., subject to impurity, decay, and gradation]. Therefore, the inquirer [into the highest good] finds no satisfaction here.
  [The objector] says: If, thinking that this [Vedic ritual] is not the highest [means], the inquirer finds no satisfaction here, then that particular fruit which is the highest should be taught.
  It is replied:
The opposite of that is better.

children.text:
tadityanena karmavidhiniṣpāditasya svargaprāptilakṣaṇasya phalasyābhisambandhaḥ / tasmādviparītaḥ śuddho 'kṣayo niratiśaya ityarthaḥ / ko 'sāvityucyate mokṣaḥ śreyān / etaduktaṃ bhavati / ubhāvapyetau praśasyau svargāpavargau, āmnāyavihitatvāt / mokṣastu praśasyataraḥ / kasmāt ? yathoktadoṣānupapatteḥ / sa hyavaśyaṃbhāvitvādaikāntikaḥ / atīndriyatvādasaṃvedyaḥ / svātmanyavasthitvāllaghuḥ sarvatra sannihitaśca / āmnāyastutatvātpraśastaḥ / sadbhirāsevitatvādaninditaḥ / yamaniyamavairāgyajñānābhyupāyaśuddherviśuddhaḥ / adravyatvādakṣayo niratiśayaśca /
  āha, kathaṃ punarayamapavargaḥ prāpyata iti ?
  ucyate, saṃyogābhāvāt / duḥkhaṃ ca pradhānam / tathā ca tantrāntareṣvapyuktam- duḥkhahetuḥ kāryakaraṇaśaktiriti / tena yadā puruṣasya saṃyogastadāviśuddhitvamasya / svaśaktiviśeṣayogātteṣu teṣu jātyantaraparivarteṣu dharmādinimittasāmarthyādāyāsamanubhavati / yadā tu pradhānasaṃyogo vinivartate tadā nimittābhāve naimittikasyāpyabhāva iti kṛtvā na punardvandvānyanubhavati /
  āha, kimarthaḥ punarayaṃ pradhānasya puruṣeṇa saha saṃyogaḥ ?
  ucyate, naitadihābhidhānīyam / vakṣyatyayamupariṣṭādācāryaḥ "puruṣasya darśanārthaḥ, kaivalyārthastathā pradhānasya / paṅgvandhavadubhayorapi saṃyoga iti" (

children.translated_text: <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 21

By the word 'that,' the connection with the fruit characterized by the attainment of heaven, which is accomplished through the injunction of ritual action, [is indicated]. Therefore, 'the opposite' means pure, imperishable, and unsurpassed — this is the meaning. What is that? It is said: <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation) is better. What is stated here is this: both heaven and liberation are praiseworthy, since both are enjoined by scripture. But <s>mokṣa</s> is more praiseworthy. Why? Because the aforementioned defects do not apply to it. For it is absolute, since it inevitably comes about. It is imperceptible, since it is beyond the senses. It is subtle, since it abides in one's own self, and it is omnipresent. It is authoritative, since it accords with scripture. It is blameless, since it is cultivated by the virtuous. It is pure, since it is attained through the purity of the means — <s>yama</s> (restraint), <s>niyama</s> (observance), <s>vairāgya</s> (dispassion), and <s>jñāna</s> (knowledge). It is imperishable and unsurpassed, since it is non-material.
  [Objection:] How then is this <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) attained?
  [Reply:] Through the absence of conjunction. And suffering is <s>pradhāna</s> (the primary cause). As stated in other systems too — 'The cause of suffering is the power of effects and instruments.' Therefore, when there is conjunction of <s>puruṣa</s> (the self), there is impurity for it. Through the connection with its particular powers, in those various transmigrations through different births, it experiences suffering due to the capacity of causes such as <s>dharma</s> (merit) and the like. But when the conjunction with <s>pradhāna</s> ceases, then, since the effect also ceases when the cause is absent, it no longer experiences the pairs of opposites.
  [Objection:] For what purpose, then, is this conjunction of <s>pradhāna</s> with <s>puruṣa</s>?
  [Reply:] This need not be explained here. The teacher will state later: 'For the purpose of the seeing of <s>puruṣa</s>, and likewise for the purpose of the isolation of <s>pradhāna</s>; like the lame and the blind, the conjunction of the two [exists]' (
From the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower. // <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 2 //

children.text: vyaktaṃ cāvyaktaṃ ca jñaśca vyaktāvyaktajñāḥ / teṣāṃ vijñānaṃ vyaktāvyaktajñavijñānaṃ tasmāt / bahuṣvaniyamādalpāco 'pi jñaśabdasya na pūrvanipātaḥ / athavā jñānasya sādhakatamaṃ vyaktam / tatpūrvakatvādavyaktasamadhigamasyetyabhihitam / yadvā vyaktaṃ ca avyaktaṃ ca te vyaktāvyakte, te vijānāti iti vyaktāvyaktajñaḥ, tadvijñānāt saṃyogo nivartate / vakṣyati caitat, "dṛṣṭā mayetyupekṣata eko dṛṣṭāhamityuparamatyanyā" iti (

children.translated_text: <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 66
Just as a man who has slipped from the top of a tree falls even without wishing to,
so too, one who knows the <s>guṇas</s> and <s>puruṣa</s> becomes liberated even without wishing to.

The manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower — these are the 'manifest-unmanifest-knower.' Their discernment is the 'discernment of the manifest, unmanifest, and knower' — from that [liberation comes]. Due to the rule that among many [compounds], the shorter term does not take first position, the word <s>jña</s> (knower) does not come first. Alternatively, the manifest is the most effective instrument of knowledge; since the comprehension of the unmanifest is preceded by that, [the order is] thus stated. Or again: the manifest and the unmanifest are <s>vyaktāvyakte</s>; one who knows them is <s>vyaktāvyaktajña</s> — from his discernment, conjunction ceases. And this will be stated: 'One [<s>prakṛti</s>] desists thinking "I have been seen"; the other [<s>puruṣa</s>] desists thinking "I have seen"' (

children.text: kiṃ cānyat / āmnāyābhihitatvāt / āmnāyanibandhano hyayamartho jñānānmokṣa iti, na yādṛcchikaḥ / katham ? evaṃ hyāha- "satyaṃ jñānamanantaṃ brahma yo veda nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ parame vyoman so 'śnute sarvān kāmān saha brahmaṇā vipaścitā /"

children.translated_text: 'From which words turn back, unable to reach it, together with the mind —

children.text: ānandaṃ brahmaṇo vidvān na bibheti kutaścana //"
children.translated_text: the wise one who knows the bliss of <s>Brahman</s> fears nothing whatsoever.'

children.text:
"tameva viditvāmṛtatvameti nānyaḥ panthā ayanāya vidyate /" tathā brāhmaṇe 'pyuktam / "tarati śokamātmavit /" "brahmavid brahmaiva bhavatīti /" tasmādāmnāyaprāmāṇyādapi manyāmahe jñānānmokṣa iti /
  āha, jñānavācino 'mṛtatvanimittābhyupagamānmahata āmnāyāntarasyānarthakyam / yadi jñānavācina āmnāyakhaṇḍakādamṛtatvamavāpyata ityetadabhyupagamyate, tena kriyāvācino mahata āmnāyāntarasyānarthakyaṃ prāptam / kiṃ kāraṇam ? na hyanāyāseneṣṭāvāptau satyām āyāsabhūyiṣṭhe karmaṇi pravartamānaḥ kṛtī bhavatīti / āha ca -
children.translated_text:
'Having known That alone, one attains immortality; there is no other path for reaching [it].' Likewise it is stated in the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>: 'The knower of the self crosses over sorrow.' 'The knower of <s>Brahman</s> becomes <s>Brahman</s> indeed.' Therefore, from the authority of scripture too, we hold that liberation comes from knowledge.
  [Objection:] Since you accept that immortality comes from the knowledge-teaching portion [of scripture], the vast remaining portion of scripture becomes purposeless. If it is accepted that immortality is obtained from the knowledge-teaching section of scripture, then the great remaining portion of scripture that teaches ritual action becomes purposeless. For what reason? Because no wise person would engage in action that is full of effort when the desired end can be obtained without effort. And it is said:

children.text: akke cenmadhu vindeta kimarthaṃ parvataṃ vrajet /
children.translated_text: If one could find honey in the <s>arka</s> plant, why would one go to the mountain?
When the desired object has been obtained, what wise person would make further effort?

What else? Because it is declared by scripture. For this doctrine — that liberation comes from knowledge — is grounded in scripture, not arbitrary. How so? For it is thus stated: 'Truth, knowledge, infinite is <s>Brahman</s>. He who knows it as deposited in the cave, in the highest heaven, enjoys all desires together with the wise <s>Brahman</s>.'

children.text:
ucyate- yadi punaḥ karmāṇyatyantakartavyatayeṣyante, jñānavācina āmnāyasya kathamarthavattā siddhā bhavati ?
  āha, samuccaye tūbhayārthavattvam / jñānakarmaṇostu samuccaye 'bhyupagamyamāne dvayorapyāmnāyārthavattā siddhā bhavati / vidvān yajeta vidvān yājayediti vacanāt, tathā sarvapuruṣāṇāṃ kratāvadhikāraḥ aśrotriyaṣaṇḍhaśūdravarjamitinyāyāt / tasmājjñānakarmaṇoḥ samuccayādiṣṭaprasiddhiḥ /
  ucyate- na, pūrvadoṣāparihārāt / yadi niyamato viduṣaiva karmāṇi kartavyānītyabhyupagamyate tena yaḥ pūrvokto doṣaḥ saṃsārābhāvaprasaṅgaḥ, tasyāparihāraḥ / kiṃ ca śāstrahāneśca / yaśca śāstramiṣṭāpūrte samupāsyate te dhūmamabhisaṃbhavantīti tadetasyāṃ kalpanāyāṃ hīyate / kiṃ cānyat- bhinnaphalatvāt / ihābhinnaphalāni dravyāṇi samuccīyante / tadyathā bhujyaṅgāni sūpādīni / abhinnaṃ teṣāṃ tṛptilakṣaṇaṃ phalamiti / na caitajjñānakarmaṇorabhinnaṃ phalam / svargāpavargahetutvāt / jñānasāmarthātkaivalyamabhinnaṃ phalamiti cet pūrveṇāviśeṣaḥ / yaduktaṃ saṃsārābhāvaprasaṃga iti tadanapahṛtameva bhavati / kiṃcānyat- śrūyamāṇaphalavirodhaśca / yacca kriyāyāḥ phalaṃ śrūyate agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāmo, rāṣṭramagniṣṭomena jayatīti tadvirudhyate / karmaṇaśca śeṣabhāvaḥ / svārthopasarjanatve satyarthāntaraniṣpādakatvāt / yathāvahantītyevamādyāḥ kriyāḥ svaṃ phalamupasarjanīkṛtya taddvāreṇa yajerupakurvantyastaccheṣabhūtā bhavanti evaṃ kriyāpi jñānaphalabhūtatvāttaccheṣabhūtā syāt /
  vidhisadbhāvāt kriyāprādhānyamiti cenna- uktatvāt / kathametat ? nāsti vidhikṛto viśeṣaḥ / upetya vā / tatrāpi tadutpatteḥ / asti hi jñānasyāpi vidhāyakaṃ śāstram / katham ? evaṃ hyāha- "ya ātmāpahatapāpmā vijighatso vipipāso vijaro vimṛtyurviśokaḥ sannyastasaṃkalpaḥ so 'nveṣṭavyaḥ sa jijñāsitavyaḥ / sarvāṃśca kāmānavāpnoti ya ātmānamanuvidya vijānātīti" prajāpatervacanaṃ śrūyate / punarapyāha- "dve vidye veditavye parā caivāparā ca" yā / tasmādvidhisadbhāvātkriyāprādhānyamiti svapakṣānurāgamātrametat / dṛṣṭārthatvādityeke /
  eke punarācāryā manyante dṛṣṭameva jñānasyājñānanivṛttilakṣaṇaṃ phalaṃ tasmānna śāstreṇa vidhīyate / kiṃ kāraṇam ? dṛṣṭārthasya hi karmaṇo na śāstraṃ prayojakam / svayamevārthitatvāttatra pravṛtterbhujyādivat / teṣāṃ jñānavidhāyakāni vākyāni tānyupāyaguṇavidhānārthamanuvādabhūtānyāśrīyante / tadyathā dadhnā juhoti, payasā juhotīti /
  yattu khalvidamucyate vidvānyajeta, vidvān yājayet, śrotriyasya ca karmaṇyadhikāra iti tasyāmayamarthaḥ- adhītya vedaṃ kriyānupūrvo ca jñātvā karmaṇi pravartitavyam / evaṃ ca sati na kaściddoṣaḥ / yadi punarniyamata evātmavidhāṃ karmaṇyadhikārastena saṃsārābhāvaprasaṃgaḥ / svābhāvikatvāt / vijñānasya śāsrasya sarvādhikāravirodhaḥ / tasmānnāsti samuccayo jñānakarmaṇoḥ /
  apara āha- satyam / nāstyanayoḥ samuccayaḥ kintarhi sarvārthā kriyā jñānaṃ pratiṣiddhārtham / ye hi ṣaṇḍhāndhavabadhirādayaḥ karmaṇo 'tyantaṃ nirākṛtāsteṣāṃ jñānādāśramāntare 'mṛtatvāvāptiḥ / itareṣāṃ tū mūlāśrame karmaṇa eveti tasya nāyaṃ vādinaḥ parihāra iti /
  ucyate- na, svasamayavirodhāt / evaṃ bruvāṇasyāsya vādinaḥ svasamaya eva virudhyate / yaduktam- vidvāṃsaḥ prajāṃ nākāmayanta, kiṃ prajayā kariṣyāmaḥ ? atha yaduktaṃ putraiṣaṇāyāśca vittaiṣaṇāyāśca vyutthāya bhaikṣacaryāṃ carantīti / na ca ṣaṇḍānāṃ putraiṣaṇāvyutthānamathavad bhavati, devakṛtatvāt / kiṃ cānyat - rahasyabhūtatvāt / rahasyabhūtaṃ hi vedānāṃ jñānam / yasmādāha- taddha smaitadāruṇirauddālakirjyeṣṭhāya putrāya provāca / idaṃ jyeṣṭhaputrāya pitā brahma prabrūyāt / praṇāyyāntevāsine nānyasmai yasmai kasmaicana / ya imāmadbhiḥ parigṛhītāṃ vasunā vasumatīṃ pūrṇāṃ dadyādetadeva tato bhūya iti /

children.translated_text: And here there are [verses]:
The supreme secret is recited at the end of the <s>Vedas</s>;
if that were intended for eunuchs and the like, then by good fortune scripture would be fruitful!

[Reply:] But if actions are held to be absolutely obligatory, how can the purposefulness of the knowledge-teaching scripture be established?
  [Objection:] Through combination, both would be purposeful. If the combination of knowledge and action is accepted, the purposefulness of both portions of scripture is established. Because of the statement 'The learned one should sacrifice, the learned one should cause sacrifice,' and because of the principle that all persons have qualification for ritual, 'except the non-Vedic-student, the eunuch, and the <s>śūdra</s>.' Therefore, from the combination of knowledge and action, the attainment of the desired end is established.
  [Reply:] No, because the earlier objection is not resolved. If it is accepted that the knowledgeable person must necessarily perform actions, then the previously stated defect — the impossibility of the absence of <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration) — is not eliminated. Moreover, because scripture would be contradicted. The scripture that says 'Those who resort to ritual and charitable works enter smoke' — that would be violated under this interpretation. Furthermore, because the fruits are different. In this world, substances with the same fruit are combined — for example, foods such as curries and the like — their common fruit being satisfaction. But knowledge and action do not have the same fruit, since they are respectively the causes of liberation and heaven. If one says that <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) is the common fruit due to the power of knowledge, then there is no difference from the earlier [objection] — the stated consequence of the impossibility of <s>saṃsāra</s> remains unresolved. Furthermore, because there is contradiction with the declared fruit. The fruit of action that is declared — 'One should offer the <s>agnihotra</s> desiring heaven,' 'One conquers a kingdom by means of the <s>agniṣṭoma</s>' — that would be contradicted. And action would become subordinate. When something serves another's purpose while being subordinated to it, it accomplishes something other [than its own end]. Just as actions such as 'carrying' and the like, having subordinated their own fruit, serve sacrifice through that [subordination] and thus become subsidiary to it — so too, action, being in the nature of a fruit of knowledge, would become subsidiary to it.
  If one argues that action is primary because injunctions exist — no, because this has been addressed. How so? There is no special [priority] created by injunction. Or even granting that, the same [objection] arises there too. For there is scripture that enjoins knowledge as well. How? For it is thus stated: 'The self that is free from evil, free from hunger and thirst, free from old age and death, free from sorrow, free from desire — that is to be sought, that is to be inquired into. He who has found and knows the self obtains all worlds and all desires' — thus the words of <s>Prajāpati</s> are heard. And again it says: 'Two kinds of knowledge are to be known — the higher and the lower.' Therefore, the claim that action is primary because injunctions exist is merely attachment to one's own position. Some say [action is primary] because [knowledge] has a visible result.
  Some other teachers hold that the fruit of knowledge is indeed visible — namely, the removal of ignorance — and therefore it need not be enjoined by scripture. For what reason? For scripture is not the motivator for an action that has a visible purpose, since one engages in it of one's own accord, like eating and the like. According to them, the scriptural statements that enjoin knowledge are taken as restating [what is already known], for the purpose of enjoining subsidiary qualities of the means — just as [the statements] 'One offers with curds, one offers with milk.'
  As for what is said — 'The learned one should sacrifice, the learned one should cause sacrifice,' and 'The one versed in scripture has qualification for ritual action' — the meaning of that is: having studied the <s>Vedas</s> and having followed the sequence of rituals, and having known, one should engage in action. Thus there is no defect. But if the qualification for ritual action belongs necessarily only to the knowers of the self, then the impossibility of <s>saṃsāra</s> follows. Because it would be natural. And [such a view] contradicts the universal qualification for the science of knowledge. Therefore there is no combination of knowledge and action.
  Another says: True, there is no combination of the two. Rather, all action is [for everyone], while knowledge is for those who are excluded [from action]. For those who are completely excluded from action — such as eunuchs, the blind, and the deaf — for them, immortality is obtained through knowledge in another <s>āśrama</s> (stage of life). But for others, [it is] through action alone in the primary <s>āśrama</s>. [However,] this is not a [valid] refutation of the [opponent's] position.
  [Reply:] No, because it contradicts his own doctrine. For this speaker's own doctrine is contradicted. As stated: 'The wise ones did not desire progeny — what shall we do with progeny?' And as stated: 'Having arisen from the desire for sons and the desire for wealth, they wander about as mendicants.' And the rising above the desire for sons does not occur for eunuchs in any meaningful way, since [their condition] is made by fate. Furthermore, because [knowledge] is of the nature of a secret. For the knowledge of the <s>Vedas</s> is secret in nature. Since it is said: 'This indeed <s>Āruṇi Auddālaki</s> told to his eldest son. This <s>Brahman</s> a father should declare to his eldest son. [He should declare it] to a student who has bowed down, to no one else whosoever. Even if someone were to give him this [earth] surrounded by waters, full of wealth — this [knowledge] would be greater than that.'
'The learned one should perform actions' — this, it is said, is stated in scripture;
but he would be like a eunuch and the like — one who is completely fallen from action.

children.text:
sa eva vartyatāṃ prājñaiḥ kiṃ nyāyyo 'tha matibhramaḥ ?
  indriyārthānurāgo vā dveṣo vā mokṣavartmani //
children.translated_text:
Let the wise ones follow that [path] — is it proper, or a delusion of mind,
  or attachment to sense objects, or aversion on the path of liberation?
That praise which is enjoined by the <s>Vedas</s>, being the cause of attaining <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation),
is commended by distinguished ones such as <s>Yājñavalkya</s> and others, from their ascertainment of truth.
This [knowledge], by those blinded by attachment to sense objects, who speak of reversed meanings —

children.text: vidyā kanyeva ṣaṇḍāya dīyamānā na śobhate //
children.translated_text: [when given to them,] this <s>vidyā</s> (knowledge), like a maiden given to a eunuch, does not shine.
Therefore, having repelled this army of false reasoning spoken by those who follow passion,
the wise one should proceed from <s>āśrama</s> to <s>āśrama</s>, like a youth.

children.text: iti śrīmadācāryeśvarakṛṣṇaviracitāyāṃ sāṃkhyasaptatau yuktidīpikānāmni vivaraṇe prathamamāhnikam //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the first chapter in the commentary called <s>Yuktidīpikā</s> on the <s>Sāṃkhyasaptati</s> (Seventy [Verses] of <s>Sāṃkhya</s>) composed by the revered master <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>.

[Objection:] You have correctly taught that liberation is attained from the discernment of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower. Now it should be taught: how is this triad to be understood?
  [Reply:] The understanding of this triad is declared in two ways — in summary and in detail. That same triad is divided into five topics. What are these topics? They are: the topic of <s>prakṛti</s> (primal nature) and <s>vikṛti</s> (modification), the topic of cause and effect, the topic of excess and non-excess, the topic of cause and caused, and the topic of object and subject. Since the topic of <s>prakṛti</s> and <s>vikṛti</s> precedes the other topics, we shall explain its divisions. That [topic] is further divided into four: something is a cause only and not an effect; something is both a cause and an effect; something is an effect only and not a cause; and something is neither a cause nor an effect.
  [Objection:] This has been taught too generally; it does not settle in our understanding. Therefore, explain by distinguishing — what is the nature of which category?
  [Reply:] Very well. It is taught:
Primordial nature (<s>mūlaprakṛti</s>) is uncaused (<s>avikṛti</s>);

  ucyate- taditaratrāpi tulyam / yathaiva hi satāmātmādīnāṃ kāraṇaṃ nopapannamevamasatāṃ śaśaviṣāṇādīnāmapīti nāsti kaścidviśeṣaḥ / tṛtīyā tu viṣādāvalyaiva koṭiḥ / evamubhayapakṣavyudāsātsvapakṣasiddhiriti cet athāpi syāt- sadasatoḥ kriyāsambandhaṃ pratyaviśeṣa upadarśyate bhavatā / tenobhayorapi pakṣayorvyudāsaḥ kṛto bhavati / na cobhayapakṣavyudāsātsvapakṣasiddhiriti / etaccāyuktam / kasmāt ? uttaratra pratiṣedhāt / sa khalveṣa vādī satkāryavādaṃ pratyācaṣṭe tasmātsvaka evainamadhikāre nivartayiṣyāmaḥ /

  ucyate, kāraṇāntarapratiṣedhāt / puruṣākartṛtvātpradhānākhyānāṃ guṇānāṃ cāvasthāntarānupapatteravikṛtitvasiddhiḥ / ihārabhyamāṇā prakṛtiḥ kāraṇāntarairīśvarādibhirārabhyate, puruṣeṇa vā, guṇairvā / kiñcātaḥ ? tanna tāvatkāraṇāntarairīśvarādibhirārabhyate / kasmāt ? pratiṣedhāt / yathā kāraṇāntarāṇi na santi tathottaratra pratiṣedhaḥ kariṣyate / idānīṃ sattvaṃ rajastamaḥ puruṣa iti padārthacatuṣṭayaṃ pratijñāyate / tatrāpi puruṣakartṛtvaṃ pratyākhyāyate / tasminpratyākhyāte guṇānāmevāvasthāntarāpekṣaḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvaḥ / sūkṣmāṇāṃ mūrtilābhaḥ kāryam / nivṛtaviśeṣāṇāmavibhāgātmanāvasthānaṃ kāraṇamityayaṃ siddhāntaḥ / tatrāstaṅgataviśeṣāṇāṃ nivṛttapariṇāmavyāpārāṇāmaṅgāṅgibhāvamanupagacchatāmupasaṃhṛtaśaktīnāṃ sarvavikārasāmyaṃ sarvaśaktipralayaṃ nissattāsattaṃ nissadasadavyaktalakṣaṇamavasthāntaramupasaṃprāptānāṃ nāstyanyatsūkṣmataramavasthāntaram, yasyedaṃ pradhānalakṣaṇamavasthāntaraṃ kāryaṃ syāt / tasmātsuṣṭhūcyate mūlaprakṛtiravikṛtiriti /
children.translated_text:
"Root" (mūla) means foundation, support — it is synonymous with "basis." That which produces is <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature). It is the root and it is <s>Prakṛti</s>, hence <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s> (root-nature). Root-nature is the root of what? Of <s>Mahat</s> (the Great One) and the rest. This is indeed the designation of <s>Pradhāna</s> (primal matter) — "<s>Mūlaprakṛti</s>." And it is unmodified (<s>avikṛti</s>), meaning it is not produced as a modification.
[Objection:] The compound is untenable because another qualifier is being introduced. The word "root" (<s>mūla</s>) is adopted to qualify <s>Prakṛti</s>, yet it introduces another qualification referring to <s>Mahat</s> and the rest. In that case, the prohibition that "terms with qualifiers do not form compounds" would apply. If one says there is no fault because an alternative compound can be prescribed — that is, if there is this fault in the present compound, an alternative compound will be prescribed: "the root of the <s>Prakṛtis</s> is <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s>" — this too is untenable. Why? Because another fault arises. Even so, by the rule "the subordinate member is placed first," and since what is expressed in the genitive is subordinate, it should be placed first. Thus it should be "<s>Prakṛtimūla</s>" ("nature-root"), not "<s>Mūlaprakṛti</s>." Therefore this alternative too is without substance.
[Reply:] Let the original compound stand. A relational word, being dependent, always forms a compound in derivation. As for the objection that the compound is untenable because another qualifier is introduced — to that we say: relational words have no independent existence apart from their correlates, so they must necessarily form compounds precisely because they carry expectancy. Just as in "<s>Devadatta</s>'s teacher's family" (<s>devadattasya gurukulam</s>), the word "teacher" (<s>guru</s>), though requiring the relational word "<s>Devadatta</s>," nonetheless forms a compound with the word "family" (<s>kula</s>) due to its relational nature — so too here, the word "root" (<s>mūla</s>), though requiring <s>Mahat</s> and the rest due to its relational nature, nonetheless forms a compound with the word <s>Prakṛti</s>. Moreover, because the meaning expressible by a sentence is apprehended even in a compound: where the meaning expressible by a sentence cannot be obtained through a compound, as in "the servant of a prosperous king," there the rule "terms with qualifiers do not form compounds" is established in grammar. But here the meaning expressible by a sentence is apprehended even when the compound exists. Therefore there is no fault. Furthermore, because of an indicatory rule (<s>jñāpaka</s>): the indicatory rule is indeed "one whose action is similar to the object acts like the object" (<s>karmavatkarmaṇā tulyakriyaḥ</s>). Likewise "the teaching of the open pronunciation of 'a'" (<s>akārasya vivṛttopadeśa</s>) and so forth. Therefore no objection should be raised here.
[Objection:] Analysis of the component parts is untenable because it is a proper-name word (<s>saṃjñā</s>). In proper-name words, the component parts are not analyzed. Just as with <s>Gajakarṇa</s> ("elephant-ear") or <s>Aśvakarṇa</s> ("horse-ear") — whose elephant? whose horse? [one does not ask].
[Reply:] No, because the meaning is coherent. Where the meaning is coherent, there is indeed analysis of component parts even in proper-name words. Just as <s>Saptaparṇa</s> ("seven-leaved") — "whose leaves are seven at each joint" — and <s>Aṣṭāpada</s> ("eight-footed") — "whose feet are eight in each row." And here the meaning is coherent; therefore there is no fault.
[Objection:] <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s> is unmodified — one should say "it is <s>Prakṛti</s>," since it is stated that "<s>Mahat</s> and the rest, the seven, are both <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Vikṛti</s> (modification)."
[Reply:] There is no need to state its <s>Prakṛti</s>-nature separately. The <s>Prakṛti</s>-nature of <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s> need not be stated. For what reason? Because it follows from the meaning itself. It is already established by the statement "<s>Mūlaprakṛti</s> is unmodified." For if stated, it would be redundant.
[Objection:] The <s>Prakṛti</s>-nature is untenable, given the acceptance of <s>satkāryavāda</s> (the doctrine of pre-existent effects). That which produces is <s>Prakṛti</s>; its state is <s>Prakṛtitva</s> (being a cause). But this does not hold when the effect already exists. Why? Because for things that already exist — the self and so forth — causation is not coherent.
[Reply:] That same [objection] applies equally to the other position. Just as causation is not coherent for existing things like the self and so forth, so too it is not coherent for non-existing things like the hare's horn and so forth — there is no difference whatsoever. The third alternative — that of poison — is indeed the only option. If one says: "By refuting both positions, one's own position is established" — that is, since you demonstrate that there is no difference between existent and non-existent with respect to their relation to action, you thereby refute both positions, and from the refutation of both positions one's own position is not established — this is improper. Why? Because of the refutation that follows later. That disputant indeed advocates <s>satkāryavāda</s>; therefore we shall refute him in his own domain.
[Objection:] The statement of "unmodified" (<s>avikṛti</s>) is purposeless, since that is already established by its being <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s>. If it is the root of all <s>Prakṛtis</s>, it must necessarily be unmodified. Otherwise, its being <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s> would be untenable. If <s>Pradhāna</s> too had another <s>Prakṛti</s> above it, its status as <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s> would not hold. Therefore, since that is already established by the statement of <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s>-nature, the mention of "unmodified" is purposeless.
[Reply:] No, because it serves to prevent an infinite regress. Just as for roots and such, a seed is the <s>Prakṛti</s>, and of that yet another, and of that yet another — thus an infinite regress — so too for <s>Mahat</s> and the rest, <s>Pradhāna</s> is the <s>Mūlaprakṛti</s>, and of that yet another — an infinite regress would follow. Lest that occur, the statement is made to prevent it.
[Objection:] No, because no reason has been taught. Undoubtedly it would be so, but no reason has been taught by you here. And it is not proper for the wise to accept what has no stated reason. Therefore this is unjustified.
[Reply:] Because any other cause is negated. Due to <s>Puruṣa</s>'s non-agency, and because the <s>guṇas</s> (constituents) called <s>Pradhāna</s> cannot assume another state [beyond the primal equilibrium], the unmodified nature is established. The <s>Prakṛti</s> being discussed here would be produced either by other causes such as <s>Īśvara</s> (God) and the like, or by <s>Puruṣa</s>, or by the <s>guṇas</s>. What of it? It is not produced by other causes such as <s>Īśvara</s>. Why? Because they are negated. The negation that no other causes exist will be made later. For now, four categories are posited: <s>Sattva</s>, <s>Rajas</s>, <s>Tamas</s>, and <s>Puruṣa</s>. Among these, the agency of <s>Puruṣa</s> is rejected. When that is rejected, the cause-effect relationship pertains only to the different states of the <s>guṇas</s> themselves. The effect is the <s>guṇas</s> in their subtle form acquiring manifest form. The cause is the state of remaining in an undifferentiated condition when specific distinctions have ceased — this is the established doctrine. For those [<s>guṇas</s>] whose specific distinctions have subsided, whose transformative activity has ceased, who do not enter into the relationship of principal and subordinate, whose powers are withdrawn, who have reached the equilibrium of all modifications, the dissolution of all powers, beyond being and non-being, beyond existent and non-existent — the state characterized as <s>Avyakta</s> (the Unmanifest) — there is no other state more subtle than this, of which this state characterized as <s>Pradhāna</s> could be an effect. Therefore it is well said: "<s>Mūlaprakṛti</s> is unmodified."
<s>Mahat</s> (the Great One) and the rest, the seven, are both <s>Prakṛti</s> (cause) and <s>Vikṛti</s> (modification).

mahānādyo yāsāṃ tā mahadādyāḥ / avayavena vigrahaḥ, samudāyaḥ samāsārthaḥ / anyathā mahānevātrāparigṛhītaḥ syāt / prakṛtayaśca vikṛtayaśca prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ / kāraṇāni kāryāṇi cetyarthaḥ / tatra mahānahaṃkārasya prakṛtiḥ pradhānasya vikṛtiḥ / ahaṃkāro 'pi tanmātrendriyaparvaṇoḥ prakṛtirvikṛtirmahataḥ / tanmātrāṇi ca bhūtaparvaṇaḥ prakṛtirahaṃkārasya vikṛtiḥ /

) iti tenaivedaṃ siddham / nārthastadarthenāpi saptagrahaṇena /

children.translated_text:
) — by that alone this is established. There is no need for the specification of "seven" for that purpose either.
[Reply:] It is for indicating the unity of <s>tattva</s> (principle) despite difference of form. For eight forms of <s>Buddhi</s> (intellect) — <s>Dharma</s> (virtue) and the rest — will be described, and <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> will be described as having three aspects — <s>Vaikārika</s> (modified), <s>Taijasa</s> (luminous), and <s>Bhūtādi</s> (elemental) — and thus as having three characteristics. Lest the difference of form lead to a difference of <s>tattva</s>, the specification of "seven" is made for this purpose.
[Objection:] Because without a reason, there can be no acceptance. Even what is stated explicitly is not accepted by those skilled in reasoning without a justification — how much less what is arrived at with difficulty. Therefore a resolution must be stated here: how is <s>Buddhi</s>, though having many forms, one single [principle]?
[Reply:] No [need to address it now], because this will be examined later. We shall examine this later: whether, even when multiple forms manifest, the entity remains the same, or whether difference of form entails difference of <s>tattva</s>. Therefore let this stand for now as established — "<s>Mahat</s> and the rest, the seven, are both <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Vikṛti</s>."

Those that begin with <s>Mahat</s> are called "<s>Mahadādyāḥ</s>" ("<s>Mahat</s> and the rest"). The analysis is by component parts; the meaning of the compound is the aggregate. Otherwise, <s>Mahat</s> alone would not be included here. Those that are both <s>Prakṛtis</s> (causes) and <s>Vikṛtis</s> (modifications) are <s>Prakṛtivikṛtis</s> — meaning they are both causes and effects. Among these, <s>Mahat</s> is the <s>Prakṛti</s> of <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-principle) and the <s>Vikṛti</s> of <s>Pradhāna</s>. <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> too is the <s>Prakṛti</s> of the <s>Tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) and the sense-organ group, and the <s>Vikṛti</s> of <s>Mahat</s>. And the <s>Tanmātras</s> are the <s>Prakṛti</s> of the gross-element group and the <s>Vikṛti</s> of <s>Ahaṃkāra</s>.
[Question:] What is the purpose of specifying "seven"?
[Reply:] The specification of "seven" is for the purpose of delimiting the boundary. For if "seven" were not specified, it would not be known how many members of the <s>Prakṛti</s>-group are designated as <s>Prakṛtivikṛti</s>. In that case, the <s>Prakṛti</s>-nature of the gross elements and the sense-organ group too would be entailed.
[Objection:] This purpose does not exist, because it is established by elimination. In your <s>Pañcaśikha</s> system there are twenty-five <s>tattvas</s> (principles). Among them it has been said "<s>Mūlaprakṛti</s> is unmodified," and it will be said "the group of sixteen is modification only; <s>Puruṣa</s> is neither <s>Prakṛti</s> nor <s>Vikṛti</s>." By elimination, exactly seven remain. Therefore there is no need for that specification of "seven."
[Reply:] It is for the purpose of including <s>Ahaṃkāra</s>. For <s>Patañjali</s> [holds that] "<s>Ahaṃkāra</s> does not exist as such," since he accepts that <s>Mahat</s> has the nature of the I-notion (<s>asmipratyaya</s>). This [specification] will serve to counter that [view].
[Objection:] No, because it is included later. This purpose does not exist, for the teacher will state explicitly later with a clear voice: "From <s>Prakṛti</s> arises <s>Mahat</s>, from that <s>Ahaṃkāra</s>" (
The group of sixteen, however, is modification only.

children.translated_text: This is the group of sixteen, being of sixteen in measure. Its measure — the suffix '-kan' [functions] in the sense of number, name, group, and <s>sūtra</s>-study. [Objection:] What then is this group of sixteen? [Reply:] The five gross elements and the eleven sense-faculties. The word 'tu' (but/only) is for the purpose of restriction. [Objection:] But this meaning can be obtained even without the word 'tu.' How? Because it has been taught earlier that 'the seven beginning with <s>mahat</s> are both <s>prakṛti</s> and <s>vikṛti</s>.' Since the precedence of <s>ahaṅkāra</s> and <s>tanmātras</s> is [thus] established, the repetition [of the text] will restrict [the reference] to the two stages of sense-faculties and gross elements. Just as in 'Five five-clawed [animals] may be eaten' — though all substances capable of remedying hunger are fit to be eaten by implication, the repetition [of the text] makes a restriction — so this should be viewed. If [you say] the restriction is for the sake of what is desired — let that be your view. If 'tu' is for restriction based on what is desired — how then is it to be understood that the sixteen-fold [group] is exclusively evolutes? [It should be understood as] 'the sixteen-fold is an evolute' — not 'let it be known [otherwise].' If so, then 'tu' is read in an inappropriate place; it should be stated 'the sixteen-fold evolute indeed.' Or, if you think the word 'tu' is read here for metrical completion and should be seen [as meaningful] only where it is faultless — this is untenable. Why? Because there is no doubt. When it has been taught that 'the seven beginning with <s>mahat</s> are both <s>prakṛti</s> and <s>vikṛti</s>' — why would we be doubtful? Therefore we see a weak purpose in its reading. But perhaps the intention is: even though this is established by meaning, nevertheless the teacher emphasizes restriction for the purpose of clear understanding. Why? Because the intentions of <s>sūtra</s>-authors are various. Just as the blessed <s>Pāṇini</s> — even though restriction is established without effort by what is desired in [rules like] 'not before kye,' 'rāt of sa' — nevertheless makes effort elsewhere in [rules like] 'ajādi,' 'guṇavacanāt,' 'stautiṇyor eva,' '<s>ṣaṇyabhāsāt</s>' — so too it should be seen here. This is untenable. Why? Because it is impossible. Or again, even granting the restrictive purpose of 'tu,' how can restriction be understood here, since products characterized as bodies and such are perceived [arising] from the gross elements too? Some offer this solution: because of the non-difference-of-meaning of bodies and such [from earth etc.], earth and so forth do not have the nature of <s>prakṛti</s> (cause). For the product of earth and such is merely a special arrangement — like a fist, knot, or earring — not a different entity. Therefore they are not <s>prakṛti</s>. But this too is untenable. Why? Because there is no distinction. For the <s>Sāṃkhyas</s>, every product is non-different [in substance from its cause]. With this reasoning, it would follow that all <s>tattvas</s> (principles) are non-<s>prakṛti</s>. And if this is not desired, it contradicts <s>satkāryavāda</s> (the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause). Others say: the restriction [that they are evolutes only] is because the gross elements do not transform — they are non-producers. This too is untenable. Why? Because of perception. For the transformation of gross elements into sprouts, curds, milk, and such is perceived directly. But [the transformation] of the other <s>tattvas</s> is grasped by inference — thus this [argument] is inferior. Therefore this is inappropriate. [Objection:] Then should it not be understood that 'the sixteen-fold is exclusively evolute'? [Reply:] It should be understood. Why? Because no other <s>tattva</s> is possible. Here, the transformation of the <s>guṇas</s> that have departed from equilibrium due to the purpose of <s>puruṣa</s> — from <s>mahat</s> etc. up to the particulars — proceeds with a rule of production of distinct <s>tattvas</s>. But from earth and such, there is no production of a distinct <s>tattva</s>. Therefore their nature is exclusively that of evolutes. And furthermore: because there is no distinct apprehending faculty. Just as when earth and such are produced from <s>tanmātras</s>, a distinct apprehending faculty characterized as a sense-organ arises from <s>ahaṅkāra</s> appropriate to it — no such distinct apprehending faculty exists for the products of earth and such, like pots etc. Therefore [they are] not a distinct <s>tattva</s>. And hence earth and such are exclusively evolutes. Furthermore: because in those [evolutes] the state of being an effect disappears just as the state of being a cause disappears in <s>pradhāna</s>. Just as there is no state subtler than <s>pradhāna</s>, and so the state of being a cause ceases therein — so the state of being an evolute ceases in them. Therefore it is properly said: this sixteen-fold [group] is exclusively evolute. [Objection:] Then what is the understanding regarding <s>puruṣa</s>? [Reply:]
<s>Puruṣa</s> is neither <s>prakṛti</s> nor <s>vikṛti</s>. || <s>ISk</s> 3 ||

Just as <s>pradhāna</s> — so too this <s>puruṣa</s>: being acted upon by other causes such as <s>Īśvara</s> (God) and others, it is not produced. Why? Because of the prohibition. Just as other causes do not exist — that prohibition will be made later. Because of equality with other <s>puruṣas</s>. All <s>puruṣas</s> are equal. And a cause-effect relationship is not seen among equals. Moreover, because of their inactivity and purity — action characterized by transformation or by motion is impossible for them due to their all-pervasiveness. Why? Because they do not produce one another. Not by the <s>guṇas</s>, because of being of a different class. Here we shall establish that the <s>guṇas</s> are non-conscious. And whatever is produced by something becomes of that [same] nature. If <s>puruṣas</s> were produced by the <s>guṇas</s>, then they too would be non-conscious — but they are conscious. Therefore they are not produced by the <s>guṇas</s> — this is established. Something is a cause only and not an effect; something is both cause and effect; something is an effect only; and something is neither cause nor effect — thus the fourfold operation of causality has been explained. This is the summary <s>sūtra</s> of the thesis. Here, what has been taught by you [teachers] should be understood as the provable (<s>prameya</s>) in this <s>śāstra</s>. || 3 ||

For this <s>puruṣa</s> does not undergo a change of state; nor indeed does a change of state arise from [another] change of state. children.translated_text: ) — so it is stated. If restriction is applied to both, the faults of both positions follow. Therefore this is inappropriate. [Objection:] If [you say] 'establishment only' — no, because of non-invariability. For sometimes this knower, even when the sign such as the sun is present, is obstructed in matters like determining direction. Therefore, because of non-invariability, the restriction 'establishment only' is inappropriate. [Reply:] As for what was said — 'the word hi has no expression, because restriction is impossible' — let the restriction be 'from <s>pramāṇas</s> only.' As for the objection about contradiction with the sage's knowledge — this is no fault. Why? Because [his knowledge] is of an already-established nature. For things whose nature is being established — because of their essential dependence [on means] — have an expectation of connection with means for the accomplishment of their own nature; but the knowledge of the supreme sage, the blessed one, is of an already-established nature. Therefore the expectation of connection with means is inapplicable to it. Or alternatively, let the restriction be 'establishment only.' As for the objection about non-invariability — that is untenable. Why? Because the <s>aṅga-aṅgī</s> (component-principal) relationship of <s>sattva</s> and the others is not fixed. Because the deficiency of <s>pramāṇa</s> is possible due to the preponderance of <s>tamas</s>. Here, the principal-component relationship of <s>sattva</s> and the others is unfixed. Due to the power of place, time, and occasion, sometimes <s>sattva</s> predominates, sometimes <s>rajas</s>, sometimes <s>tamas</s>. And the predominance of <s>sattva</s>, because it is of the nature of illumination, is [itself] <s>pramāṇa</s>. When <s>tamas</s> predominates, then, <s>sattva</s> being overpowered by it, the product of that [sattva] — inference with its three-temporal members — arises. Therefore, even when the sign such as the sun is operative, [the knower] is obstructed in matters like determining direction. But otherwise, there is no loss of the [pramāṇa's] own nature. But for one who does not accept that <s>pramāṇa</s> is obstructed due to a deficiency of its accomplishment, the loss of the own nature of <s>pramāṇas</s> follows. How? For this is their own nature: the determination of the provable. Therefore it is proper — the word 'hi' is for the purpose of restriction. [Objection:] Many <s>pramāṇas</s> are accepted by the teachers; does your honor approve all of them? [Reply:]

That which is measured is the provable (<s>prameya</s>). The establishment of the provable is <s>prameyasiddhi</s>. 'Establishment' means ascertainment, understanding — such is the meaning. 'That by which [something] is measured' is the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). The suffix <s>lyuṭ</s> denotes the instrument. That [<s>pramāṇa</s>] is one only, since <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) is accepted as one; but due to limiting adjuncts, it is regarded as divided — [into] perception, inference, and so forth. Without depending on that adjunct-created division, and accepting the commonality of being a determiner of the provable, the singular designation is made — 'from <s>pramāṇa</s>.' From this, 'establishment of the provable' should be understood. How? Like rice etc. Just as rice etc. — the provable — is measured by a <s>prastha</s>-measure etc. — the <s>pramāṇa</s> — so here too the provable — <s>vyakta</s> (manifest) etc. — is determined by the <s>pramāṇa</s> — perception etc. Now, what is the purpose of the word 'hi' (indeed) here? It is for the purpose of restriction. [Objection:] If so, the word 'hi' has no [proper] expression. Because of the impossibility of restriction. For in this <s>sūtra</s>, restriction is in no way possible. Therefore it is proper that the word 'hi' has no [significative] expression. [Reply:] If [you say] 'of the provable only' — no. Because of the impossibility of anything else. For restriction applies to an entity only when deviation is possible — for example, 'This is a cow only, not a horse; this is <s>Devadatta</s> only, not <s>Yajñadatta</s>.' But there is no possibility that both the provable and the non-provable are objects of <s>pramāṇa</s>-determination, which would necessitate restricting 'of the provable only.' [Objection:] If [you say] 'from <s>pramāṇas</s> only' — no, because of the absurd consequence of contradicting the sage's knowledge. For your position is that the knowledge of the supreme sage, the blessed one, is innate and not preceded by <s>pramāṇa</s>. And innate things — both natural and derivative — [include] <s>dharma</s> and others (
The <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is accepted as threefold. || <s>ISk</s> 4c ||

children.translated_text: What then is 'threefold'? <s>Vidhā</s> means 'kind'; three kinds of it — that is 'threefold,' meaning of three types. By this, the following is stated: the one <s>sattva</s> characterized as <s>buddhi</s>, appearing as if divided due to benefit from powers — [powers] whose distinct forms are delimited by specific effects, generated by the aid of various causes — becomes expressible by words such as 'seen' [i.e., perception] etc. But it is not the case that, as for those of other systems, cognitions whose range is produced by sense-organs impinging on objects exist here — [cognitions] which, when conceptualized, would be three independent <s>pramāṇas</s>. [Objection:] How then do the powers characterized as <s>pramāṇa</s> come to have distinct forms [even though residing] in the same substance? [Reply:] Like <s>sattva</s> and the others. Just as <s>sattva</s> and the other <s>guṇas</s>, even when residing in a single substance such as sound, do not have a confusion of their forms due to the distinction of their effects such as illumination — or just as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, even when residing in a single substance, [are distinct] because they are apprehended by different faculties — or just as the powers characterized as agent, instrument, location, recipient, source, and object, even when residing in a single substance, have their own natures — delimited by specific effects — not confused — so this should be viewed. [Objection:] If [one power's] generation [requires] another power, then [it requires] another substance? [Reply:] No, because [we] do not accept [that]. For we do not accept the recklessness of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇabhaṅga</s>) without reasoning — not even under threat of the stick! But that is not the occasion [for this discussion] — let that stand for now. [Objection:] How then is it understood that <s>pramāṇa</s> is exactly threefold and not of many kinds? [Reply:]
Because it is established by all <s>pramāṇas</s>. || <s>ISk</s> 4b ||

children.translated_text:
And all those <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) are all the <s>pramāṇas</s>. The state of being established is establishedness. The establishedness of all <s>pramāṇas</s> is 'being established in all <s>pramāṇas</s>.' Establishedness means inclusion — that is the meaning. Therefore, because of being established in all <s>pramāṇas</s>. 'In that very threefold <s>pramāṇa</s>' — this is the completion of the sentence. Since all <s>pramāṇas</s> postulated by others are included in this very threefold <s>pramāṇa</s> — this much being stated, this is said: 'because of being established in all <s>pramāṇas</s>.' Alternatively, that which is established among all <s>pramāṇas</s> is 'established in all <s>pramāṇas</s>' — this is a locative compound according to the rule 'with siddha, śuṣka, pakva, and bandha,' just as one says '<s>Sāṃkāśya</s>-established' or '<s>Pāṭaliputra</s>-established.' Its nature is <s>pramāṇa</s>-establishedness; therefore, because of being established in all <s>pramāṇas</s>. 'Of which threefold <s>pramāṇa</s>?' — this is the completion of the sentence.
But by what characteristic is the threefold <s>pramāṇa</s> established?
It is said: by mutual distinction. We shall demonstrate how the others are not distinct from these three.
[Objection:] But what then is that threefold <s>pramāṇa</s>?
It is said:
Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony. // <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 4a //

children.translated_text: Perception and inference, and verbal testimony together with analogy,
<s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) and <s>abhāva</s> (absence) are the means that establish what is to be established.

Thus. Among these, perception (<s>dṛṣṭa</s>) is the determinate cognition that arises from the operation of a sense organ that has apprehended its object. Inference (<s>anumāna</s>) is the subsequent cognition regarding the other relatum, preceded by the perceptual ascertainment of one of two invariably concomitant things. Authoritative testimony (<s>āptavacana</s>) is the certainty regarding an entirely imperceptible object, mediated by a trustworthy source. This is merely the enumeration. The <s>ācārya</s> (teacher) himself will state the fundamental definition: 'Perception is the determinate cognition of each respective object,' and so forth.
[Objection:] The threefold division is untenable, because we hear of fewer or more. Some from other systems accept four <s>pramāṇas</s>, based on the statement: 'Perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony are the <s>pramāṇas</s>.' Similarly, others say six:
