children.translated_text: In accordance with previous practice, even without the actual object, from words alone there arises
cognition in manifold ways, following the pattern of one's own prior experience.

— so it is declared. Others hold these to be nine, together with <s>sambhava</s> (inclusion), <s>aitihya</s> (tradition), and <s>ceṣṭā</s> (gesture). The <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> and <s>Bauddhas</s> hold that there are only perception and inference. In this regard, how is it determined that <s>pramāṇa</s> is precisely threefold, and not fewer or more?
It is said: What then is this thing called <s>upamāna</s> (analogy)?
[Objection:] <s>Upamāna</s> is the means of establishing the unknown through similarity with what is well-known. 'Well-known' means already cognized; through similarity with that, the ascertainment of what is to be established — that is, what is unknown — is <s>upamāna</s>. The procedure of cognition is as follows: one who has not encountered a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) asks someone who has cognized a <s>gavaya</s>, for the purpose of recognizing it: 'What does a <s>gavaya</s> look like?' That person tells him: 'A <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow.' Then the inquirer, whose own form of the <s>gavaya</s> was entirely unperceived, having received the impression produced by the knowledge of similarity with the well-known object as explained by the informant, cognizes: 'Surely, a <s>gavaya</s> looks like this.' Another says: rather, <s>upamāna</s> is said to be the cognition of the connection between a name and its referent — 'this is that object, this word is its name' — which arises when one, having received the impression from knowledge of similarity with a well-known object generated by authoritative testimony, subsequently perceives that object through direct perception.
If so, then analogy and tradition are [merely] verbal testimony, since they are established through authoritative instruction. For it is by the force of authoritative instruction that the inquirer, upon encountering the unknown <s>gavaya</s>, recognizes it through the statement 'a <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow,' not from mere similarity. Therefore, analogy is not separate from verbal testimony. And as for what is set up as a separate <s>pramāṇa</s> called <s>aitihya</s> (tradition), such as 'thus indeed spoke <s>Yājñavalkya</s>' — that too, since it depends on a particular speaker, is not something different from verbal testimony.
[Objection:] No, because it depends on similarity. For if analogy were authoritative instruction, then just as in cases like 'in heaven there are <s>Apsarases</s>' or 'the northern <s>Kurus</s>' — where cognition occurs through authoritative instruction alone without invoking similarity — so too it should be here. But one who wishes to communicate about the <s>gavaya</s> employs a statement that contains similarity with something well-known, not merely a bare statement. The inquirer too cognizes from that very [similarity-laden statement], not from mere words. Therefore, a separate account of this must be given. If one thinks that it is included within verbal testimony because of the operation of words — that this object characterized by similarity with something well-known operates in the cognition of the <s>gavaya</s> not alone but accompanied by the operation of words, and therefore it is included therein — that too is untenable. Why? Because the same consequence would apply to <s>vīta</s> (affirmative) and <s>avīta</s> (negative) [forms of inference] as well. For <s>vīta</s> and <s>avīta</s> reasoning too, when employed for communicating to others, depend on the operation of words. The consequence would follow that they too are authoritative testimony. And this is undesired. Therefore, analogy is not authoritative instruction.
[Reply:] It is said: there is no non-deviation of similarity, because it serves merely as an expedient means. The cognition of the <s>gavaya</s> by the inquirer is established solely from the trustworthiness of the informant. But he, out of skill, thinking 'this matter is difficult to establish,' employs similarity with something well-known. Therefore, when the informant employs similarity as an expedient means for communicating about the <s>gavaya</s>, what arises is not something different from verbal testimony. And if the status of separate <s>pramāṇa</s> is accepted for things of this kind, then too little is said by asserting four <s>pramāṇas</s>. Why then should one not additionally enumerate hand gestures, eye-closing, and the like? Moreover, because it depends on a particular speaker: for where cognition arises from the force of the object itself, the cognizer does not look to a particular speaker [to determine] 'this has a perceived referent, this has an unperceived referent' — as in inference. But in analogy there is dependence on a particular speaker. Therefore, it is not something different from verbal testimony. And this must necessarily be understood thus: for one who thinks that cognition of the <s>gavaya</s> comes from similarity with the well-known alone, there should be cognition even from 'a <s>gavaya</s> is like a horse' — but this cannot be, because it would be false knowledge. As for what is said — that <s>upamāna</s> is the cognition of the connection between a name and its referent — that too is untenable. Why? Because of the consequence of infinite regress. For example, when among many seated persons one asks 'Which one here is <s>Devadatta</s>?', another replies: 'The one with the crown, with earrings, broad-chested, with coppery elongated eyes.' Then too there would be cognition of the connection between name and referent, and hence the consequence of a separate <s>pramāṇa</s> — thus there would be an infinite regress of <s>pramāṇas</s>. And this is undesired. Thus, analogy from another is not a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>. When one oneself perceives both a cow and a <s>gavaya</s> and discriminates 'as this one is, so is that one,' then, since that object has been ascertained by another <s>pramāṇa</s>, it does not constitute a [separate] <s>pramāṇa</s>. Therefore, it is well said that analogy and tradition are authoritative testimony, since they are established through authoritative instruction.
What else? <s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>sambhava</s> (inclusion), <s>abhāva</s> (absence), and <s>ceṣṭā</s> (gesture) are established through inference — 'are [not separate] testimony' is to be supplied. Among these, <s>arthāpatti</s> is where, having previously observed the invariable concomitance of two things, upon subsequently seeing or hearing one of them, there arises cognition of the other. From seeing: as when one perceives <s>guḍa</s> (jaggery) and cognizes sweetness, which is the object of another sense organ. From hearing: as when one hears the word '<s>guḍa</s>' and cognizes sweetness, which is not denoted by the word. There is another kind of <s>arthāpatti</s>: where, having observed the invariable concomitance of two properties, one postulates the co-occurrence of their respective opposites. This is of two kinds: deviating and non-deviating. The deviating kind is as follows: when it is said 'whatever has parts is non-eternal,' it is presumed that what is without parts is eternal. But since this is not observed in the case of <s>karma</s> (action) and the like, due to its non-universality, it does not constitute a <s>pramāṇa</s> at all. But the invariably concomitant, non-deviating kind — as when, having observed a lion and a boar meeting in a thicket, one subsequently sees the lion alone emerging with its body marked by the boar's wounds, and cognizes 'the boar has been defeated' — that is inference. How so? Because the victory and defeat of the lion and boar have an invariable connection. When, upon perceiving the victory of the lion, one cognizes the invariably concomitant defeat of the other, what else could this be other than inference? For when a cognizer has ascertained the aggregate of both relata, and upon one relatum becoming perceptually present, there arises cognition of the other relatum — that is inference. Thus <s>arthāpatti</s> is of this nature, and therefore it cannot be separate from it.
<s>Sambhava</s> (inclusion) is where, when a <s>droṇa</s> (a measure) or a <s>prastha</s> (a sub-measure) is mentioned, the presence of half-<s>droṇas</s> and so forth is ascertained. This too is just <s>arthāpatti</s> through the postulation of co-occurrence. How so? Because the word '<s>droṇa</s>' applies to a substance of the stated measure, not to less, not to more. When '<s>droṇa</s>' is stated, the presence of its sub-parts, which are eternally co-existent and denoted by other words, is ascertained — that is just <s>arthāpatti</s>. And that has been said to be inference.
<s>Abhāva</s> (absence): just as the existence of fire is cognized from the presence of smoke, so too the absence of fire is cognized from the absence of smoke — this has been stated to be <s>arthāpatti</s> through the postulation of the co-occurrence of opposites. When the postulation of co-occurrence is deviating, it is simply the absence of a <s>pramāṇa</s> — as in the case of iron balls, embers, and the like, where the absence of smoke does not entail the absence of fire. But where there is invariable concomitance, as in 'whatever is produced is non-eternal,' there it is inference. How so? Because of the applicability of co-occurrence, just as with the relation between being produced and being non-eternal.
Others, however, describe <s>abhāva</s> differently: when it is said '<s>Caitra</s> is not in the house,' the cognition arises that he is outside. In that case, the absence from the house being the cause of the cognition of presence outside is just <s>arthāpatti</s> through the postulation of the co-occurrence of opposites. How so? Just as in the case '<s>Devadatta</s> does not eat during the day yet is fat' — where, from the observation of corpulence as the counterpart of not eating, eating is ascertained at the time opposite to day, namely at night — so too here, by the force of the statement of absence from the house, the opposite is postulated with respect to its counterpart. Otherwise, if mere absence were intended, one would simply say '<s>Caitra</s> does not exist.' And <s>arthāpatti</s> is inference.
<s>Ceṣṭā</s> (gesture) is a certain bodily action such as striking the belly, making <s>añjali</s> (salutation gesture), and so forth, that indicates one's intention. It is called a <s>pramāṇa</s> because it communicates hunger and the like, which are not otherwise perceived. And that is just inference. Why? Because a bodily action that is performed as a concomitant of the desire to eat and so forth, if it conveys its concomitant, then it cannot be maintained to be separate from inference.
[Objection:] Then <s>pratibhā</s> (intuition) will be a separate <s>pramāṇa</s>.
[Reply:] It is said: What is this thing called <s>pratibhā</s>?
[Objection:] In this beginningless <s>saṃsāra</s> (cycle of existence), among gods, humans, and animals, with respect to external objects such as women and the like, which are undifferentiated [in themselves], the cognition that arises as differentiated — in the forms of a corpse, a beloved, food, and so forth — depending on the impressions of previous practice, and which serves as a factor in determining what is to be done: that is <s>pratibhā</s>. And thus it has been said:

children.translated_text: All people follow it as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge);
practical activities proceed even among animals under its influence.

For one who has practiced a certain object as pleasant and so forth, cognition arises from the mere word alone, even without that actual object. For example, when it is said 'a tiger dwells here,' even without the actual external object, sweating, trembling, and the like occur due to the force of habitual practice alone. Therefore, <s>pratibhā</s> (intuition) itself, because it serves as a factor in determining what is to be done for gods, humans, and animals, is a <s>pramāṇa</s>. And it has been said:

children.text: ucyate pratibhāyā dṛṣṭādivyatirekena rūpāntarānupapatteḥ / avacanamityanuvartate / yadi pūrvābhyāsavāsanāpekṣaḥ pratyayaḥ pratibhetyupagamyate tena tarhi asau pratyakṣamanumānamāptavacanaṃ cetyetadāpannam / kasmāt ? yato na dṛṣṭādivyatirekeṇa pratyakṣarūpaṃ kadācidapyupalabhāmahe / tasmānna tebhyo 'rthāntaraṃ pratibhā / ārṣapratyayasambhavādayuktamiti cet- syādetat, astyārṣo hi dṛṣṭādivyatirekeṇa sarvapadārtheṣu sāṃsiddhikaḥ pratyayaḥ / sa prātibho bhaviṣyatīti / etaccāpyayuktam / kasmāt ? uktatvāt / uktametat siddharūpaṃ bhagavataḥ paramarṣerjñānam / ato na pramāṇāpekṣamiti / yogināmiti cenna, anabhyupagamāt / na hi yogināmapramāṇapūrvakaṃ jñānamiti yathā tathā vakṣyāmaḥ / sa laukika iti cet na / aniścitatvāt / syādetat- asti laukikaḥ pratyayo dṛṣṭādivyatirekeṇa / tadyathā santamase vrajato drāgiti vijñānamutpadyate - asti me pratīghāti dravyaṃ purastādūrdhvamavasthitamiti / tacca naivam / kasmāt ? aniścitatvāt / na hi tatra niścaya utpadyate idaṃ taddravyamasti purato vā vyaktamastīti / na cāniścitaṃ pramāṇajñānamiṣyate / kiṃcānyat- anavasthāprasaṃgāt / yadi caivaṃjātīyato 'pi pratyayaḥ pramāṇamabhyupagamyate tenānavasthā prāpnoti / kiṃ kāraṇam ? anavasthānādvikaraṇasya / kāmakrodhalobhayaviṣādadvārako vikalpaḥ samyaṅmithyā vā yasmādaneka utpadyate tasmānna laukikaḥ pratyayaḥ pratibhā / yattu khalvidamucyate- abhyāsavāsanāpekṣāsatsvapi vyāghrādiṣu pratipattirutpadyate / iti / satyametat / sā tu mithyājñānatvātpramāṇatvena na parigṛhyate ityayamadoṣaḥ / tasmāt siddhaṃ dṛṣṭādivyatirekeṇa rūpāntaranupapatteḥ pratibhāyāḥ pṛthaganabhidhānam / tataśca sarvapramāṇasiddhatvāt trividhaṃ pramāṇamiṣṭamiti sthitametat // 4 //
children.translated_text: It is replied: because of the impossibility of a form different from perception and the rest for <s>pratibhā</s> (intuition). 'There is no statement' continues from above. If it is accepted that the cognition called <s>pratibhā</s> depends on the <s>vāsanā</s> (latent impression) from previous practice, then it falls under perception, inference, and authoritative testimony. Why? Because we never perceive a form of perception apart from the seen and so forth. Therefore, <s>pratibhā</s> is not something different from them. If one objects that it is inappropriate because of the possibility of an <s>ārṣa</s> (seer's) cognition — one might say: there exists indeed the <s>ārṣa</s> cognition, a naturally arisen cognition regarding all objects, distinct from perception and so forth; that will be <s>pratibhā</s>. But this too is inappropriate. Why? Because it has already been stated. It was stated that the knowledge of the blessed supreme <s>ṛṣi</s> (sage) is of a perfected nature; therefore it does not depend on means of valid knowledge. If one objects regarding <s>yogins</s> — no, because it is not accepted. For we shall explain in what manner the knowledge of <s>yogins</s> is not without a prior means of valid knowledge. If one says it is mundane — no, because of its indeterminate nature. One might say: there exists a mundane cognition apart from perception and the rest. For example, when one walks in total darkness, a sudden cognition arises: 'there is an obstructing substance before me, standing upright.' But this is not so. Why? Because of its indeterminate nature. For no certainty arises there: 'this particular substance exists' or 'something is definitely before me.' And indeterminate knowledge is not accepted as valid cognition. Moreover — because of the consequence of infinite regress. If cognition of this sort too is accepted as a means of valid knowledge, then infinite regress would follow. For what reason? Because of the instability of the discriminating faculty. Since manifold conceptual constructions — whether right or wrong — arise through the doors of desire, anger, greed, and despair, therefore no mundane cognition constitutes <s>pratibhā</s>. As for what is indeed said — 'even in the absence of latent impressions from prior practice, cognition arises regarding tigers and the like' — this is true. But since it is false knowledge, it is not accepted as a valid means of knowledge, and thus there is no fault. Therefore it is established that, because of the impossibility of a different form apart from perception and so forth, <s>pratibhā</s> is not separately mentioned. And since it is established through all valid means of knowledge, the position that the means of valid knowledge are threefold stands firm.
<s>Kārikā</s> 5

children.translated_text: One asks: let this be so. But because the definition has not been stated, there is no understanding of it. Therefore the definition should be stated. For the definition of perception and the rest is unsettled, due to the diversity of views. Some say: 'Knowledge born from the contact of sense organ and object, which is non-verbal, non-erring, and of the nature of determinate judgment, is <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception).' Likewise others: 'That which is produced from the contact of self, sense organ, mind, and object — that is different [from inference].' Still others: 'The cognition born when there is proper contact of <s>puruṣa</s> (the person) with the sense organs — that is <s>pratyakṣa</s>.' The <s>Vārṣagaṇa</s>s say: 'It is the functioning of hearing and the other [sense organs].' Others say: 'That which is free from conceptual construction.' Thus the definition is unsettled. Therefore there is no understanding of perception and the rest. Hence the definition should be stated. It is replied:
Ascertainment directed toward each object is <s>dṛṣṭa</s> (the perceived, i.e., perception).

children.translated_text: ) — he will also state. That which operates toward the object is <s>prativiṣaya</s> (directed toward each object). What is that? The sense organ. The ascertainment that occurs in that [sense organ] is <s>prativiṣayādhyavasāya</s> (ascertainment directed toward each object). That which falls upon the activity of sense organs that have apprehended their objects, which has the form of illumination due to the predominance of <s>sattva</s> over <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> — that is <s>dṛṣṭa</s> (the perceived). That <s>dṛṣṭa</s> means <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) — this is the meaning. This is the means of valid knowledge. The favor of the power of consciousness that accompanies it is the result. The objects to be known are sound and the rest. In the same way, the relationship of means and result should be understood in what follows also. One asks: is this result something different from the means of valid knowledge, or is it not different? How can it first be not different? One asks: why? Because it has the form of apprehension. For knowledge has the form of apprehension, and by its very arising the object is apprehended — so whence the distinction of result? It is replied: how then would the status of being an instrument obtain? One says: the status of being an instrument is due to conventional usage. For the arising of knowledge, though having the form of apprehension, is understood in the world as possessing activity when it has the appearance of the object — thus the status of being an instrument is accepted through conceptual construction, not in ultimate reality. It is replied: the result is indeed something different. Because of the difference of substrate. For the means of valid knowledge called ascertainment has its locus in <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), while the result characterized as favor has its locus in <s>puruṣa</s> (the person). And it is not fitting for things with different substrates to be identical. As for what was said — 'knowledge itself is the result because it has the form of apprehension' — that is untenable. Why? Because it is unestablished. For just as objects such as a pot cannot be determined as having this form or not having this form without knowledge, so too knowledge cannot be determined as having the form of its object or not without the cognition of <s>puruṣa</s>. And the <s>śāstra</s> (scripture) states: 'Through its conjunction, the non-conscious [intellect] appears as if conscious' (
<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 20

children.translated_text: ) — because of this statement. Therefore, without the cognition of <s>puruṣa</s>, the claim that knowledge has the form of apprehension is unestablished from the standpoint of <s>Sāṃkhya</s>. And the discussion should proceed on the basis of what is accepted by both sides. If one objects: 'It is unjustified because of the non-existence of <s>puruṣa</s>' — no, because it will be demonstrated later. In the section 'Because the aggregate serves another's purpose,' we shall establish the existence of <s>puruṣa</s>. Therefore it is established for the proponent of ascertainment as the means of valid knowledge that the result is indeed something different from the means of valid knowledge. One asks: if ascertainment is the means of valid knowledge, how does the common usage '<s>pratyakṣa</s> (perceptible) object' become meaningful? It is replied: the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' [is applied] to the object because it is measured by that [perception], and because it is caused by that. Just as a heap of rice measured by a <s>prastha</s> (measure) becomes designated by the word '<s>prastha</s>,' so an object measured by <s>pratyakṣa</s> would be designated by the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>.' One objects: no, because the same consequence would apply elsewhere too. If the word '<s>pratyakṣa</s>' applies to the object because it is measured by perception, then an object measured by inference should be called '<s>anumāna</s>' (inference), and an object measured by verbal testimony should be called '<s>śabda</s>' (word). But fire, heaven, and so forth are not designated by the word for the means of valid knowledge [that establishes them]. Therefore the analogy is faulty. Furthermore, the intuitive knowledge that arises for <s>yogins</s> dwelling in the stages of meditation, which transcends inference and scripture, should be additionally enumerated. Why? For pleasure and the like are not grasped by the activity of hearing and the other [sense organs], and the knowledge of <s>yogins</s> is supersensory. But when the matter is treated as stated here, those too are objects, and what prevents the ascertainment of them from being perceptual?

Those that pervade are <s>viṣaya</s>s (objects), namely sound and the rest. Or alternatively, those that are perceived — this is the meaning. And they are of two kinds: specific and non-specific. The specific ones have the nature of earth and the rest, and are apprehended by beings such as ourselves. The non-specific ones have the nature of <s>tanmātra</s>s (subtle elements) and are apprehended by <s>yogins</s> and those of the upward stream. And the master will state this later: 'The five <s>buddhīndriya</s>s (cognitive sense organs) have both specific and non-specific objects' (

  ucyate- karaṇāntarāṇāṃ tu sandehanivṛttyartham / evaṃ tarhi śrotrādīnāmanyatamamantaḥkaraṇaṃ cetyetad dvāradvāribhāvena catuṣṭayaṃ viṣayaṃ prati vartate / tasmādadhyavasāyagrahaṇaṃ kriyate sandeho mā bhūditi /
  āha- astvatra sandehaḥ, naikena kenacit kaścidviṣaya upādīyate / tena vayaṃ sarveṣāṃ pratyakṣatvaṃ pratipatsyāmahe /
  ucyate- sarvābhyupagame hi śāstrahāniḥ / yadi punaḥ sarveṣāmeva pramāṇatvamabhyupagamyate tena yacchāstramekameva darśanaṃ khyātireva darśanamiti taddhīyate / vakṣyati cācāryaḥ "ete pradīpakalpāḥ" (

) tadvirudyate / tasmādadhyavasāyagrahaṇaṃ kartavyam / sandeho mā bhūditi /
  āha- na, sandehamātrametad bhavati / sarvasandeheṣu caitadupatiṣṭhate- vyākhyānato viśeṣapratipattirna hi saṃdehādalakṣaṇam / tatrādhyavasāyo dṛṣṭamiti vyākhyāsyāmaḥ /
  ucyate- muktasaṃśayaṃ cendriyavṛttipratipatteḥ / syādetat, yadyatra sandehaḥ syāt / naivātra sandehaḥ prāptaḥ, kintarhi śrotrātivṛttereva grahaṇam /
  āha- kiṃ punaḥ kāraṇaṃ yena nimittāviśeṣe 'pi śrotrādivṛtterevātra grahaṇaṃ prāpnoti, nāntaḥkaraṇasyaiva pratyakṣatvam ?
  ucyate- tatra ca mukhyā śrotrādivṛttiḥ / kasmāt ? sākṣādviṣayagrahaṇasāmarthyāt / nāntaḥkaraṇam, taddvāreṇa pratipatteḥ / gauṇamukhyayośca mukhye sampratipattiḥ / tadyathā- gauranubandhyaḥ ajo 'gnīṣomīya iti vāhīko nānubadhyate /
  āha- yadīyaṃ śrotrādivṛttireva pratyakṣamityabhupeyate ka evaṃ sati doṣaḥ syāt ?
  ucyate- rāgādiviṣayaṃ yadvijñānaṃ liṅgaliṅgipūrvakam, yogināṃ ca dhyānabhūmikāsu viharatāmanumānāgamatītaṃ prātibhaṃ yadvijñānamutpadyate tadupasaṃkhyeyaṃ syāt / kutaḥ ? na hi sukhādayaḥ śrotrādivṛttibāhyāḥ, yogināṃ cātīndriyaṃ jñānamiti / yathānyāsaṃ tu kriyamāne te 'pi viṣayāḥ, teṣāṃ yo 'dhyavasāyastasya pratyakṣatvaṃ kena vāryate ?
  āha- prativiṣayagrahaṇaṃ tarhi kimartham ?
  ucyate - prativiṣayagrahaṇamasadvyudāsārtham / adhyavasāyo dṛṣṭamitīyatyucyamāne mṛgatṛṣṇikālātacakragandharvanagarādiṣu api yo 'dhyavasāyastad dṛṣṭamiti / prativiṣayagrahaṇāttu teṣāṃ vyudāsaḥ kṛto bhavati /
  āha- yadyevaṃ viṣayādhyavasāya ityeva cocyatām / kimpratigrahaṇena ?
  ucyate- pratigrahaṇaṃ sannikarṣārtham / viṣayādhyavasāyo dṛṣṭamitīyatyucyamāne viṣayamātre sampratyayaḥ syāt / pratigrahaṇe punaḥ kriyamāṇe pratirābhimukhye vartate / tena sannikṛṣṭendriyavṛttyupanipātī yo 'dhyavasāyastad dṛṣṭamityupalabhyate /
  āha- kasya punaratīndriyasannikarṣe pratyakṣatvaṃ prāpnoti ?
  ucyate- anumānasya / kasmāt ? taddhi liṅgadarśanādasannikṛṣṭe viṣaye bhavati /
  āha- anumānasyāprasaṅgaḥ / sāmānyavihitasya viśeṣavihitena bādhanāt / sāmānye hi viṣayamātre 'dhyavasāyasya pratyakṣatvaṃ vidhāya viśeṣe liṅgaliṅgipūrvake 'numānaṃ śāsti / sāmānyavihitaṃ ca viśeṣavihitena bādhyate, yathā taddhi brāhmaṇebhyo dīyatāṃ takraṃ kauṇḍinyāyeti /
  ucyate- smṛtestarhi pratyakṣatvaṃ prāpnoti / tatrāyamapavādo nābhiniviśata iti /
  āha na, smṛteḥ, pramāṇādhikārāt / pramāṇādhikāro 'yam / na ca smṛtyā kiṃcit pramīyate / smṛteḥ pramite 'rthe prādurbhāvāt /
  ucyate- saṃśayasya tarhi prāpnoti /
  na saṃśayasya, adhyavasāyagrahaṇāt / adhyavasāyo hi dṛṣṭamityucyate / na ca saṃśayo 'dhyavasāyo 'niścitatvāt /
  ucyate- indriyāntarākūtaviṣaye tu prasaṅgaḥ / evaṃ tarhīndriyārthasannikṛṣṭendriyavṛttyupanipātīti doṣo na bhavati /
  āha- rāgādyupasaṃkhyānam / yadi sannikṛṣṭendriyavṛttyupanipātī yo 'dhyavasāyastad dṛṣṭamityabhyupeyate, tena rāgādiviṣayaṃ vijñānamatīndriyatvātpratyakṣaṃ na prāpnoti / tasyopasaṃkhyānam kartavyam /
  ucyate- na tarhīdaṃ pratigrahaṇamindriyaviśeṣaṇaṃ viṣayaṃ viṣayaṃ prati yo vartate tasmin yo 'dhyavasāyastad dṛṣṭamiti / kintarhi- adhyavasāyaviśeṣaṇaṃ viṣayaṃ viṣayaṃ prati yo 'dhyavasāya iti /
  āha- adhyavasāyaviśeṣaṇamiti cet, śabdādyupasaṃkhyānam / śabdādīnāmeva tena pratyakṣatvaṃ prāpnoti / teṣāmupasaṃkhyānaṃ kartavyaṃ prāpnoti / kiṃ kāraṇam ? antaḥkaraṇasya taiḥ sannikarṣānupapatteḥ / pratigrahaṇaṃ sannikarṣārthamiti pūrvamatisṛṣṭaṃ bhavatā / taccedānīmantaḥkaraṇaviśeṣaṇam / na cāntaḥkaraṇasya śabdādibhiḥ sannikarṣa upapadyate, śrotrādivaiyarthyaprasaṅgāt / dvāridvārabhāvasyāpaghātaprasaṅgācca / tasmātsudūramapi gatvā pratigrahaṇaṃ pratyākhyānānna mucyate / rāgādyupasaṃkhyānādveti /
  ucyate- astu tarhīndriyāṇāṃ prati viṣayagrahaṇaṃ viśeṣaṇam / yattūktaṃ rāgādīnāmupasaṃkhyānaṃ kartavyamiti tatra brūmaḥ / ekaśeṣanirdeśāt siddham / evaṃ tarhi prativiṣayādhyavasāyaśca prativiṣayādhyavasāyaśca prativiṣayādhyavasāya iti sarūpāṇāmekaśeṣaḥ kariṣyate / tatraikena bahiraṅgasyaindriyasya pratyakṣasya parigrahaḥ / dvitīyenāntaraṅgasya prātibhasyeti rāgādiviṣayaṃ yogināṃ ca yadvijñānaṃ tat saṃgṛhītaṃ bhavatīti vyākhyātaṃ pratyakṣam /

) that is contradicted. Therefore, the term 'ascertainment' (<s>adhyavasāya</s>) should be adopted. [The objection] 'there should be no doubt' [is addressed as follows]:
He says: No — this is merely a doubt. And in all doubts this [principle] applies: 'From explanation, the apprehension of the specific [meaning arises]; for from doubt alone, [a definition] is not faulty.' Therefore we shall explain that 'ascertainment is perception' (<s>dṛṣṭa</s>).
It is said: [It must be] free from doubt, because of the apprehension of sense-organ activity. [The objection]: This would [hold] if there were doubt here. But doubt has not arisen here; rather, it is the apprehension of the activity of the ear and other [sense-organs] alone.
He says: What then is the reason that, even though there is no distinction of cause, only the activity of the ear and other [sense-organs] yields apprehension here, and not the directness of the internal organ (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) itself?
It is said: There, the activity of the ear and other [sense-organs] is primary. Why? Because of their capacity to apprehend objects directly. Not the internal organ, since apprehension [of objects] is through its mediation [by the senses]. And between the secondary and the primary, the understanding falls on the primary. For example: 'A cow is the <s>anubandhya</s> [victim]; a goat is the <s>Agnīṣomīya</s> [offering]' — [here] a <s>Vāhīka</s> [man] is not bound [as the victim, even though he is also an animal].
He says: If this activity of the ear and other [sense-organs] alone is accepted as perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), what fault would there be?
It is said: The cognition whose object is passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the like, preceded by the mark and the marked, and the intuitive (<s>prātibha</s>) cognition that arises for <s>yogins</s> abiding in the stages of meditation — transcending inference and scripture — would have to be additionally enumerated. Why? Because pleasures and the like are not external to the activity of the ear and other [senses], and the knowledge of <s>yogins</s> is suprasensory. But when [the definition] is formulated as stated, those objects too [are included], and the perception-nature of their ascertainment — by what is it prevented?
He says: Then what is the purpose of the term 'each object' (<s>prativiṣaya</s>)?
It is said: The specification 'each object' is for the exclusion of the unreal. If one merely says 'ascertainment is perception,' then even the ascertainment regarding mirages, fire-wheels, cities of the <s>Gandharvas</s>, and the like would be perception. But through the specification 'each object,' the exclusion of those is accomplished.
He says: If so, let it simply be said 'ascertainment of an object' (<s>viṣayādhyavasāya</s>). What is the need for the prefix '<s>prati</s>'?
It is said: The prefix '<s>prati</s>' is for the purpose of [indicating] contact. If one merely says 'ascertainment of an object is perception,' there would be conviction regarding any object whatsoever. But when the prefix '<s>prati</s>' is employed, '<s>prati</s>' functions in the sense of 'facing toward.' Therefore, the ascertainment that arises from the occurrence of proximate sense-organ activity directed toward each object — that is perceived as perception.
He says: But for whom does perception arise in suprasensory contact?
It is said: For inference. Why? Because that [inference] arises regarding an object not in proximity, from the observation of a mark (<s>liṅga</s>).
He says: There is no occasion for [the objection about] inference. Because the specific rule overrides the general rule. For having established in the general [case] that the ascertainment of any object whatsoever is perception, [the teacher] teaches in the specific [case] that what is preceded by mark and the marked is inference. And the general rule is overridden by the specific rule — just as 'Let that buttermilk be given to the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>; [but specifically] to <s>Kauṇḍinya</s>.'
It is said: Then memory (<s>smṛti</s>) would [also] attain the status of perception. For this exception does not attach to it.
He says: No, not memory, because this is the domain of the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). This is the domain of <s>pramāṇas</s>. And nothing is cognized by memory [as a <s>pramāṇa</s>], since memory arises with regard to an object already cognized.
It is said: Then it would apply to doubt.
Not to doubt, because of the term 'ascertainment.' For it is said that 'ascertainment is perception.' And doubt is not ascertainment, because of its unsettled nature.
It is said: But there is the implication regarding the object of the intention of another sense-organ. If so, then [the definition] 'arising from the occurrence of proximate sense-organ activity directed toward the sense-object' would not be faulty.
He says: The additional enumeration of passion (<s>rāga</s>) and the like [is needed]. If it is accepted that ascertainment arising from the occurrence of proximate sense-organ activity is perception, then cognition whose object is passion and the like — being suprasensory — would not attain the status of perception. Its additional enumeration must be made.
It is said: Then this prefix '<s>prati</s>' does not qualify the sense-organ — [meaning] 'the ascertainment that operates toward each object' — but rather qualifies the ascertainment — 'the ascertainment toward each object [that is] ascertainment.'
He says: If it qualifies ascertainment, then the additional enumeration of sound and the like [is needed]. For then only sound and the like would attain the status of perception. Their additional enumeration would have to be made. What is the reason? Because there is no possibility of contact of the internal organ with those [sense objects]. The prefix '<s>prati</s>' was previously conceded by you to be for the purpose of contact. And now that [qualifies] the internal organ. But contact of the internal organ with sound and the like is not possible, because there would be the implication of the uselessness of the ear and other [sense-organs]. And because there would be the destruction of the door-and-doorkeeper relationship. Therefore, even having gone very far afield, the prefix '<s>prati</s>' cannot escape refutation. [This is] because of the additional enumeration of passion and the like.
It is said: Then let the specification 'each object' qualify the sense-organs. As for what was said — that the additional enumeration of passion and the like must be made — to that we say: it is established from the single-remainder statement (<s>ekaśeṣa</s>). In that case, 'ascertainment of each object' and 'ascertainment of each object' and 'ascertainment of each object' — a single-remainder (<s>ekaśeṣa</s>) of identical forms will be made. Of these, by the first, the external, sense-based perception is encompassed; by the second, the internal, intuitive [perception] — thus the cognition whose object is passion and the like, and the knowledge of <s>yogins</s>, is included. Thus perception has been explained.
He says: Now inference should be stated.
It is said:

It is replied: because of the absence of that [common feature], there is no application [of the term] to the other [means of knowledge]. In the case of other means of valid knowledge, there is no common ground. How so? That by which one infers is <s>anumāna</s> (inference). But no one infers by means of fire and the like — therefore there is no designation by the same word. One asks: for what purpose is the word '<s>adhyavasāya</s>' (ascertainment) included? It is replied: for the purpose of preventing over-extension. If it were merely said '<s>prativiṣayaṃ dṛṣṭam</s>' (perception is what is directed toward each object), then whatever operates toward an object — whether as a helper or as an obstructor — all of that would be entailed as perception. But when the word '<s>adhyavasāya</s>' is included, there is no fault. One objects: no, because of the context of means of valid knowledge. The word '<s>adhyavasāya</s>' has no purpose. Why? Because this is the context of means of valid knowledge. And nothing that operates toward an object without ascertainment serves as a measure of anything. Therefore we shall understand ascertainment by implication alone. Just as when it is said in the context of study, 'Let the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>s be brought,' only those who are studying are brought. It is replied: but it is for removing the doubt regarding other instruments. In that case, the four — one or another of hearing and the other [sense organs] together with the inner organ — operate toward the object in the relation of door and doorkeeper. Therefore the word '<s>adhyavasāya</s>' is included so that there may be no doubt. One objects: let there be doubt here — no single entity alone apprehends any object. Therefore we shall understand all of them as constituting perception. It is replied: if all were accepted [as means of knowledge], there would be the loss of the [Sāṃkhya] doctrine. If the status of being a means of valid knowledge were accepted for all of them, then the doctrine that states 'only one is the seeing, the seeing alone is the seeing' would be destroyed. Inference (<s>anumāna</s>) is declared to be threefold.

anumānaṃ triprakāramācāryairākhyātam / pūrvavat, śeṣavat, sāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ ca / tatra pūrvamiti kāraṇamucyate / yasya hi yat kāraṇaṃ sa loke tatpūrvaka ityucyate / yathā tantupūrvakaḥ paṭo, devadattapūrvako yajñadatta iti / pūrvamasyāstīti pūrvavat / śeṣa iti vikāranāma, śiṣyata iti kṛtvā / tathā coktam- na śeṣo 'gneranyasya jātamityasti / nāpatyamanyena jātaṃ sambhavatītyarthaḥ / śeṣo 'syāstīti śeṣavat /
  tatra pūrvavat yadā kāraṇamabhyuditaṃ bhaviṣayattvaṃ kāryasya pratipadyate / tadyathā meghodaye bhaviṣyattvaṃ vṛṣṭeḥ /
  āha- naitadastyudāharaṇamanekāntāt / na hi meghodayo 'vaśyaṃ vṛṣṭeḥ kāraṇaṃ bhavati, vāyvādinimittapratibandhasambhavāt /
  ucyate- yadi tarhi kāraṇaśaktiṃ sahakāriśaktyantarānugṛhītāmapratiyoginīṃ dṛṣṭvā kāryasya vyaktiṃ pratipadyate / tadyathā yadā lauhadaṇḍādisādhanasampanne vyāpāravatā kumbhakāreṇādhiṣṭhitāṃ mṛdamupalabhya ghaṭasya, tadā pūrvavat /
  śeṣavat- yadā kāryanirvṛtiṃ dṛṣṭvā kāraṇasadbhāvaṃ pratipadyate / tadyathā kumārakaṃ dṛṣṭvā dvayasamāpattim /
  āha- naitadastyudāharaṇam / anekāntāt / na hi dvayasamāpattipūrvaka eva prāṇabhṛtāṃ prādurbhāvo, droṇādīnāmanyathotpattiviśeṣaśravaṇāt /
  ucyate- yadā tarhi prabhānuraṃjitamantarikṣaṃ dṛṣṭvā candrārkayorudayaṃ pratipadyate tadā śeṣavat /
  āha- etadapi nāstyudāharaṇam / anekāntāt / na hi prabhānurāgo 'ntarikṣe candrārkanimitta eva bhavati / kintarhi digdāhādinimitto 'pi /
  ucyate - yadā tu nadīpūraṃ dṛṣṭvā vṛṣṭiṃ pratipadyate tadā śeṣavat /
  etadapi nāstyudāharaṇam / anekāntāt / nadīpūrasya hi nimittamanekavidhaṃ bhavatīti himilayanasetubhaṃgagajakrīḍādi / tasmādayuktametat /
  ucyate yadā tarhi parṇaṃ dṛṣṭvā śālūkaṃ pratipadyate, aṃkuraṃ vā dṛṣṭvā bījamiti tadā śeṣavat /
  athavā punarastu pūrvakamevodāharaṇam / yattūktaṃ- anekāntāditi atra brūmaḥ- vītāvītasāmarthyāt / vītāvītābhyāṃ hetubhūtābhyāmabhipretārthasiddhiriti vakṣyāmaḥ / prasaṃgidharmāntaranivṛttimukhena cāvītaprayogaḥ / tatra yadā prasaṃgināṃ himavilayanādīnāṃ deśakālaliṅgaiḥ pratiṣedhaḥ kriyate tadā muktasaṃśayaṃ pratipattirbhavati / deśastāvattad yathā- dakṣiṇāpathe nāsti himavilayanasambhavaḥ / kālato yathā prāvṛṭkāle / liṅgato 'pi yasmānmudgagavedhukaśyāmākakāṣṭhasūtraśakṛtprabhṛtīnāmanupalambhastathoṣmakaluṣatvādīnāmupalambhaḥ / tasmāt pariśeṣato medhyā evāpa iti / tasmānnānekāntaḥ / evaṃ kṛtvā pūrvāṇyapyudāharaṇāni upapannāni bhavanti / deśādivicārasāmarthyāt /
  sāmānyatodṛṣṭaṃ nāma yatraikadārthayoravyabhicāramupalabhya deśāntare kālāntare ca tajjātīyayoravyabhicāraṃ pratipadyate / tadyathā kvaciddhūmāgnisambandhaṃ dṛṣṭvā kvaciddhūmāntareṇāgnyantarasyāstitvaṃ pratipadyate /
  āha- naitadastyudāharaṇam / aviśeṣaprasaṅgāt / sarvatraiva hyanumāne kvacidarthayoravyabhicāramupalabhyānyatra tajjātīyayorarthayoravyabhicāraṃ pratipadyate / tadyathā kvacit sādhanavato mṛtpiṇḍād ghaṭaniṣpattimupalabhyānyatra sādhanavataḥ piṇḍāntarādghaṭāntaraniṣpattiṃ pratipadyate, tathaikatra nadīpūrād vṛṣṭimupalabhyānyatra nadīpūrāntarādvṛṣṭyantaramavasīyate / tathā ca sati trayāṇāmaviśeṣaprasaṃgaḥ /
  ucyate- yadā tarhi sahabhuvāmekasya viśiṣṭaguṇamupalabhya śeṣāṇāmapi tadvattvamanumīyate tadā sāmānyatodṛṣṭam / tadyathā vṛkṣādekasya phalasya pākamupalabhya śeṣāṇāṃ vṛkṣāntarāṇāṃ ca pāko 'numīyate / āha- etadapi nāstyudāharaṇam / anekātantāt / na hi sarveṣāṃ phalānāṃ tulyakālaṃ pāko bhavati / pūrvāparakālaniṣpannatvāt, nimittabhedācca / ucyate- yadā tarhi samudrādekamudababinduṃ prāśya śeṣasya lavaṇatānumīate / sthālyāṃ vaikaṃ pulākamupalabhya śeṣāṇāṃ pāko 'numīyate tadā sāmānyatodṛṣṭam / āha- naitadastyudāharaṇam / akṛtsnasaṅgrahāt / vakṣyatyayamupariṣṭādācāryaḥ "sāmānyatastu dṛṣṭādatīndriyāṇāṃ pratītiranumānāditi" (

In this way, when the means of valid knowledge is so conceived, through the apprehension of the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion in causes, effects, and their aggregates, there would be comprehension of <s>tanmātra</s>s (subtle elements), <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego-principle), and <s>pradhāna</s> (primal matter). But not of <s>puruṣa</s> (the person), because objects of that class are not apprehended. It is replied: when, through observing the invariable concomitance of one property with another in a certain case, one apprehends a property of a different class that has never been directly perceived, based on the observation of the first property — then that is <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (inference based on general observation). For example, having observed that <s>Devadatta</s>'s going results in reaching another place, one infers going for the stars — which have never been directly seen [to move] — from their reaching another place. Similarly, having observed that the height of palaces and so forth is preceded by growth, one infers growth for herbs and trees from observing their height. One objects: this is not a valid example either, because there is no distinction from the previous [type]. You have already stated that the comprehension of cause from effect is of the <s>śeṣavat</s> type. Here too, the comprehension of the cause characterized as motion from the effect characterized as reaching another place [is the same]. Therefore there would be the consequence of no difference between <s>śeṣavat</s> and <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>. It is replied: no, because there is no fixed rule. For our position is that where a cause is invariably comprehended through an effect, that is <s>śeṣavat</s>. But that fixed rule does not obtain in <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>. Why? Because of the generality of being an aggregate. Proof based on the generality of serving another's purpose is also observed. As it is said: 'Due to non-deviation, specific [instances] that are understood become demonstrators.' It is also observed between the general [features] of what is to be proved and the means of proof, as in: 'Sound is impermanent, because it is produced.' In that case, there would be the abandonment of the thesis of the one who asserts a fixed rule. By this, the fallacious reasons — the unestablished, the contradictory, and the inconclusive — are refuted. For since they cause doubt, error, and ignorance, they are non-demonstrative. Thus inference has been explained. One asks: what is the definition of authoritative testimony? It is replied:

Inference is stated by the <s>ācāryas</s> (teachers) to be of three kinds: <s>pūrvavat</s> (based on the antecedent), <s>śeṣavat</s> (based on the remainder), and <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (based on general observation). Among these, '<s>pūrva</s>' (antecedent) means 'cause.' For that which has something as its cause is called in the world 'preceded by that.' Just as cloth is preceded by threads, and <s>Yajñadatta</s> is preceded by <s>Devadatta</s>. 'It has an antecedent' — thus '<s>pūrvavat</s>.' '<s>Śeṣa</s>' (remainder) is a name for a modification (<s>vikāra</s>), because it 'remains' (<s>śiṣyate</s>). And thus it is said: 'The remainder of fire is not produced by another' — meaning, offspring is not produced by another. 'It has a remainder' — thus '<s>śeṣavat</s>.'
Among these, <s>pūrvavat</s> is when, upon observing the cause, one apprehends the future existence of the effect. For example, upon the rising of clouds, one apprehends the future existence of rain.
He says: This is not a [valid] example, because of inconclusiveness. For the rising of clouds is not necessarily the cause of rain, since there is the possibility of obstruction by wind and other intervening causes.
It is said: Then when, having observed the power of the cause accompanied by the power of auxiliary [causes], unobstructed, one apprehends the production of the effect — for example, when one observes clay presided over by an active potter equipped with instruments such as an iron rod and the like, and [apprehends] a pot — then [that is] <s>pūrvavat</s>.
<s>Śeṣavat</s>: when, having seen the production of an effect, one apprehends the existence of the cause. For example, having seen a young boy, one [infers] the union of a couple.
He says: This is not a [valid] example, because of inconclusiveness. For the birth of living beings is not exclusively preceded by the union of a couple, since we hear of the special origins of <s>Droṇa</s> and others being otherwise.
It is said: Then when, having seen the sky illuminated by radiance, one apprehends the rising of the moon or sun — then [that is] <s>śeṣavat</s>.
He says: This too is not a [valid] example, because of inconclusiveness. For the redness of the sky is not caused solely by the moon and sun; rather, it can be caused by the burning of the horizons and the like.
It is said: Then when, having seen the flooding of a river, one apprehends rain — then [that is] <s>śeṣavat</s>.
This too is not a [valid] example, because of inconclusiveness. For the cause of a river's flooding is of many kinds — the melting of [Himalayan] snow, the breaking of a dam, the sport of elephants, and so forth. Therefore this is unjustified.
It is said: Then when, having seen a leaf, one apprehends a lotus root (<s>śālūka</s>), or having seen a sprout, one [apprehends] a seed — then [that is] <s>śeṣavat</s>.
Alternatively, let the previous example stand. As for what was said — 'because of inconclusiveness' — to that we say: because of the power of the refuted and unrefuted (<s>vītāvīta</s>). We shall explain that the establishment of the intended meaning is through two reasons — the refuted and the unrefuted. And the employment of the unrefuted is through the negation of alternative properties. When the alternative [explanations] such as the melting of snow and the like are negated through the marks of place, time, and indication, then the apprehension becomes free from doubt. As for place: in the southern region (<s>Dakṣiṇāpatha</s>), there is no possibility of snow-melting. As for time: during the rainy season. As for indication: because [there is] non-observation of moss, <s>Gavedhuka</s> grass, <s>Śyāmāka</s> grain, wood, threads, dung, and the like, and the observation of warmth, turbidity, and the like. Therefore, by elimination, the waters are indeed from rain. Therefore there is no inconclusiveness. Having established [it] in this way, the previous examples too become valid, through the power of the investigation of place and the like.
<s>Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (inference by general observation) is that where, having observed the invariable concomitance of two things in one place, one apprehends their invariable concomitance in another place and time among things of the same class. For example, having observed the connection of smoke and fire in one place, one apprehends the existence of another fire from another [instance of] smoke elsewhere.
He says: This is not a [valid] example, because of the implication of non-distinction. For in every inference, having observed the invariable concomitance of two things in one place, one apprehends the invariable concomitance of things of the same class elsewhere. For example, having observed the production of a pot from a lump of clay that possesses the means [of production] in one place, one apprehends the production of another pot from another lump elsewhere. Similarly, having observed rain from a river-flood in one place, one infers another rain from another river-flood. And if so, there would be the implication of non-distinction among the three [types of inference].
It is said: Then when, having observed a distinctive quality of one among co-existents, one infers the same quality for the rest — then [that is] <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>. For example, having observed the ripening of one fruit on a tree, one infers the ripening of the remaining [fruits] and of other trees.
He says: This too is not a [valid] example, because of inconclusiveness. For not all fruits ripen at the same time, since they are produced at earlier and later times, and because of the difference of causes.
It is said: Then when, having tasted a single drop of water from the ocean, one infers the saltiness of the rest; or having found a single grain of rice [partially cooked] in a pot, one infers the cooking of the rest — then [that is] <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s>.
He says: This is not a [valid] example, because of incomplete coverage. For the <s>ācārya</s> will state further on: 'From that which is seen in general, the understanding of suprasensory [objects] is through inference' (
<s>Āptaśruti</s> (trustworthy revelation) is <s>āptavacana</s> (authoritative testimony). (<s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 5)

āptā nāma rāgādiviyuktasyāgṛhyamāṇakāraṇaparārthāḥ vyāhṛtiḥ / śravaṇaṃ śrutiḥ / āptā cāsau śrutirāptaśrutiḥ / athavā āptāsyāstītyāptaḥ / akāro matvarthīyaḥ / tadyathā tundo ghaṭa iti / āptebhyaḥ śrutirāptaśrutiḥ / āptaśrutiścāptaśrutiḥ / sarūpāṇimityekaśeṣaḥ / tatra pūrveṇāptaśrutigrahanena pratipādayati apuruṣabuddhipūrvaka āmnāyaḥ, svatantraḥ puruṣaniḥśreyasārthaṃ pravartamāno niḥsaṃśayaṃ pramāṇamiti / dvitīyena manvādinibandhanānāṃ ca smṛtīnāṃ vedāṅgatarketihāsapurāṇānāṃ śiṣṭānāṃ nānāśilpābhiyuktānāṃ cāduṣṭamanasāṃ yadvacastatpramāṇamityetasiddhaṃ bhavati / tuśabdo 'vadhāraṇārthaḥ / āptaśrutirevāptavacanaṃ na śabdamātram /
  evaṃ sati yaduktaṃ tantrāntarīyaiḥ śiṃśapādiśabdānāṃ nirvikalpamanumāne 'ntarbhāvastrilakṣaṇatvāditi tadayatnataḥ pratikṣiptaṃ bhavatīti vyākhyātāni pramāṇāni / etaiḥ pūrvoktaṃ prameyaṃ yathāsvaṃ pratipattavyamiti // 5 //
children.translated_text: <s>Āpta</s> (trustworthy) means: an utterance of one who is free from passion and the like, whose motive is not discernible, and which serves another's purpose. Hearing is <s>śruti</s> (revelation). And it is <s>āpta</s> (trustworthy) and <s>śruti</s> (what is heard), hence <s>āptaśruti</s>. Or alternatively, one who possesses what is trustworthy is <s>āpta</s> — the suffix 'a' has the possessive sense, as in '<s>tuṇḍa</s>' meaning 'one having a belly (i.e., a pot).' <s>Śruti</s> from the <s>āpta</s>s (trustworthy ones) is <s>āptaśruti</s>. And <s>āptaśruti</s> is indeed <s>āptaśruti</s> — being of the same form, there is retention of one [compound]. Therein, by the first [compound] '<s>āptaśruti</s>,' it is demonstrated that the sacred tradition (<s>āmnāya</s>) — which is not preceded by a person's intellect, which is independent, and which operates for the supreme good of persons — is unquestionably a means of valid knowledge. By the second [compound], it is established that the speech of those with uncorrupted minds — including the <s>smṛti</s>s (remembered traditions) composed by <s>Manu</s> and others, the <s>Vedāṅga</s>s, logic, <s>itihāsa</s>s (histories), <s>Purāṇa</s>s, the learned, and those skilled in various crafts — is a means of valid knowledge. The word 'tu' serves the purpose of restriction: <s>āptaśruti</s> alone is <s>āptavacana</s> (authoritative testimony), not mere word. This being so, what was stated by proponents of other systems — that non-conceptual [cognition of] words like '<s>śiṃśapā</s>' (a type of tree) and the like falls within inference because of having the three characteristics — is effortlessly refuted. Thus the means of valid knowledge have been explained. The objects to be known mentioned earlier should be understood through these [means], each in its appropriate way.
<s>Kārikā</s> 6–7

āha- astu tāvadakṣarānnikarṣabhājāmarthānāṃ pratyakṣeṇopalabdhiḥ / asannikarṣabhājāmapi copalabdhasambandhānāmanumānena / ye tvatīndriyā bhāvāsteṣāmubhayavailakṣaṇyānnāsti pratyakṣānumānābhyāmupalabdhiḥ / āgamikatve sarvavādasiddhiprasaṃgaḥ / ityato 'tyantamevāgrahaṇaṃ prāptam / tatra yaduktametāvadbhiḥ pramāṇaiḥ sakalapadārthāvabodha iti etadayuktam /
  ucyate- syādetadevaṃ yadyekarūpamevānumānamadhītaṃ syāt, kiṃ tarhi trividham / tatra satyameva pūrvavaccheṣavatī prāganubhūtasambandhaviṣayaphale iti kṛtvā na tābhyāmaśeṣapadārthādhigamo 'bhyupagamyate /
children.translated_text: One objects: let there be apprehension through perception of those objects that are within the range of the senses. And let there be [apprehension] through inference of those not within range but whose connection has been previously observed. But as for those entities that are supersensory — because of their dissimilarity to both — there is no apprehension through perception or inference. If they were to be established through scripture, there would be the consequence that all doctrines would be established. Therefore complete non-apprehension would follow. Hence what was said — that there is comprehension of all objects through this many means of valid knowledge — is unjustified. It is replied: this would be so if inference were acknowledged to be of only one form. But in fact it is of three kinds. Among these, it is true that the <s>pūrvavat</s> and <s>śeṣavat</s> types have as their result [cognition of] objects whose connection has been previously experienced — therefore it is not accepted that all objects without exception are comprehended through these two.
But through <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> (inference based on general observation), the establishment of supersensory [objects] is through inference. (<s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 6a)

  tasya prayogamātrabhedāddvaividhyam / vītaḥ avīta iti / tayorlakṣaṇamāmananti-

children.translated_text: When the reason is employed in its own form for establishing the thing to be proved,
that is <s>vīta</s> (affirmative); the other, through the exclusion of alternatives, is defined as the remainder.

This <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> inference — through it the comprehension of supersensory objects should be understood. How? Just as, having observed the co-presence of being produced and being impermanent in a pot, one infers impermanence elsewhere in sound and the like from observing their being produced — similarly, since fragments and the like are established as having the same class-nature as sandalwood and the like and thus as being preceded by those [causes]; since the causal complex, having the same class-nature as pleasure and the like, is established as preceded by those; and since beds and the like, being aggregates, are established as serving another's purpose — so too the causal complex, being an aggregate, is established as serving another's purpose. Thus everything that is desired is encompassed. But for those who hold that <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> is the same as <s>śeṣavat</s>, since it demonstrates through the channel of effects, there would be the consequence of non-apprehension of <s>puruṣa</s>. If one objects that there is no fault because of the figurative attribution of activity as an effect — one might say that even though <s>puruṣa</s> has no effect, the apprehension of <s>puruṣa</s>, <s>avyakta</s> (the unmanifest), <s>mahat</s> (the great principle), <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), and the <s>viśeṣa</s>s (specific elements) is through their respective activities at the present time. Why? Because the power of their activity, figuratively spoken of as an effect, connects itself to them. But this is unjustified. Why? Because a different reason is stated [by the teacher]. If the apprehension of <s>puruṣa</s> through activity were easily established, the master would not have stated the purposefulness of aggregates as the reason. And that [purposefulness] is not a form of activity — therefore one must necessarily accept that <s>śeṣavat</s> and <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> are different things. Therefore it is established: the comprehension of supersensory objects is through <s>sāmānyatodṛṣṭa</s> [inference]. Its twofold nature is due solely to a difference in the manner of application: <s>vīta</s> (affirmative) and <s>avīta</s> (negative). They state the definition of these two:

For the nature of <s>sādhana</s> (the means of proof) is twofold: general and specific. Of these, the general is the essential nature of the object that coexists with the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) and is properly relied upon as the cause of its apprehension. The specific, on the other hand, includes measure, positive correlation, the fact that composites serve another's purpose, and so forth. Here, when the <s>hetu</s> (reason), with reference to the opponent's thesis, is adduced in its true nature for establishing the <s>sādhya</s>, it is called <s>vīta</s> (affirmative inference). But when, having set aside through exclusion the <s>prasaṅgins</s> (incidentally connected alternatives) that are other than one's own <s>sādhya</s>, it is adduced for establishing the <s>sādhya</s> by the method of residue, then it is called <s>avīta</s> (negative inference). For example: if the origination of the world is not possible from atoms, <s>puruṣa</s>, <s>Īśvara</s> (God), <s>karma</s>, fate, time, inherent nature, or chance, then by residue it must be from <s>pradhāna</s> (primal matter) — this is the <s>avīta</s> type. Now, when the <s>vīta</s> type of reason is to be communicated by a speaker who places in the mind of the listener a cognition having the same form as the cognition established in his own mind, it is first brought into the form of a statement — since it is impossible to transfer meaning to another's mind without a verbal statement, the component statement is devised.
The components of that [statement] are: desire to know, doubt, purpose, possibility of attainment, and removal of doubt — these constitute the limbs of exposition. <s>Pratijñā</s> (thesis), <s>hetu</s> (reason), <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example), <s>upasaṃhāra</s> (application), and <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion) are the limbs for conveying [knowledge] to another.
Of these, the desire to know is <s>jijñāsā</s> (curiosity). Someone approaches another and says: "I wish to know <s>puruṣa</s> (the self). Does it exist or not?" When asked "What is the source of your doubt?", he replies: "Because what is not perceived has been seen in both ways." Here, what is not perceived has been seen in two ways: as existent and as non-existent. The existent [but imperceptible includes] the far side of the disk of the sun and moon, and so forth; the non-existent [includes] the horn of a hare, and so forth. And this self too is not perceived. Hence the doubt: does it exist or not? When asked "What is the purpose of this inquiry?", he explains: the attainment of the truth of the <s>śāstra</s> (authoritative teaching), and from that, the attainment of <s>mokṣa</s> (liberation). How so? If this self exists, then from the knowledge of its being not a <s>prakṛti</s> (primal cause), its indifference, its all-pervasiveness, and so forth — which is the opposite of the delusion of non-selfhood — the attainment of <s>apavarga</s> (final release) is inevitable, as has been stated: "From the knowledge of the manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower, <s>mokṣa</s> is attained" — thus the <s>śāstra</s> becomes meaningful. But if it is determined that [the self] does not exist, then by <s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s> (inference from general observation), other entities likewise do not exist; having abandoned the sage's doctrine as largely deceptive, through the removal of the view that grasps at a self, one attains the supreme <s>nirvāṇa</s> (extinction), characterized by the cessation of the afflictions of the three realms, which is the supramundane, unsupported, void object of meditation. And this matter can be determined, since the three <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) are available. This being established, the ascertainment of the <s>sādhya</s> after removing the doubt is the <s>pratijñā</s> (thesis). The ascertainment of the <s>sādhya</s> — namely, "<s>puruṣa</s> exists" — that is the <s>pratijñā</s>.
The concise statement of the <s>sādhana</s> (means of proof) is the <s>hetu</s> (reason). That by which [the <s>sādhya</s>] is proved is the <s>sādhana</s>, i.e., the <s>liṅga</s> (inferential mark). <s>Samāsa</s> means abbreviation. The concise statement of the <s>sādhana</s> is the <s>sādhana-samāsa-vacana</s>. The word <s>sādhana</s> is used to exclude its semblances, for those are not [true] <s>sādhana</s>, since they cause doubt and error. The word <s>samāsa</s> is used to allow scope for the other components. The mere indication of the <s>liṅga</s> is the <s>hetu</s>. But its elaboration, characterized by coexistence with the <s>sādhya</s>, constitutes the other components — this is what is meant.
Here, the illustration, the exemplification, is the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example). The demonstration that the <s>sādhana</s> coexists with the <s>sādhya</s> — that is the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>. For instance: "It is observed that things which act in combination serve another's purpose, such as beds, seats, chariots, and shelters." As for the negative [example], since in the <s>avīta</s> type the nature consists in the exclusion of the properties of other incidentally connected [alternatives], it is included within that, and for that purpose the <s>vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta</s> (example by dissimilarity) is stated.
The subsumption of the <s>sādhya</s> and the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> under a single operation is the <s>upanaya</s> (application). The bringing together under a single operation of the <s>sādhya</s>, characterized by the fact that the eye and other [organs] serve another's purpose, and of the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, namely beds and the like. Since the <s>sādhya</s> and the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> are different things, a single operation does not directly apply. Therefore, since there is no direct exemplification of the one by the other, the single operation is figuratively applied through a common property: "As this is, so is that." Just as beds and the like, being composite, serve another's purpose, so too the eye and other [organs] must serve another's purpose. That other [which they serve] is <s>puruṣa</s>.
On account of that [foregoing argumentation], the repetition of the <s>pratijñā</s> is the <s>nigamana</s> (conclusion). The restatement made with reference to the <s>hetu</s>, <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, and <s>upasaṃhāra</s> is the <s>nigamana</s>. Namely: "Therefore, <s>puruṣa</s> exists." The combination of these components, having a distinct meaning through their mutual connection, is taught to be a <s>vākya</s> (statement). And when multiple statements, their own meanings becoming subordinate, are joined with one another as serving a further purpose, then the entire <s>śāstra</s> too is understood to be one [unified] statement.
[Objection:] The non-mention of <s>jijñāsā</s> (desire to know) and so forth [is justified], because even without them the meaning is grasped by itself. And because conveying [knowledge] to another is like one's own ascertainment. For just as conviction arises in oneself, so too another should be convinced — this is reasonable. And when one is apprehending the meaning by oneself, <s>jijñāsā</s> and the rest have no function therein. Therefore, their inclusion even for the sake of [communicating to] another is not to be posited. Moreover, the statement of doubt is purposeless, since the meaning is already understood. For the proponent and opponent are each certain of their own positions; there is no purpose in mutual questioning about doubt. Furthermore, the statement of purpose and possibility of attainment [is unnecessary], since their understanding follows from the very acceptance of the proof. For the activity of great [thinkers] without purpose is not possible. Nor is there activity regarding an impossible object, such as leveling the <s>Himavat</s> (Himalayas). Therefore, stating these is purposeless. [Counter-reply:] "If [you say] that when they are present, [the result] is present" — it might be argued: when <s>jijñāsā</s> and the rest are present, there is activity toward the ascertainment of truth; when absent, there is not; therefore these too will be [parts of the] proof. But this too is untenable. Why? Because of overextension. Since activity is observed when the self, the inner organ, the senses, light, and the object are present, those too would have to be parts of the proof. And this is undesirable. Therefore <s>jijñāsā</s> and the rest are purposeless. [Further objection:] The <s>pratijñā</s> and the rest are ill-formulated. How so? Because the ascertainment of the <s>sādhya</s> applies to the other components as well. If the ascertainment of the <s>sādhya</s> is called <s>pratijñā</s>, then the ascertainment of the <s>hetu</s> or of the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> too should be called <s>pratijñā</s>, since there is no difference in the ground. For the word <s>sādhya</s> has a general application and cannot be restricted to a particular [referent] without [special] effort. Moreover, the definition of <s>hetu</s> is untenable, since the <s>sādhana</s> has not been [previously] specified. For one who states the definition "the concise statement of the <s>sādhana</s> is the <s>hetu</s>" should first specify what the <s>sādhana</s> is; then it should be said "the concise statement of that is the <s>hetu</s>" — but this has not been done. Therefore this definition is faulty. Furthermore, [the word] <s>samāsa</s> (concise) would lead to the exclusion of detailed [exposition]. For if the word <s>samāsa</s> is employed, what follows is that the detailed elaboration of the proof, such as "the observed co-occurrence of a single class among the varieties that are internal, of the nature of cause and effect," and so forth, would not be the <s>hetu</s>. Therefore the use of <s>samāsa</s> is undesirable. [Sub-objection:] "There is no fault, since it is the <s>liṅga</s> that is stated" — it might be thought: for us, the <s>liṅga</s> is the <s>sādhana</s>, and it has been specified here; therefore the objection is imposed due to one's own dullness of mind, not due to our error. But this too is improper. Why? Because that [<s>liṅga</s>], being divided in two ways, functions as proof in five ways. For that <s>liṅga</s> is accepted as being of two kinds: <s>vīta</s> and <s>avīta</s>, and is thus divided in two. And within that, the <s>vīta</s> has five subdivisions. Therefore it is impossible to call one [component] extracted from the totality the <s>liṅga</s>. Furthermore, the definition of <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> is untenable, since accepting it as either word or referent leads to undesirable consequences. "The illustration of that is the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>" — here, is the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> the word by which the <s>sādhya</s> and <s>sādhana</s> are illustrated? Or the referent in which they are illustrated? What follows from this? If the word is accepted, then the definition of <s>upanaya</s> (application) is undermined. Why? Because the single operation "as stated, so is the <s>sādhya</s>" would not be possible. But if the referent is accepted, then since the referent is not a component of the statement, there would be a contradiction with the five-component [doctrine]. Furthermore, [the objection is that] there is no difference between <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, <s>upanaya</s>, and <s>nigamana</s>, since the meanings of <s>hetu</s> and <s>pratijñā</s> are [already] stated [in them]. The character of being proof, defined as the invariable concomitance with the <s>sādhya</s>, is what is conveyed in both <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> and <s>upanaya</s>. And since the <s>nigamana</s> [merely repeats] the content of the <s>pratijñā</s>, its status as a separate component is not justified.
[Reply:] To the statement that <s>jijñāsā</s> and the rest need not be mentioned because one reaches the status of a component through one's own ascertainment, and therefore they need not be stated for conveying [knowledge] to another — to this we say: No, because it has already been stated. It has been stated above that <s>jijñāsā</s> and the rest are limbs of exposition. And the exposition of <s>śāstra</s> is undertaken by the wise for the benefit of all — not for oneself or for those of equal understanding. When it is so conceived, for those who are to be instructed, these are by no means purposeless. Otherwise there would be a contradiction with what has been said: "The determination of the learned in the teaching of <s>śāstra</s> is for the benefit of those who are in doubt, in error, and uninstructed." Moreover, because no absolute rule is accepted. For we do not say that their statement is absolutely necessary; rather, when the opponent asks "What do you wish to know?", it must necessarily be stated in words. "By what property? Is it eternal or non-eternal?" "What is the source of doubt?" "From its having form." But for one who does not ask, these need not be stated to him. [Objection:] "If they are purposeless somewhere, the consequence applies everywhere." [Reply:] No, because the same consequence would apply to the others [i.e., <s>pratijñā</s> etc.] as well. For the <s>pratijñā</s> and the rest too may sometimes not be stated; would it then follow that they are never to be stated? And thus you yourself have said: "For someone, something is already well-known; therefore even the statement of one [side] alone can be a proof, just as a word, because it conveys two meanings, [sometimes renders] the statement of both unnecessary." As for what was said — that the statement of doubt is purposeless because [the positions] are already determined — this is incorrect. Why? Because it has been stated: when there is a question, that statement is made. By this, [the objections regarding] purpose and possibility of attainment are also answered. For whoever asks "What is the purpose of this?" or "Is this matter possible?" — to him this is to be stated. As for what was said — "when they are present, [the result] is present" — [we reply:] No, because this is not accepted. We do not say: "Because <s>jijñāsā</s> and the rest are present, the ascertainment of truth is present; therefore they are components." Rather, for the person toward whom these function as limbs in [producing] understanding, for that person they are the means of proof. As for what was said — that because the <s>pratijñā</s> is accepted as stating the <s>sādhya</s>, the same consequence applies to <s>hetu</s> and <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> — this is improper. Why? Because that understanding [of what <s>pratijñā</s> is] arises when <s>jijñāsā</s> and the rest are present. Although the word <s>sādhya</s>, without qualification, denotes other things too since it is established [in a general sense], nevertheless, for the person toward whom <s>jijñāsā</s>, doubt, purpose, and possibility of attainment [function], the ascertainment of the <s>sādhya</s> after removing his doubt is the <s>pratijñā</s> — not so for <s>hetu</s> and <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>. Therefore this [objection] is incorrect. Moreover, because there is no contradiction when they are present [in the other components]. When <s>jijñāsā</s> and the rest do occur with respect to the <s>hetu</s> or the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> — as in "Is sound produced or not?" or "Is cognition permanent or momentary?" — then indeed the ascertainment of that becomes a <s>pratijñā</s> [in its own right]. As for what was said — that the definition of <s>hetu</s> is untenable because the <s>sādhana</s> has not been specified — this is incorrect. Why? Because it is well-known in common usage. Just as you, in stating the definition of <s>pratijñā</s> as "the thesis desired to be established as <s>sādhya</s>," do not [separately] define <s>sādhya</s> — why? — because "what is to be established is <s>sādhya</s>" is well-known in common usage — similarly, we, in stating the definition of <s>hetu</s> as "the concise statement of the <s>sādhana</s>," do not [separately] define <s>sādhana</s>. Why? Because "that by which something is proved is <s>sādhana</s>" is well-known in common usage. Or [alternatively], because <s>anumāna</s> (inference) has already been specified. For the <s>liṅga</s> is our <s>sādhana</s>, and it has been specified. As for what was said — that because of the <s>vīta</s> and <s>avīta</s> division, the proof functions in five ways — to this we say: this is improper. Why? Because of the force of the word <s>samāsa</s>. It is precisely for this reason that the word <s>samāsa</s> is employed — so that it may be understood that the <s>hetu</s> is merely the statement of the essential nature of the <s>sādhana</s>, while the elaboration constitutes the other components. By this, the objection of excluding detailed exposition is addressed. How? Because that is not the meaning of the word <s>samāsa</s>. As for what was further said — that the definition of <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> is untenable because of undesirable consequences whether word or referent is assumed — let it be the word that is the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>. As for what was said — that the definition of <s>upanaya</s> would be undermined — this is untenable. Why? Because when [the operation] is impossible in one [domain], the function is understood with respect to the other related [domain]. When it is impossible in the word, we shall understand the function with respect to the referent. Or alternatively, let the referent be the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>. As for what was said — that the five-component doctrine is contradicted because the referent is not a component of the statement — when it is impossible in the referent, we shall understand the function with respect to the word. As for what was said — that <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, <s>upanaya</s>, and <s>nigamana</s> are not separate components because they merely state the meanings of <s>pratijñā</s> and <s>hetu</s> — this is no fault. Why? Because this has not been asserted [by us]. For we do not assert this. Rather: the statement of the <s>prameya</s> (object of knowledge) is the <s>pratijñā</s>; the mere statement of the form of the <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) is the <s>hetu</s>; the demonstration of its coexistence with the <s>prameya</s> is the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>; the subsumption of the <s>sādhya</s> and <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> under a single operation through a common property is the <s>upanaya</s>; the indication of the combined functioning [of all components] for establishing the <s>sādhya</s> is the <s>nigamana</s>. Therefore this [objection] is improper. Moreover, just as one can posit a single thing as having the nature of proof [in multiple aspects], so too there is no fault in positing [multiple components for it]. Just as a statement and its meaning are the primary [signifier and signified] of words and referents, and since they have a non-different object — having established in the mind a single, partless, and sequenceless object, speakers describe it as differentiated through the extraction of capacities such as being graspable by the ear, being impermanent, being produced, being an object of knowledge, and so forth, [applying labels like] <s>sādhya</s>, <s>sādhana</s>, and doubt — yet the unity of the statements of <s>sādhya</s>, <s>sādhana</s>, and doubt is not entailed by their having a single object as their property. Similarly, the statement of the capacities of a single <s>sādhana</s> — namely, its property of being the <s>sādhya</s>, its coexistence with [the <s>sādhya</s>], and so forth — through <s>hetu</s>, <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, and the rest constitutes separate components for us. Therefore, what was said — that <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, <s>upanaya</s>, and <s>nigamana</s> are not separate components because they state the meanings of <s>pratijñā</s> and <s>hetu</s> — is improper. Therefore it is well said that the <s>vīta</s> [inference] has ten components.
The teachers consider it proper to employ the [<s>vīta</s>] first. What is the reason? Because [doing otherwise would] contradict the definition of <s>avīta</s>. For the defining characteristic of <s>avīta</s> is the support of the <s>sādhya</s> by the method of residue. If, when the subject possessing the property of <s>pradhāna</s> has been established through its own positive nature with positive correlation, the application is made merely by negating the opponent's positions, then the characteristic of the method of residue is undermined. Why? Because here the negation alone is stated first. Therefore, just as the manifest does not arise from atoms and so forth due to contradiction with the reasons, so too it could be supposed that it does not arise from <s>pradhāna</s> either due to the absence of reasons. Hence the exclusion of that [supposition] too would have to be derived from the <s>avīta</s> [inference]. In that case, what residue would there be? But when the subject has been delimited through its own positive nature, then the application [of the method of residue] is properly formulated: "If the manifest does not arise from atoms and so forth, then by residue, the manifest arises from <s>pradhāna</s> alone" — this is stated on the basis of the positive correlations and so forth mentioned above. Therefore the employment of <s>vīta</s> first is established. Thus, through <s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s> (inference from general observation), the comprehension of supersensible objects is [demonstrated].
[Objection:] No, because those that are not apprehended through any other means of knowledge are not grasped [by this inference either]. If it is accepted that everything beyond the senses is comprehended through <s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa anumāna</s> (inference from general observation), then the consequence is that even those objects whose non-apprehension is due to there being no other means [of knowing them] should be grasped by that very [inference]. For example —
Due to excessive distance, excessive proximity, impairment of the sense organs, instability of the mind,
subtlety, concealment, suppression, and intermixture with what is similar. (<s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 7)
