Here, <s>hetu</s> (cause) and <s>kāraṇa</s> (cause) are synonymous. That which possesses it is <s>hetumat</s> (caused). <s>Nitya</s> means permanent. What is not permanent is <s>anitya</s> (impermanent). That which pervades is <s>vyāpin</s> (pervasive). What is not pervasive is <s>avyāpin</s> — the meaning is 'not omnipresent.' That which is accompanied by activity is <s>sakriya</s> (active). <s>Aneka</s> means differentiated. <s>Āśrita</s> means dependent. <s>Liṅga</s> means that which is endowed with defining characteristics. Those which are divided are <s>avayavas</s> (parts) — the meaning is 'they are apprehended separately.' That which has parts is <s>sāvayava</s> (composite). <s>Paratantra</s> means dependent on another. These properties beginning with 'caused' and ending with 'dependent' are the unexceptionable and exclusive attributes of <s>vyakta</s> (the manifest), distinct from <s>Pradhāna</s> (primordial nature) and <s>Puruṣa</s> (consciousness).
  [Objection:] 'Caused' is non-specific, since it applies everywhere. For all three — <s>vyakta</s>, <s>avyakta</s> (the unmanifest), and <s>Puruṣa</s> — possess a cause, so this should be listed as a non-distinguishing property.
  [Reply:] No, because of the specification of a productive cause. Even though the property of being caused is common to <s>vyakta</s>, <s>avyakta</s>, and <s>Puruṣa</s>, we shall specify a particular kind of cause — namely a productive cause (<s>kāraka</s>). And that belongs only to <s>vyakta</s> and not to the others, so this will not be a non-distinguishing property.
  [Objection:] That is untenable, because no specification is provided. The word <s>hetu</s> (cause) is a general term. And general terms do not settle upon a specific meaning without connection to a qualifier through context, meaning, or another word. Therefore a specification should have been supplied, but it is not. Hence these are non-distinguishing properties.
  [Reply:] No, because when a term that applies to all is predicated of one subject, it indicates eminence. Here, when a property that could apply to all is predicated of a single subject, eminence is understood from that. Just as when one says 'the young man is a great eater,' since eating applies to everyone, what is understood is 'this one eats eminently' — so too here the teacher says '<s>vyakta</s> is caused' precisely in this sense of eminence. From this we shall understand eminence. And what is this eminence? When both a productive cause (<s>kāraka</s>) and an inferential indicator (<s>jñāpaka</s>) are possible, only the productive cause is intended. Or alternatively, because of connection with the word <s>anitya</s> (impermanent) — for the teacher, having said 'caused,' then reads 'impermanent.' From the connection with this other word, the cause that is concomitant with impermanence is understood to be intended here. And what is the cause concomitant with impermanence? The productive cause (<s>kāraka</s>).
  [Objection:] Even so, this is untenable. Why? Because that applies in both cases. For the followers of other systems hold that destruction is seen in cloth and similar things, for both that which is produced and that which is manifested, without exception. Either a refutation of that should be stated, or one should not say that '<s>vyakta</s> is impermanent in two ways.'
  [Reply:] No, because a one-sided doctrine would follow. For every debater must necessarily accept something as permanent. Even destruction itself, at the very least, is not an object that is not expressed by word and cognition. If that were so, this would be a one-sided doctrine (<s>ekāntavāda</s>). And that is not accepted by those who reason properly. Moreover, if it were conceived thus, even the compounded (<s>saṃskṛta</s>) would be perishable. Therefore it is exceedingly rash to assert destruction for both the produced and the manifested.
  [Objection:] Impermanence is untenable, given the acceptance of <s>satkāryavāda</s> (the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause). For just as there is no origination from what is non-existent, likewise there should be no destruction of what exists. And if destruction of the existent is accepted, then at the time of cosmic dissolution (<s>pralaya</s>), the origination of the <s>tattvas</s> and other things that had been destroyed — origination from what would then be non-existent — would overthrow <s>satkāryavāda</s>. Therefore it is improper to say '<s>vyakta</s> is impermanent.'
  [Reply:] No, because our position is the withdrawal of manifestation (<s>vyaktyapagama</s>). We who always assert the indestructibility of what exists do not contradict <s>satkāryavāda</s>. Rather, when a particular configuration arises from the mutual combination of causes, and then a contrary power manifests, the manifestation (<s>vyakti</s>) is concealed — this is what is meant by the word 'destruction.' And thus the <s>Vārṣagaṇas</s> teach: 'This entire triple world departs from manifestation; it does not depart from existence, because destruction is precluded. And due to the absence of combination, there is subtlety; and due to subtlety, non-apprehension. Therefore the withdrawal of manifestation is what is called destruction. And that is of two kinds: for the <s>tattvas</s>, lasting until the next creation-dissolution cycle; for other things, lasting for some interval of time.'
  [Objection:] This is improper. Why? Because of a contradictory position. The followers of <s>Śākyaputra</s> (the Buddha) maintain that everything cognizable is momentary, except space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and cessation (<s>nirodha</s>). Either a refutation of their view must be stated, or one should not say that '<s>vyakta</s> is impermanent in two ways.'
  [Reply:] No, because we do not accept their reason. Even the learned do not find any evidence (<s>liṅga</s>) for the claim that the triple world is destroyed at every moment. Therefore this does not establish itself in our cognition.
  [Objection:] Because destruction is observed at the end. Here, whatever is seen to perish at its end is observed to be momentary — just as with lamp flames, cognitions, and sounds. And there is destruction at the end for compounded things (<s>saṃskāras</s>), therefore they are called momentary.
  [Reply:] That is untenable, because it remains to be proved. Here, extension by analogy (<s>atideśa</s>) is made from what is established — just as a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) is known from a <s>go</s> (cow). But the momentariness of lamp flames, cognitions, and sounds is not established. Therefore this amounts to nothing.
  [Objection:] This is not unestablished. Why? Because no increase is observed. For if a new flame were to arise in the interval of fuel while the previous flame had not perished, there would also be an increase in size, but that is not seen. Therefore the lamp flame does not persist. Furthermore, because of the absence of a support. The flame arises dependent on its support [the fuel], and that support, even as it is being produced, is itself being consumed — so it is not reasonable for the flame to persist without a support. There would also be the absurd consequence that a flame would persist even when its fuel is exhausted. Furthermore, because of the absurd consequence of the splitting of light by an obstruction placed on top. If one accepts that flames persist, then when an obstruction is placed upon them from above, the light would be split in two like a thread. And this is undesirable. Therefore there is no persistence of flames in a lamp. By this, sound is also answered. How? If sound too were not destroyed, then from the impact of swift wind and water currents, since at every moment a new sound would appear and the prior sound would not be destroyed, there would be an increase. But that is not observed. Furthermore, because of direct perception. For it is established by direct perception that a sound produced by a hand-clap does not exist after the moment of its production. And if one says it is manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>), that is not so, because no fixed rule is observed. A fixed rule regarding causes is observed for sounds that differ according to differences in what is expressed and the speaker. But this does not hold for things apprehended by the same sense organ. Furthermore, because of being heard separately. Sound is heard at a location separate from the location of the cause of manifestation. And this is not observed for manifestable things such as pots. As for momentary cognition, the causes of its destruction have already been stated above. Therefore, what was said — that because the momentariness of lamp flames, cognitions, and sounds remains to be proved, compounded things are not momentary — this is improper.
  [Reply:] Regarding what was said about the non-observation of increase, we say: this is improper. Why? Because of the apprehension of a specific difference. When one says 'momentary,' a specific time-measure is being relied upon, and from the absence of increase and similar observations, only destruction as such is sometimes inferred. But that destruction belongs to flames that persist for one moment — but that they do not persist for even two moments, this is without proof and is merely a dogmatic assertion. What learned person would accept it? As for what was said about the splitting of light by the descent of an obstruction, that too is improper. Why? Because it is untenable either way. Consider: is it the case that what is observed to be split in two is non-momentary, or that what is not observed to be split is momentary? What follows from this? If one accepts that what is split in two is non-momentary, then the absurd consequence is that a thread would be non-momentary. But if one holds that what is not observed to be split is momentary, then what is the example here? Why? Because a thesis without an example has no standing. By this, the increase of sound is also answered. As for what was further said about the non-persistence of sound produced by a hand-clap — there the objector himself has said 'because it is manifestable.' And what was said — that sound is not manifestable because a fixed rule is observed — that is improper, because it is not one-sided. Just as white and black are invariably conveyed by the words 'white' and 'black,' yet they are not thereby non-manifestable; similarly, the fixed relation of sound to speaker and thing spoken may hold, yet sound need not be non-manifestable. And what was also said — that sound is not manifestable because of the impossibility of spatial difference between the manifestable and its manifester — that too is improper. Why? Because it is established as in the case of the eye. Just as there is a manifestable-manifester relationship between the eye and form even when they are in different locations, so too it may be with sound. Therefore sound too is not momentary. As for cognition, we shall state the cause of its momentariness in its own proper section. Therefore what was said — that compounded things are momentary like lamp flames, cognitions, and sounds because destruction is observed at the end — that is improper.
  [Objection:] Then, the momentariness of lamps and all other entities follows. From what? From the absence of a cause for persistence. If an entity is accepted to have perished, then it follows that since there is no impediment to the destruction of this thing immediately upon its origination, the absolute permanence (<s>kūṭasthatva</s>) of all entities would follow.
  [Reply:] No, because of the fitness of a cause. For the domain of all beings is such that origination occurs through the force of <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions), and that very state of being is sufficient for their persistence. When there is destructibility but the <s>saṃskāra</s> is still operative, there is merely a lapse from stability — therefore entities persist for some time. And there is no absurd consequence of absolute permanence. Furthermore, because of the absurd consequence of the destruction of the continuum (<s>santati</s>). For if destruction is accepted immediately upon origination, then the continuum too, since destruction is observed at its end, would be destroyed. And of that continuum too, destruction would follow in the same way. And then, with the triple world appearing and vanishing like a flash of lightning — momentarily seen and then destroyed — in the absence of it all, the absurd consequence of the annihilation of <s>saṃsāra</s> (the cycle of existence) would follow. Therefore it is improper to say that destruction occurs simultaneously with origination.
  If one says there is no fault because the cause persists — one might think: the previously originated entity serves as the cause for the origination of the next; and that one for the one after it; and thus there is no severance of the continuum; but from contact with a contrary entity, there is a lapse from such origination on both sides. This too is improper. Why? Because of the abandonment of the prior reason. It was previously stated that what is to be destroyed does not persist beyond a moment even through the application of <s>mantras</s> and medicines. But now it is said that the continuum that is to be destroyed persists precisely by the force of a cause — this is an abandonment of the prior reason.
  If one says momentariness follows from the absence of a cause of destruction — one might say: no cause of destruction is found for entities; therefore dissolution is intrinsic; therefore what prevents it from occurring simultaneously with origination?
  This too is improper. Why? Because it is not accepted. For who would accept that destruction is without a cause? Rather, as was stated previously, the persistence of entities is due to the nature of things, and their cessation occurs through connection with a contrary substance, whether <s>ādhyātmika</s> (relating to the self) or other.
  If one says it is improper because of the absurd consequence of the destruction of destruction — if absence too is conceived as having a cause, then it too, like a pot, would be subject to destruction. And this is undesirable. Therefore destruction is without a cause.
  [Reply:] This is improper. Why? Because our position is the withdrawal of manifestation (<s>vyaktyapagama</s>). This objection would indeed hold against one who maintains the real destruction of entities. But for us, destruction is the withdrawal of manifestation. And how will that be contested, since it is caused?
  Therefore, compounded things are not momentary because of the absence of a cause of destruction. And for yet another reason they are not momentary. Why? Because of the absurd consequence of non-apprehension. Here, non-apprehension of what is non-existent is observed — just as of a second head. And according to them, pots and such things do not exist beyond a moment. Therefore the absurd consequence of their non-apprehension would follow.
  If one says there is no fault because of the origination of a similar thing — one might say: even though the pot ceases simultaneously with its origination, another pot just like it originates, and upon its cessation yet another, and thus apprehension is unbroken, like the continuity observed in flame, river-current, and so forth.
  This too is improper. Why? Because of the absence of a cause. This would be so if at that time there were a cause for the origination of a similar thing. But there is none, since cessation has already occurred. Therefore this is unfounded.
  If one says it is established because the previously originated entity serves as the cause — that is not so, because it is well known that production comes from a material cause (<s>upādāna</s>). Here in the world, the production of a pot is well known to come from a material cause called a lump of clay. But at that time the lump of clay does not exist [on the momentarist's view]. Furthermore, because no sequence is apprehended. Here, the production of a pot from a palanquin and such things is apprehended in a sequence. But there is no such sequence [in the momentarist's account]. Furthermore, because of the absence of the aggregate of instrumental causes. Here, the production of a pot is well known from the aggregate of the potter, the stick, the wheel, the string, and the slab. But the occurrence of these is not possible there [in the momentarist's account]. Furthermore, because what is to be produced from that does not produce something other than itself. Here in the world, the production of a pot from a pot is not well known. And an example that is not well known is no example at all.
  If one says it is like cognition and sound — one might say: just as a cognition produces another similar cognition, and a sound produces another sound, so too a pot may produce a pot.
  This too is false. Why? Because it is established — for it is also well known to us that from a cognition another cognition arises, and from a sound another sound. [But this does not apply to pots.] Therefore this is mere babbling. So what was said — that because of the origination of a similar thing, the apprehension 'this is the same' is unbroken even given the momentariness of entities — that is improper.
  Furthermore, there is yet another reason. Because at the time of the effect's origination, the cause has ceased. When the cause does not exist, the effect does not originate — otherwise the absurd consequence of the simultaneous apprehension of two pots would follow. But when the effect originates, the cause has ceased — thus origination without a seed is entailed. And this is undesirable, because of the absurd consequence of perpetual origination.
  If one says there is no fault because of the capacity of the cause in what has not yet originated — one might say: as long as the effect has not originated, the cause serves a purpose; once originated, the cause's activity would be purposeless; and the cause does exist when the effect has not yet originated; therefore origination is not without a seed.
  This too is improper. Why? Because of the absurd consequence of origination even in the absence [of the cause]. Consider: let the threads be divided into atoms or thrown into fire — even then, since their destruction is well established, can one claim that a cloth originates from them? Therefore this is a delusion.
  If one says origination and cessation of cause and effect occur simultaneously, like the two pans of a balance — one might say: just as the two pans of a balance rise and fall simultaneously, so too origination and destruction of effect and cause occur simultaneously.
  That too is improper. Why? Because no cause-effect relationship is observed there. What is this — clinging to foam while drowning in water? For the lowering of one pan of the balance is a state of that single thing, and it serves as the cause for the rising of the second pan. But in your view, the destruction of the cause and the origination of the effect occur simultaneously, and no cause-effect relationship between them can be conceived. Therefore this is improper.
  If one says the establishment of momentariness follows from the apprehension of specific differences — one might think: if there is no cessation of entities immediately upon origination, then what accounts for the difference in bodies and such things caused by breath, exhalation, and fatigue, and the difference in lotuses, stones, and such things caused by contact with cold and heat? And the apprehension of bells and such things that are initially without sound and later possess sound — therefore momentary destruction is not refuted.
  This too is improper. Why? Because it has already been answered. The reply has been stated here above — that in the absence of a cause, the absurd consequence of non-origination would follow. Furthermore, because no different configuration is apprehended. For here we do not apprehend a configuration different from and contrary to the prior configuration. Therefore let it be understood that they are non-different. The apprehension of specific differences, however, is due to the manifestation of a different power through the influence of another substance. And it has been said: 'The withdrawal of manifestation is what is maintained, due to the loss of the prior configuration. In the absence of that [loss], the specific difference of this [entity] is not established...'

sattvaṃ laghu prakāśakamiṣṭamupaṣṭambhakaṃ calaṃ ca rajaḥ /
  guru varaṇakameva tamaḥ
children.translated_text: <s>Sattva</s> is light and illuminating; <s>rajas</s> is stimulating and moving; <s>tamas</s> is indeed heavy and obscuring.

evaśabdaḥ pratyekaṃ pariśamāpyate / sattvaṃ laghu prakāṣakameveṣṭam / yat kiṃcitkāryakaraṇe laghu prakāśaṃ ca tatsattvarūpamiti pratyavagantavyam / tatra kāryasya tāvadudgamaheturdharmo laghutvam, karaṇasya vṛttipaṭutvahetuḥ / prakāśastu pṛthivīdharmasya cchāyālakṣaṇasya tamasastiraskāreṇa dravyāntaraprakāśanam / karaṇasyāpi grahaṇaṃ saṅkalpābhimānādhyavasāyaviṣayeṣu yathāsvaṃ pravartamānam /
  upaṣṭambhakaṃ calameva rajaḥ / yaḥ kaścidupastambhaścalatā copalabhyate tadrajorūpamityavagantavyam / tatropastambhaḥ prayatnaḥ, calatā kriyā / sā ca dvividhā, pariṃṇāmalakṣaṇā praspandalakṣaṇā ca / tatra pariṇāmalakṣaṇayā sahakāribhāvāntarānugṛhītasya dharmiṇaḥ pūrvadharmātpracyutiḥ / praspandalakṣaṇā prāṇādayaḥ karmendriyavṛttayaśca vacanādyāḥ / bāhyānāṃ dravyāṇāmutpatananipatanabhramaṇādīni /
  guru varaṇakameva tamaḥ / yatkiṃcid gauravaṃ varaṇaṃ copalabhyate tattamorūpamiti pratyavagantavyam / tatra gurutvaṃ kāryasyādhogamanaheturdharmaḥ karaṇasya vṛttimandatā / varaṇamapi kāryagataṃ ca dravyāntaratirodhānam / karaṇagatā cāśuddhiḥ prakāśapratidvandvibhūtā / ityeṣa sattvādīnāmavyatikareṇa svabhāvopalambho yata eṣāṃ nānātvamavasīyate /
  yatpunaretaduktaṃ strīkṣatramegheṣu svabhāvavyatikaropalambhādeko guṇastrirūpaḥ, sarve vā sarvarūpā, rūpāntarasya vā sata utpattiriti atra brūmaḥ na, guṇabhūtasya bhaktita upakārātpradhānarūpopapatteḥ / iha guṇabhūtasya bhaktitaḥ pradhānopakāritve sati bhaktitastadrūpopapattirdṛṣṭā / tadyathā kṣīrādeḥ / taddhi mukhādiṣu dṛṣṭapratilabdhapravṛttiḥ pittasya svena rūpeṇāṅgabhāvaṃ gacchaṃstasyopakārāttiktaṃ saṃpadyate / na ca tathā sadeva / sattvamapi straiṇaguṇabhūtaṃ sapatnīrajasaḥ svena rūpeṇāṅgabhāvaṃ gacchaṃstasyopakārādduḥkhaṃ saṃpadyate / tamaso mohaḥ / evaṃ kṣātraṃ rajaḥ āryadāralakṣaṇasya sattvasya dasyulakṣaṇasya ca tamasaḥ / evaṃ medhyaṃ tamaḥ kārṣike sattvasya proṣitadayitāyāśca rajasaḥ / tasmānnāsti guṇānāṃ svābhāvavyatikaraḥ / kiṃ cānyat / aguṇabhūtānāṃ svabhāvagrahaṇāt / yadā caite 'ṅgabhāvamapagacchanto madhyasthāstulyasaṃskārāśca pratipadyante tadā svarūpeṇaiva / tasmādasaṃkīrṇaṃ guṇarūpam /
  āha- na, sandehāt / ubhayathā hi rūpāntaragrahaṇaṃ kṣīrādiṣu dṛṣṭam / tādrūpyāttaiśca vipariṇatānāṃ guṇabhāvācca / yathoktaṃ tatra kathamidamekāntena niścīyante guṇabhāvātsattvādīnāṃ rūpāntaragrahaṇaṃ na punastādrūpyādeveti ?
  ucyate- grahaṇavikalpopalambhāt / yadi straiṇaṃ sattvaṃ tādrūpyādeva sapatnyā tena gṛhyate tena bharturapi tathā grahaṇaprasaṃgo madhyasthānāṃ tulyasaṃskārāṇāṃ ca / aniṣṭaṃ caitat / tasmād bhākto 'yaṃ guṇavikalpopalambhaḥ / kiṃ cānyat / uttarakālaṃ svarūpagrahaṇānnivṛttānuśayābhiścaikārthatāmupagatābhiḥ sapatnībhiḥ svenaiva rūpeṇa straiṇasya sattvasya grahaṇamupalabhyate / svagṛhasamavasthitaiścāryadāraiḥ kṣatriyāṇām / niṣpannaśasyaiśca kṛṣīvalairmeghānām / tasmādbhākto 'yaṃ grahaṇavikalpopalambhaḥ / tasmādyuktametat anyo 'nyajananavṛttayo guṇāḥ, na ca saṃkīrṇasvabhāvā iti /
  yatpunaretaduktam anyonyamithunatvānupapattiḥ, sattvasyetaravirodhāt, ityatra brūmaḥ - asti cāyaṃ virodho guṇānāṃ
children.translated_text:
The word 'eva' (indeed) is to be completed with each individually. <s>Sattva</s> is indeed light, illuminating, and pleasant. Whatever is light and luminous in an effect or instrument should be understood as being of the nature of <s>sattva</s>. In that regard, lightness is the property that causes the rising up of an effect, and for an instrument it is the cause of sharpness of function. Illumination, moreover, is the revealing of other substances by the concealment of darkness, which has the character of shadow and is a property of earth. For the instrument as well, it is apprehension — operating respectively in the domains of cognition (<s>grahaṇa</s>), ideation (<s>saṅkalpa</s>), self-reference (<s>abhimāna</s>), and determination (<s>adhyavasāya</s>).
<s>Rajas</s> is indeed stimulating and moving. Whatever stimulation and movement is perceived should be understood as being of the nature of <s>rajas</s>. Of these, stimulation is effort (<s>prayatna</s>), and movement is activity (<s>kriyā</s>). And that is twofold: characterized by transformation (<s>pariṇāma</s>) and characterized by vibration (<s>praspanda</s>). Of these, by transformation-characterized activity, there is the falling away of a substance-possessor — assisted by auxiliary conditions — from its prior property. Vibration-characterized activity includes <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest, the functions of the organs of action such as speech and so on. For external substances, it includes rising up, falling down, revolving, and the like.
<s>Tamas</s> is indeed heavy and obscuring. Whatever heaviness and obscuring is perceived should be understood as being of the nature of <s>tamas</s>. Of these, heaviness is the property that causes the downward movement of an effect, and for an instrument it is sluggishness of function. Obscuring, with respect to effects, is the concealment of other substances; with respect to instruments, it is impurity that stands opposed to illumination. This is the apprehension of the essential natures of <s>sattva</s> and the rest without mutual intermixture, from which their plurality is ascertained.
Now, as to what was said — that from the observation of intermixture of natures in women, warriors, and rain clouds, there is a single <s>guṇa</s> with three forms, or all possess all forms, or there is the origination of a different form from an existing one — to this we say: No, because from the subordinate service of that which has become an accessory (<s>guṇabhūta</s>), the assumption of the principal's form is justified. Here, when that which has become an accessory renders subordinate service to the principal, it is observed that it assumes the form of that principal accordingly. Just as with milk and the like. For milk, having obtained its operation as observed in the mouth and other organs, becoming an accessory of bile through its own form, becomes bitter through service to it. Yet it is not intrinsically so. Likewise, <s>sattva</s>, having become an accessory of feminine qualities, becoming an accessory of <s>rajas</s> (its co-wife, as it were) through its own form, becomes painful through service to it. From <s>tamas</s> comes delusion. Similarly, <s>rajas</s> is martial (<s>kṣātra</s>) — being an accessory of <s>sattva</s> characterized as noble wives and of <s>tamas</s> characterized as bandits. Similarly, <s>tamas</s> is cloud-like (<s>medhya</s>) — being an accessory of <s>sattva</s> in the case of the farmer and of <s>rajas</s> in the case of the woman whose beloved has gone abroad. Therefore there is no natural intermixture of the <s>guṇas</s>. Moreover, because in their non-accessory state their own natures are apprehended. When these, not entering into an accessory relation, become neutral and of equal disposition, then they exist in their own form alone. Therefore the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> is unmixed.
[Objection:] No, because of doubt. For the assumption of a different form in milk and the like is observed in both ways — both from identity of nature and from having become an accessory of those. As stated there, how can this be determined with certainty that it is from the accessory relation that <s>sattva</s> and the rest assume a different form, and not simply from identity of nature?
[Reply:] Because of the observation of differentiated apprehension. If feminine <s>sattva</s> were apprehended by the co-wife merely from identity of nature, then there would be the unwanted consequence that the husband too would apprehend it in the same way, as would those who are neutral and of equal disposition. And this is undesired. Therefore this observation of differentiated quality is figurative (<s>bhākta</s>). Moreover, at a later time, when the co-wives, having withdrawn their residual impressions and arrived at a state of common purpose, apprehend the feminine <s>sattva</s> in its own form alone — this is perceived. Likewise with noble wives staying in their own homes perceiving warriors, and with farmers whose crops have ripened perceiving rain clouds. Therefore this observation of differentiated apprehension is figurative. Hence this is established: the <s>guṇas</s> generate and function through one another, yet they are not of mixed nature.
Now, as to what was said — that mutual pairing is unjustified because <s>sattva</s> is opposed to the others — to this we say: This opposition of the <s>guṇas</s> does indeed exist,
their functioning is purposive, like a lamp. // <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 13 //

kimutpadyata iti vākyaśeṣaḥ / tadyathā vartijyotistailānāṃ parasparavirodhe 'pi pradīpakaraṇaikakāryasādhanabhāvopagatānāṃ vṛttaya ekatra saṃmūrchitāḥ sahabhāvaḥ prakṛṣṭamapi kālamanubhavanti evaṃ sattvarajastamasāṃ sati virodhe mahadādyekakāryasādhanabhāvopagatānāṃ vṛttaya ekatra mūrchitāḥ saha bhavantīti /
  yuktyabhāvādasiddhiriti cet syānmatam - kā punaratra yuktiryena virodhināmekakāryatā bhavatīti ?
  ucyate- guṇapradhānabhāvāt / guṇabhūto hi pratiyogī pradhānabhūtena tadupakarakatvānna virudhyata iti saṃsargeṇa varttitumutsahate / tulyabalayostu dvayoḥ satyameva sahāvasthānasya nāsti sambandhaḥ / tathā ca bhagavān vārṣagaṇyaḥ paṭhati rūpātiśayā vṛttyatiśayāśca virudhyante / sāmānyāni tvatiśayaiḥ saha vartante / tadyathā jalāgnī pacanīyasvedanīyeṣu kāryeṣu, chāyātapau ca sūkṣmarūprakāśane, śītoṣṇe ca prajāvasthitau / evaṃ tatsiddhaḥ pradīpavatsattvarajastamasāṃ virodhe 'pi sahabhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: [Objection:] As to what was said — that from the distinction of essential natures such as lightness and the rest, the plurality of the <s>guṇas</s> is established — to this we say:
If <s>sattva</s> and the other <s>guṇas</s> are distinct from each other due to differences in characteristics,
then, since each possesses two characteristics, six <s>guṇas</s> would result.

The completion of the sentence is: 'what is produced?' Just as the wick, flame, and oil, despite their mutual opposition, having entered into the state of accomplishing the single effect of producing a lamp, their functions, merged together in one place as co-existence, endure even for a long time — so too, despite the opposition among <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s>, having entered into the state of accomplishing the single effect of <s>Mahat</s> (the Great) and the rest, their functions, merged together in one place, co-exist.
[Objection:] If it be said that this is unestablished due to the absence of reasoning — what reasoning is there by which those that are mutually opposed have a single effect?
[Reply:] Because of the relation of principal and subordinate. For the opposing party that has become subordinate does not oppose the one that has become principal, since it serves as its instrument — and thus it is able to function in conjunction. But for two of equal strength, there is truly no possibility of co-existence. And so the venerable <s>Vārṣagaṇya</s> teaches: 'Excesses of form and excesses of function are mutually opposed. But generalities co-exist with excesses.' Just as water and fire in cooking and sweating operations, shade and sunlight in the illumination of subtle forms, and cold and heat in the sustenance of living beings. Thus it is established that, like a lamp, there is co-existence of <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> despite their opposition.

children.text: yadi laghvādilakṣaṇabhedātsattvādīnāṃ nānātvaṃ mitho 'bhyupagamyate tena laghutvaprakāśatvayorapi bhedo 'sti guṇadvayaprasaṃgaḥ / evamupastambhacalatābhyāṃ gauravavaraṇābhyāṃ ca dvayaṃ dvayamiti ṣaḍguṇāḥ prāpnuvanti / atha mataṃ laghutvaprakāśayorabheda iti pṛthaganabhidhānaṃ prāptam / tadbhede vā grahaṇabhedamanicchataḥ prāpto laghutvādibhede 'pi guṇābhedastathā caiko guṇa iti prāptam / yatpunaretaduktaṃ guṇabhūtasya bhaktita upakārātpradhānarūpāpattiriti,

children.translated_text: If <s>sattva</s>, upon becoming an accessory, becomes painful,
then, since the assumption of a different form is not withdrawn, the earlier fault is not removed.

If the plurality of <s>sattva</s> and the rest is accepted on the basis of the difference in characteristics such as lightness and the rest, then there is also a difference between lightness and illumination — resulting in the unwanted consequence of two <s>guṇas</s>. Likewise, stimulation and movement would be two, and heaviness and obscuring would be two — thus six <s>guṇas</s> would result. If, on the other hand, it is held that lightness and illumination are non-different, then they should not have been stated separately. Or, if one who does not wish to accept difference of apprehension despite their being stated differently, then even with the difference of lightness and the rest, non-difference of the <s>guṇas</s> follows — and thus it would follow that there is a single <s>guṇa</s>. Now, as to what was said — that from the subordinate service of an accessory, the assumption of the principal's form results:

children.text:
yadi hi rajaso 'ṅgabhāvamupagacchatsattvamupakārāttadrūpaṃ bhavati tena pratijñātasya rūpāntarasyopasaṃhārāttrairūpyaṃ guṇānāmekaikasya prāptam rūpāntarasya vā sata utpattiḥ / tasmātpūrvadoṣāparihārātpratijñāmātramevāyaṃ samādhiḥ / yadapyuktaṃ aguṇabhūtānāṃ svabhāvagrahaṇāditi /
  aṅgabhāvānapekṣaṃ tu grahaṇaṃ nāstyṛṣerapi /
  paramarṣerapi guṇānāṃ kāryameva pratyakṣaṃ na śaktimātreṇāvasthānamasaṃvedyatvāt / tatra cāṅāṅgibhāvagamanamanivāryam / tasmāddoṣamanicchatā guṇā parityājyāḥ / nāsti vā sudūramapi gatvā tatsaṃkaradoṣaparihāraḥ /
  ucyate- yattāvaduktaṃ lakṣaṇabhedād guṇanānātvavādino lakṣaṇadvayayogādekaikasya guṇaṣaṭtvaprasaṃga iti tanna / kasmāt ? dvayorguṇapradhānabhāvānupapatteḥ / ihārthāntarasyārthāntareṇa guṇapradhānabhāvo bhavati / yathā strīkṣatramegheṣu vyākhyātam / na ca laghutvaprakāśayorupastambhacalanayorgauravavaraṇayośca mithau guṇapradhānabhāvo 'sti, tadanarthāntaraṃ dharmāsta iti nāsti ṣaṭtvaprasaṃga iti / kiṃ ca aprasiddhatvāt / na hyetatkvacitprasiddham yathā yāvanto dharmāstāvanto dharmiṇa iti / na cāprasiddhena vyavahāraḥ / kiṃca pṛthaktvaikāntaprasaṅgāt / lakṣaṇabhedānnānātvapratijñasya sarvārthānāṃ svasāmānyalakṣaṇayogātsvato 'rthāntaramiti pṛthaktvaikāntaprasaṃgaḥ / athaitadaniṣṭaṃ na tarhi vaktavyaṃ lakṣaṇabhedād guṇānāṃ ṣaṭtvamiti / yatpunaretaduktaṃ aṅgabhūtasya pradhānarūpāpatteḥ pūrvadoṣānivṛttiriti tadapyayuktam / kasmāt ? bhaktyabhidhānāt / asakṛdadhītamasmābhirbhākto 'yaṃ guṇānāṃ grahaṇavikalpa iti / na ca bhaktiḥ paramārtha ityasthāne yatnaḥ / yatpunaretaduktaṃ aguṇabhūtānāṃ sattvādīnāmṛṣerapyaviṣayatvamiti satyametat / yattūktaṃ kāryasya viṣayabhūtatvādaṅgāṅgibhāvagamanaṃ guṇānāṃ sakalasatkāryamapekṣate / tathā strīkṣatrameghāḥ prakṛtāsteṣvaṅgabhāvamagacchata iti vijñāyata iti / sāmānyaśabdānāṃ hi prakaraṇādviśeṣe 'vasthānaṃ bhavati / tadyathā bhojanakāle saindhavamānayetyukte lavaṇe saṃpratipattirnāśvādiṣu / tasmātprakaraṇamanapekṣya mahati tantre doṣābhidhānaṃ bālavākyasthānīyam / evaṃ guṇalakṣaṇopadeśātsiddhaṃ traiguṇyam // 13 //
children.translated_text:
For if <s>sattva</s>, upon entering into an accessory relation with <s>rajas</s>, assumes its form through service, then from the non-withdrawal of the admitted assumption of a different form, each <s>guṇa</s> would have three forms — or there would be the origination of a different form from an existing one. Therefore, since the earlier fault is not avoided, this solution is merely an assertion. And as to what was said — that in their non-accessory state the own natures of <s>sattva</s> and the rest are apprehended:
But even for a sage, there is no apprehension independent of the accessory relation.
Even for the highest sage, only the effect of the <s>guṇas</s> is perceptible — not their existence as mere potency, since that is unknowable. And in that case, the entering into the relation of principal and accessory is unavoidable. Therefore, one who wishes to avoid the fault must abandon the <s>guṇas</s> altogether. Or else, even going very far, there is no avoidance of the fault of their intermixture.
[Reply:] As to what was first said — that for one who maintains the plurality of the <s>guṇas</s> on the basis of characteristic-differences, there is the unwanted consequence of six <s>guṇas</s> because each possesses two characteristics — that is not so. Why? Because the relation of principal and subordinate between the two is unjustified. Here, one thing enters into a principal-subordinate relation with another thing, as was explained in the case of women, warriors, and rain clouds. But between lightness and illumination, between stimulation and movement, and between heaviness and obscuring, there is no mutual principal-subordinate relation — they are not different things but properties of the same substance — therefore there is no unwanted consequence of six. Furthermore, because it is not well-established. For this is nowhere well-established — that there are as many substance-possessors as there are properties. And one does not deal with what is not well-established. Moreover, because of the unwanted consequence of absolute separateness. If the plurality follows from characteristic-differences, then since all things possess the characteristics of their own universals, each would be something different from itself — leading to the unwanted consequence of absolute separateness. If this is undesired, then one should not say that from characteristic-differences there result six <s>guṇas</s>. Now, as to what was said — that from the assumption of the principal's form by the accessory, the earlier fault is not removed — that too is unjustified. Why? Because it was stated to be figurative. We have explained repeatedly that this differentiated apprehension of the <s>guṇas</s> is figurative (<s>bhākta</s>). And what is figurative is not ultimate reality — therefore the effort is misplaced. As to what was said — that even for a sage, <s>sattva</s> and the rest in their non-accessory state are not objects of knowledge — that is true. But as was said, since the effect is an object of knowledge, the entering of the <s>guṇas</s> into the relation of principal and accessory presupposes the entire doctrine of <s>satkārya</s> (pre-existence of the effect in its cause). Thus women, warriors, and rain clouds are the subjects under discussion, and it is known that in them the <s>guṇas</s> enter into accessory relations. For general terms come to rest on particulars by virtue of context. Just as when at mealtime one says 'bring the <s>saindhava</s> (rock salt),' the understanding is of salt, not of horses and the like. Therefore, finding fault with a great system without regard to context is tantamount to the words of a child. Thus, from the teaching of the characteristics of the <s>guṇas</s>, the doctrine of the three <s>guṇas</s> (<s>traiguṇya</s>) is established. // 13 //
<s>Kārikā</s> 14

children.text:
āha- avivekyādiridānīṃ gaṇaḥ kathaṃ pratipattavya iti ?
  ucyate-
children.translated_text:
[Objection:] How is the group beginning with non-discrimination (<s>aviveka</s>) now to be understood?
[Reply:]
The group beginning with non-discrimination is established from the three <s>guṇas</s>.
(<s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 11)
. [Question:] How is this known?
That which is three-<s>guṇa</s>-d is non-discriminating, objective, common, non-conscious, and productive — thus
From the absence of the opposite of that.

children.text:
yasmādguṇaviparyayaḥ kṣetrajñaḥ / tatra viṣayatvamacetanatvaṃ prasavadharmitvaṃ ca na bhavatīti purastātpratipādayiṣyāmaḥ / tasmātpariśeṣato vyakte eteṣāṃ dharmāṇāmavirodhaḥ /
  āha, tathā pradhānamiti prāguktaṃ (ka- 11) bhavatā / tadidānīṃ kathaṃ pratipattavyam pradhānamapi triguṇādiyuktamiti ?
  ucyate
children.translated_text:
Since the opposite of the <s>guṇas</s> is the <s>kṣetrajña</s> (the knower of the field, i.e., <s>Puruṣa</s>). In that case, objectivity, non-consciousness, and productiveness do not apply to it — this we shall demonstrate further on. Therefore, by the method of residual determination, there is no contradiction of these properties in the manifest (<s>vyakta</s>).
[Objection:] You have previously stated that <s>Pradhāna</s> (the Primal Cause) is likewise (possessing these properties) (<s>kā.</s> 11). How is it now to be understood that <s>Pradhāna</s> too possesses the three <s>guṇas</s> and the rest?
[Reply:]
The unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>) is also established, since the effect has the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> of its cause. // <s>Īśvarakṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 14 //

children.text: iha kāraṇaguṇātmakaṃ kāryaṃ dṛṣṭaṃ paṭādi / vyakte ca traiguṇyādyupalabhyate / tasmātkāraṇamapyasya tathājātīyakamiti śakyamanumātum / siddhāntamātropadarśanametadācāryaḥ karoti / nyāyaṃ tu yathokteṣu pradeśeṣūpapādayiṣyāmaḥ // 14 //
children.translated_text: Here, the effect is observed to have the nature of the <s>guṇas</s> of its cause, as in the case of cloth and the like. And in the manifest (<s>vyakta</s>), the three <s>guṇas</s> and the rest are perceived. Therefore its cause too can be inferred to be of the same kind. The <s>ācārya</s> (teacher) here presents merely the statement of the established doctrine. The reasoning, however, we shall demonstrate in the places already indicated. // 14 //
<s>Kārikā</s> 15

children.text:
āha, kāryadharmasya kāraṇopalabdhau hetumadādiprasaṃgaḥ, aviśeṣāt / yadi kārye dṛṣṭasya dharmasya kāraṇe sadbhāvo 'bhyupagamyate prāptau hetumadādīnāmapi dharmāṇāṃ kāryadṛṣṭatvātpradhāne prasaṃgaḥ / atha kāryopalabdhau tulyāyāṃ hetumadādayo neṣyante na tarhītareṣāmapi kāraṇāvasthitirastīti /
  ucyate na, svarūpavirodhitve tadapavādavijñānāt / kāraṇaguṇātmakatvātkāryasyetyanena liṅgena hetumadādayo 'pi kāraṇe prasajyante / teṣāṃ tu kāryakāraṇarūpavirodhitvādapavādo vijñāyate / katham ? yadi tāvaddhetumadādayo vyakte dṛṣṭatvātpradhāne vyañjante, kṛtakatvātkāryameva tanna kāraṇamiti prāptam / anityatvācca svayamucchidyamānamananugrāhakamavyāpitvādibhiścānantavikārotpādanaśaktihīnam / ahetumadādayaḥ pradhāne 'bhyupagamādvyakterapi prāpyante tādṛśāḥ kāraṇāsambhavātkāryameva tanna bhavatīti prāptam / avivekyādayastūbhayatrāpi bhavanto netaretarasvarūpavirodhinaḥ / tasmātkāryakāraṇabhāvābhyupagamāddhetumadādyapavādaḥ, itareṣāṃ ca kāraṇasadbhāvaḥ siddhaḥ /
  yaduktaṃ kāraṇaguṇātmakatvātkāryasyāvyaktamapi siddhamiti tadayuktam / kasmāt ? vyaktāvyaktayoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvāprasiddheḥ / siddhe hi vyaktāvyaktayoḥ kāraṇatve etadevaṃ syāt / tattvasiddham / tasmādayuktametat /
  viśeṣānabhidhānādubhayasāmyamiti cet syānmatam, yathā bhavānāha vyaktāvyaktayoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo 'prasiddhaḥ, evaṃ vayaṃ vakṣyāmaḥ- tayoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvāprasiddhirapyasiddhā / na ca kvacidviśeṣo 'styubhayasāmyaṃ bhaviṣyatīti / taccāyuktam / kasmāt ? sadbhāvāsiddheḥ / satyam, anabhidhīyamāne viśeṣe syādubhayasāmyam / avyaktasya tu sadbhāva evāsiddha ityayaṃ viśeṣaḥ / tasmādayuktametadapīti /
  kāryasya kāraṇapūrvakatvādvyaktasya ca kāryatvādavyaktasadbhāve pratipattiriti cet syādetat / kāryaṃ kāraṇapūrvakaṃ dṛṣṭam / ghaṭādikāryaṃ cedavyaktaṃ pramitatvāttasmādidamapi kāraṇapūrvakaṃ bhavitumarhati / yacca tasya kāraṇaṃ tadavyaktamiti / taccānupapannam / kasmāt ? anekāntāt / ihākasmikī ca kāryasyotpattirdṛṣṭā / tadyathendradhanuṣaḥ / asataśca bhrāntimātrāt / tadyathā māyāsvapnendrajālamṛgatṛṣṇikālātacakragandharvanagarāṇām / sataśca kāraṇāt / tadyathā mṛdādibhyo ghaṭādīnām / kāryaṃ cedavyaktamataḥ saṃśayaḥ kimindradhanurvadakasmādasya prādurbhāvo 'tha māyādivadasato 'tha kāraṇātsato ghaṭavaditi ?
  ucyate- nākasmikamasatpūrvaṃ vyaktam / kasmāt ?
children.translated_text: One objects: if a property of the effect is found in the cause, the consequence would be that properties such as being caused and so forth would also [be found in the cause], since there is no distinction. If it is accepted that a property seen in the effect exists in the cause, then the properties of being caused and so forth — since they too are seen in the effect — would apply to <s>pradhāna</s> (primal matter) as well. If, despite the equal observation in the effect, the properties of being caused and so forth are not accepted [in the cause], then the presence of the other [properties] in the cause is also not [established]. It is replied: no, because when there is a contradiction with the essential nature, the exception is recognized. By the inferential mark 'because the effect has the nature of the qualities of the cause,' being caused and so forth too would apply to the cause. But since they contradict the essential nature of cause and effect, the exception is recognized. How? If being caused and so forth, being seen in the manifest, are to be manifested in <s>pradhāna</s>, then since [<s>pradhāna</s>] is produced, it would follow that it is an effect and not a cause. And since it is impermanent, it would be self-destroying, incapable of sustaining, and due to non-pervasiveness and so forth, lacking the power to produce infinite modifications. If being uncaused and so forth are accepted in <s>pradhāna</s>, then they would also apply to the manifest — and since such a cause would be impossible, it would follow that there is no effect at all. But [properties like] non-discrimination and so forth, existing in both, do not contradict the essential nature of either. Therefore, from the acceptance of the cause-effect relationship, the exception of being caused and so forth [follows], and the presence of the other [properties] in the cause is established. As for what was said — 'because the effect has the nature of the qualities of the cause, the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest) too is established' — that is unjustified. Why? Because the cause-effect relationship between the manifest and the unmanifest is not established. For this would be so only if the causal relation between the manifest and the unmanifest were established. But that is precisely what needs to be proved. Therefore this is unjustified. If one says there is equality on both sides because no distinguishing feature has been stated — one might say: just as you say the cause-effect relation between manifest and unmanifest is not established, so too we shall say: the non-establishment of their cause-effect relation is itself not established. And since there is no distinguishing feature anywhere, there would be equality on both sides. But this is unjustified. Why? Because the existence [of the unmanifest] is not established.
Because of the finitude of the differentiated [products].

children.text: yatparimitaṃ tasya sata utpattirdṛṣṭā / tadyathā mūlāṅkuraparṇanāladaṇḍavusatuṣaśūkapuṣpakṣīrataṇḍulakaṇānām / parimitā mahadahaṃkārendriyatanmātramahābhūtalakṣaṇabhedāḥ / tasmātsatkāraṇapūrvakāḥ / yadeṣāṃ kāraṇaṃ tadavyaktam /
children.translated_text: That which is finite is seen to arise from something that exists. For example, the root, sprout, leaf, stalk, stem, chaff, husk, awn, flower, milk, grain, and particles [of a plant]. The differentiated products characterized as <s>mahat</s> (the great principle), <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), the sense organs, <s>tanmātra</s>s (subtle elements), and the gross elements are finite. Therefore they are preceded by an existing cause. That which is their cause is the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest).

children.text: // iti yuktidīpikāyāṃ sāṃkhyasaptatipaddhatau tṛtīyamāhnikaṃ prathamaṃ ca prakaraṇaṃ samāptam //
children.translated_text: Thus ends the third day's session and the first section in the <s>Yuktidīpikā</s>, a commentary on the <s>Sāṃkhyasaptati</s> (Seventy [Verses] of <s>Sāṃkhya</s>).

children.text:
āha- kasmādastyavyaktam ? asadbhedānāmapi parimāṇadarśanāt / anekānta iti cet syānmatam, asti hi māyāsvapnendrajālānuvidhāyināmapi bhedānāṃ parimāṇamiti / tasmādanaikāntiko heturiti /
  tacca naivam / kasmāt ? na hi teṣāṃ niyamo 'sti, etāvadbhirevotpattavyaṃ nānyairiti / mahadādayastu pralayakāle tirobhūtāstāvanta evotpadyante /
  āha, parimāṇānavasthānaṃ kāladvayānupalabdheḥ / satyaṃ, sāmprate kāle mahadādayo yuktaparimāṇāḥ pratyakṣānumānopalabdheḥ / atītānāgatayostu kālayornāsti prasiddhiḥ / tasmādayuktametat /
  ucyate na, viparyaye pramāṇānupalabdheḥ / idānīmetāvanto bhedā ityetacchakyamanumātum atītānāgatayostu kālayornāsti prasiddhiḥ / tasmānna bhedānavasthāprasaṃgaḥ /
  āha, bhedābhedānavasthānāt / mahadādīnāṃ ye bhedā devamanuṣyatiryañco ghaṭādayaśca teṣāmaśakyaṃ parimāṇaṃ paricchettum / sāmānye 'ntarbhāvādayuktamiti cet syānmatam, asti śarīrāṇāṃ mahābhūtasāmānyaṃ ghaṭādīnāṃ ca pṛthivīsāmānyaṃ, tatparimāṇādete 'pi parimitā iti / tadayuktam / kasmāt ? abhāvāt / nahi vaḥ sāmānyaṃ dravyādarthāntarabhūtamasti / sārūpyamātre sāmānyaparikalpanāt /
  ucyate na, tattvāntarānupapatteḥ / tattvabhedena parimitā bhedā ityetadvivakṣitaṃ yathoktamasmābhiruktaṃ ca yadyasti tattvāntaramucyatām / yatpunaretaduktaṃ sāmānyasyārthāntarabhūtasya bhavatpakṣe 'nupapattiriti satyametat / tathāvidhenāpi tu tena saṃvyavahāro na pratiṣidhyate iti vakṣyāmaḥ / tasmātsiddhaṃ bhedānāṃ parimāṇādastyavyaktam /
  kiṃ cānyat /
children.translated_text: One objects: why does the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest) exist? Because finitude is observed even in non-existent differentiated products. If one says this is inconclusive — one might hold: the differentiated products of illusion, dreams, and magic too have finitude; therefore the reason is inconclusive. But this is not so. Why? Because there is no fixed rule for those — [there is no rule that] 'only this many must be produced and no others.' But <s>mahat</s> and the rest, having disappeared at the time of dissolution, arise again in exactly the same number. One objects: the finitude is not stable, because [it is] not observed at two times. True, at the present time <s>mahat</s> and the rest have a definite number, as apprehended through perception and inference. But for the past and the future times, there is no established knowledge. Therefore this is unjustified. It is replied: no, because no means of valid knowledge is found for the contrary. It can be inferred that at present there are this many differentiated products, but for the past and future times there is no established knowledge [to the contrary]. Therefore there is no consequence of the instability of differentiated products. One objects: because of the instability of differentiated products and their sub-products. The sub-products of <s>mahat</s> and the rest — gods, humans, animals, pots, and so forth — cannot have their number determined. If one says this is unjustified because of inclusion in the universal — one might hold: bodies have the universal nature of the gross elements, and pots and the like have the universal nature of earth; from the finitude of those [universals], these too are finite. But that is unjustified. Why? Because [universals as separate entities] do not exist. For in your view, the universal is not something different from substance and the rest. [You hold that] universals are conceived merely from similarity of form. It is replied: no, because another category is untenable [as an alternative]. What is intended is that the differentiated products are finite in terms of the distinction of categories — as stated by us. And we have said: if there is another category, let it be stated. As for what was further said — 'in your system the universal as a separate entity is untenable' — this is true. But we shall explain that conventional usage with such [universals] is not thereby precluded. Therefore it is established: because of the finitude of the differentiated products, the <s>avyakta</s> exists. Moreover:
Because of co-occurrence.

children.text:
iha yena bhedānāṃ samanupagatistasya sattvaṃ dṛṣṭam / tadyathā mṛdā ghaṭādīnām / asti ceyaṃ sukhaduḥkhamohaiḥ śabdādīnāṃ samanugatiḥ / tasmātte 'pi santi ye ca sukhādayo 'stamitaviśeṣāstadavyaktam / tasmādastyavyaktam /
  āha, nāsiddhatvāt / sukhādibhiḥ śabdādayo 'nugamyanta ityetadaprasiddham kena kāraṇena pratipattavyamiti ?
  ucyate- tadbuddhinimittatvāt / iha śabdasparśarūparasagandhānāṃ sannidhāne svasaṃskāraviśeṣayogātsukhaduḥkhamohākārāḥ prāṇināṃ buddhaya utpadyante / yacca yādṛśīṃ buddhimutpādayati tattenānvitam / tadyathā candanādibhiḥ śakalādayaḥ / tasmānnāsiddhiḥ samanvayasyeti /
  āha, asiddha evāyaṃ samanvayaḥ / kasmāt ? vilakṣaṇakāryotpattidarśanāt / na hyayaṃ niyamaḥ kāraṇasadṛśameva kāryamutpadyate / kiṃ tarhi vilakṣaṇaṃ agnidhūmaśabdādi / katham ? na hyagnistṛṇādisvabhāvako 'gnisvabhāvako vā dhūmaḥ / na ca bherīdaṇḍādisvabhāvaḥ śabdaḥ / tasmātsukhādyanugatāḥ śabdādaya itīcchāmātram /
  ucyate na, viśeṣitatvāt / sukhādisvarūpāḥ śabdādayaḥ, tatsannidhāne sukhādyākārapratyayotpattirityetadādita evāsmābhirviśeṣitam / tasmānna bhinnajātīyāsta iti / yattu khalvidamucyate 'gnyādīnāṃ vilakṣaṇānāmutpattidarśanātpradhānabhedānāmatajjātīyaprasaṃga iti tadayuktam / kasmāt ? abhiprāyānavabodhāt / naiva brūmo yo yasya vikāraḥ sa tajjātīyaka iti / kiṃ tarhi yo yajjātīyakaḥ sa tasya vikāra iti / tasmādayuktametat / kiṃcānyat udāharaṇāprasiddheḥ / na caitadudāharaṇaṃ prasiddhaṃ agnyādayaḥ svakāraṇajātiṃ nānuvidadhatīta / kasmāt ? balavīryānuvidhānāt / tadyathā agnerdhūmasya ca tvakcandananalikādisnigdhatānuvṛttestaikṣṇyādyanuvṛtteśca / bherīvikāraḥ śabdo na tu yathā bherīrūpamavasthitam / pradīpeneva tu daṇḍābhighātena vyajyata iti sādhyametat / na caikaiko rūpādīnāṃ dravyākāraḥ samudāyadharmatvāt / tasmānna bherīvikāraḥ śabdaḥ / tatra yaduktaṃ vilakṣaṇakāryotpattidarśanādasiddho 'nvaya ityetadayuktam / tasmādyuktametat samanvayādastyavyaktamiti /
  kiṃ cānyat /
children.translated_text: Here, that by which the differentiated products are pervaded — its existence is observed. For example, clay [pervades] pots and the like. And there is this co-occurrence of pleasure, pain, and delusion with sounds and the other [objects]. Therefore those [pleasure, pain, and delusion] too exist; and that in which the specific [objects] have merged — that is the <s>avyakta</s> (unmanifest). Therefore the <s>avyakta</s> exists. One objects: no, because it is unestablished. That sounds and the like are pervaded by pleasure and the rest — by what means is this to be understood? It is not established. It is replied: because they are the cause of [corresponding] cognitions. Here, in the presence of sounds, touches, forms, tastes, and smells, cognitions having the form of pleasure, pain, and delusion arise in living beings due to the conjunction with their particular dispositions. And whatever produces a cognition of a certain kind is pervaded by that [quality]. For example, pieces of sandalwood and the like [are pervaded by fragrance]. Therefore the co-occurrence is not unestablished. One objects: this co-occurrence is indeed unestablished. Why? Because effects of a dissimilar nature are observed to arise. For there is no rule that only an effect resembling the cause arises. Rather, dissimilar [effects arise], such as fire, smoke, sound, and so forth. How? For smoke does not have the nature of grass and the like [which is its fuel], nor does it have the nature of fire. And sound does not have the nature of the drum, stick, and so forth. Therefore, that sounds and the like are pervaded by pleasure and the rest is mere wishful thinking. It is replied: no, because [the matter] has been specified. That sounds and the like have the nature of pleasure and the rest, and that in their presence cognitions having the form of pleasure and the rest arise — this was specified by us from the very beginning. Therefore they are not of a different class. As for what is said — 'because effects of a dissimilar nature such as fire and the like are observed to arise, the consequence would be that the products of <s>pradhāna</s> are not of the same class' — that is unjustified. Why? Because our intention is not understood. We do not say: 'whatever is a modification of something is of the same class as that.' Rather, we say: 'whatever is of the same class as something is a modification of that.' Therefore this is unjustified. Moreover, because the example is not established. This example — that fire and the like do not follow the class of their own cause — is not established. Why? Because they follow the power and energy [of the cause]. For example, fire and smoke
and because [something] proceeds from its capacity.

children.text:
iha yāvatī kācilloke pravṛttirupalabhyate sā sarvā śaktitaḥ / tadyathā kumbhakārasya daṇḍādisādhanavinyāsalakṣaṇāyāśca śakteḥ sannidhānād ghaṭakaraṇe pravṛttirasti / vyaktasya ceyaṃ kāryatvāttadbhāve pravṛttiriti / atastasyāpi śaktyā bhavitavyam / yāsau śaktistadavyaktam / tasmādastyavyaktamiti /
  āha, prākpravṛtteḥ śaktyabhāvaḥ, pravṛttyanupalabdheḥ / yadi śaktipūrvikā pravṛttiriti manyadhvaṃ tena yāvatpravṛttirnopalabhyate tāvacchaktirnāstītyetadāpannam / kasmāt ? satyāṃ śaktyāṃ kāryābhāve svarūpābhāvaprasaṃgāt / yadi khalvapi vidyamānā śaktiḥ kenacitprabandhena kāryaṃ notpādayecchaktitaraśaktetyetadāpannam / tasmātsahakāribhāvāntarasannidhānātpravruttisamakalāmevārthānāṃ śaktaya utpadyante / tāśca tāvadeva pradhvaṃsante /
  tatra yaduktaṃ prākpravṛtteḥ śaktidarśanādvyaktasyāpi niṣpādikā śaktirastītyetadayuktam / kiṃ cānyat bhedābhedakalpanānupapatteḥ / iha pradhānameva vā śaktiḥ syāt pradhānādvā bhinnā ? kiṃ cātaḥ ? tadyadi tāvatpradhānameva śaktistena kārye bhedācchaktibhedo 'vasīyata iti śaktibhedātpradhānanānātvaprasaṃgaḥ / pradhānaikatvādvā tadavyatiriktānāṃ śaktīnāmekatvaprasaṃgaḥ / tataśca kāryanānātvābhāvaḥ / atha mā bhūdayaṃ doṣa iti pradhānādarthāntarabhāvaḥ śaktīnāmabhyupagamyate tena bhinnānāṃ śaktīnāṃ pravṛttitaḥ siddhau pradhānasiddhirnāstītyetadāpannam / kiṃ cānyat / svarūpābhidhānaṃ ca / pradhānasya śaktimātrādapyarthāntaratvamabhyupagamya rūpamīdṛkpradhānaṃ svāvasthāyāmiti, taccāśakyamabhidhātum / tasmād bhedābhedakalpanānupapatterakalpanīyā śaktiriti /
  ucyate- yaduktaṃ prākpravṛtteḥ śaktyabhāvaḥ pravṛttyanupalabdheriti, atra brūmaḥ nāprasiddhatvāt / kāraṇaṃ śaktiḥ kāryaṃ pravṛttiḥ / na ca kāryānupalabdhau kāryābhāva ityetalloke prasiddham / yatpunaruktaṃ kāryaniṣpattau śakteḥ svarūpahānamiti atra brūmaḥ na, pradīpadṛṣṭāntāt / yadyathā pradīpasya ghaṭādiprakāśanaśaktirasti / atha ca kuḍyādyāvaraṇasāmarthyānna ghaṭādīnprakāśayituṃ śaknoti / na ca śakyate vaktuṃ pradīpasya prakāśanaśaktiraśakteti / evamanyeṣāmapi bhāvānāṃ prākprarutterapi śaktiḥ syāt / na cāpravṛttidarśanādasyāḥ svarūpahānaṃ syāt / yattūktaṃ sahakāribhāvāntarasannidhānātpravṛttisamakālamevārthānāṃ śaktiprādurbhāva iti atra brūmaḥ- tadaprasiddhiḥ śaktyapekṣatvāt / iha sarvaḥ kartā svagatāṃ śaktimapekṣya tadyogyatayā sahakāribhāvāntaramupādatte, sā cetprākpravṛtterna syātsādhanānāṃ viṣayasvabhāvānavadhāraṇādanupādānaprasaṃgaḥ / aniṣṭaṃ caitat / tasmātprākpravṛtteḥ śaktiḥ / yatpunaretaduktaṃ tāvadeva pradhvaṃsaṃ iti atra brūmaḥ na, kāryaniṣṭhādarśanāt / yadi pravṛttisamakālameva pradhvaṃsaḥ iti atra brūmaḥ na, kāryaniṣṭhādarśanat / yadi pravṛttisamakālameva pradhvaṃsaḥ syātkāryaniṣṭhaiva na syāt / tannimittatvātkāryasya asti tvasau / tasmānna pravṛttisamakālameva śatipradhvaṃsaḥ / sadṛśasandhānotpatyā kāryaniṣṭheti cenna / vināśasamakālotpattyasambhavāt / athāpi syādekasyāṃ śaktau kṣaṇasādhyamaṃśamavasāya vinaṣṭāyāmanyattatsadṛśaṃ śaktyantaramutpadyate, tasminvinaṣṭe 'nyaditi / evaṃ śaktisantānātkāryaniṣṭhā bhavatīti / etadapyayuktam / kasmāt ? vināśakālotpattyasambhavāt / ko hyatra heturyena vināśasamakālamanyacchaktirūpaṃ kāryamavasīyayati na punaḥ prāktanamevāvasthitamiti ? kiṃ cānyat / kauṭasthyadoṣaparihārāt / kṣaṇottarakālāvasthāne ca bhāvānāṃ yo doṣa upāttaḥ kauṭasthyaprasaṃga iti tasya parihāra uktaḥ / tasmānnāsti śaktīnāṃ pravṛttikāle vināśaḥ / pravṛttyuttarakālamapi nāsti / kasmāt
? punaḥ pravṛttidarśanāt / śaktyantarotpattau pravṛtyuttarakālamapi iti cet na, hetvabhāvāt / ko hyatra nirbandhaḥ tasyāṃ vinaṣṭāyāmanyā pravṛttyantaraheturbhavati naiva punaḥ saiveti ? kṛtārthatvādi cet na anabhyupagamāt / na hyekaghaṭārthā śaktirabhyupagamyate / tatra yenaiva hetunā ekaṃ ghaṭamavasāya na vinaśyati tenaiva yāvanti kartavyānīti / tasmāttriṣu kāleṣu śaktayo 'vatiṣṭhante /
  yatpunaretaduktaṃ bhedābhedakalpanānupapattiriti, atra brūmaḥ- astu pradhānādabhinnā śaktiḥ / na tasya nānātvaṃ śaktyekatvaṃ vā prasajyate / kasmāt ? saṃkhyāvyavahārasya buddhyapekṣatvādbuddhinimittasya cāsatkāreṇa pradhānaśaktisvabhāvāt, ihāyaṃ saṃkhyāvyavahāro buddhyapekṣaḥ / katham ? yadabhinnāṃ buddhimutpādayati tadekaṃ, pradhānāvasthāyāṃ ca śaktayo 'stamitaviśeṣatvādabhinnāṃ buddhimutpādayanti / tasmādekaṃ tatpravṛttikāle viśeṣāvagrahaṇe bhedaṃ pratipadyate, devaśaktirmanuṣyaśaktirityādi / tasmānnāsāmekatvamato na bhedābhedakalpanānupapattiriti / vyakte darśanācchaktīnāmavyakte pratipattiriti cet syādetat / vyakte śaktipravṛttī dṛṣṭe na cāvyakte / kvacidanyato vyaktamevaitasmāddhetoḥ siddhyati nāvyaktamityetaccāyuktam / kasmāt ? sāmānyatodṛṣṭāntātsiddheḥ / yathaiva hi devadattādhārayā kriyayā tasya deśāntaraprāptimupalabhyātyantādṛṣṭaṃ jyotiṣāṃ deśāntaraprāptergamanamanumīyate evaṃ pravṛtteḥ śaktiniyamitatvādvyaktasya ca pravṛttibhūtatvādavaśyamatyantādṛṣṭā śaktirabhyupagantavyeti siddhaṃ śaktitaḥ pravṛtterastyavyaktam /

Here, whatever activity is observed in the world, all of it proceeds from <s>śakti</s> (power). For example, the potter's activity in making a pot arises from the presence of means such as the rod, etc., and the power characterized by their arrangement. And this activity of the manifest (<s>vyakta</s>), because of its being an effect, consists in the presence of that [power]. Therefore, it too must possess a power. That which is this power — that is the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>). Therefore, the unmanifest exists.
  [The objector] says: Prior to activity, there is no power, because activity is not observed. If you think that activity is preceded by power, then as long as activity is not observed, it follows that power does not exist. Why? Because if power exists but there is no effect, there would be the consequence of the loss of its essential nature. And if indeed an existing power, through some sequence, does not produce its effect, it follows that the power is not truly a power. Therefore, due to the presence of auxiliary conditions, the powers of things arise simultaneously with activity, and they perish at that very same time.
  Therefore, what was said — that from the observation of power preceding activity, the manifest too has a productive power — this is improper. Moreover, because of the untenable nature of the supposition of both identity and difference. Here, is the power identical with <s>pradhāna</s> (primordial matter) itself, or is it different from <s>pradhāna</s>? What follows from this? If the power is identical with <s>pradhāna</s>, then since the difference of powers is determined from the difference of effects, the plurality of <s>pradhāna</s> would follow from the plurality of powers. Or, from the oneness of <s>pradhāna</s>, the oneness of the powers that are not different from it would follow. And consequently, there would be no plurality of effects. If, to avoid this defect, the powers are accepted as being something different from <s>pradhāna</s>, then it follows that when [things are] established through the activity of distinct powers, <s>pradhāna</s> itself is not established. Moreover, there is [the problem of] stating its essential nature. Even accepting that <s>pradhāna</s> is something different from the mere powers, 'the nature of <s>pradhāna</s> in its own state is such-and-such' — this cannot be stated. Therefore, because of the untenable nature of the supposition of both identity and difference, power is inconceivable.
  It is replied: As for what was said — that prior to activity there is no power because activity is not observed — to this we say: No, because [the non-existence of power] is not established. The cause is the power; the effect is the activity. And it is not established in the world that the non-existence of the effect means the non-existence of the effect [i.e., of the cause]. As for what was further said — that at the accomplishment of the effect, the power loses its essential nature — to this we say: No, from the analogy of the lamp. Just as a lamp has the power of illuminating a pot, etc., and yet, due to the obstructive capacity of a wall, etc., it cannot illuminate the pot, etc. — and yet it cannot be said that the lamp's power of illumination is not a power. Likewise, for other entities too, even prior to activity, there may be a power; and from the observation of non-activity, there would be no loss of its essential nature. As for what was said — that due to the presence of auxiliary conditions, the manifestation of powers of things occurs simultaneously with activity — to this we say: That is not established, because of the dependence on power. Here, every agent, having regard to its own inherent power, takes up the auxiliary means appropriate to it. If this [power] did not exist prior to activity, there would be the consequence of non-adoption [of means], because the nature of the objects as suitable instruments could not be determined. And this is undesirable. Therefore, power exists prior to activity.
  As for what was further said — that they perish at that very same time — to this we say: No, because they are observed to persist in the effect. If destruction were simultaneous with activity, they would not persist in the effect. But they do persist, because the effect is caused by them. Therefore, the destruction of power is not simultaneous with activity. If [you say] the persistence in the effect is through the arising of a similar successor — no. Because of the impossibility of arising at the same time as destruction. Even if [you suppose] that when one power, having accomplished its momentary portion, is destroyed, another similar power arises, and when that is destroyed, another, and so on — so that from this continuum of powers there is persistence in the effect — this too is improper. Why? Because of the impossibility of arising at the time of destruction. For what reason is there here by which one should determine that at the same time as destruction another power-form arises as its effect, rather than that the previous one simply persists? Moreover, because the defect of immutability (<s>kauṭasthya</s>) is avoided. The defect that was raised — namely the consequence of immutability from the persistence of entities beyond [their] moment — the answer to that has been stated. Therefore, there is no destruction of powers at the time of activity. Nor is there [destruction] after the time of activity. Why? Because activity is observed again. If [you say] this is due to the arising of a different power after the time of activity — no, because there is no reason [for this]. For what compulsion is there that when one [power] is destroyed, another becomes the cause of another activity, rather than the same one [continuing]? If [you say] because [the power] has accomplished its purpose — no, because that is not accepted. For the power is not accepted as being for the purpose of a single pot. Therefore, by the very same reason by which it does not perish after completing one pot, [it persists for] however many [pots] are to be made. Therefore, powers persist through all three times.
  As for what was further said — that the supposition of identity and difference is untenable — to this we say: Let the power be non-different from <s>pradhāna</s>. Neither its plurality nor the oneness of the powers would follow. Why? Because numerical convention depends on cognition, and because <s>pradhāna</s> and power are by nature [determined by] the constructive activity of cognition. Here, this numerical convention depends on cognition. How? What produces an undifferentiated cognition, that is one. And in the state of <s>pradhāna</s>, the powers, because their particularities are submerged, produce an undifferentiated cognition. Therefore, that is one. At the time of activity, due to the apprehension of particularities, it comes to be differentiated — 'the power of a god,' 'the power of a human,' and so forth. Therefore they are not one; hence there is no untenable nature of the supposition of identity and difference.
  If [you say] from observation in the manifest, [we should infer] powers in the unmanifest — [the argument would be:] the activity of powers is seen in the manifest, but not in the unmanifest. In some cases, from this reason, only the manifest would be established, not the unmanifest. And this too is improper. Why? Because establishment [is possible] through a general analogy (<s>sāmānyato dṛṣṭa</s>). For just as, from the movement of <s>Devadatta</s> and the activity of carrying, his reaching another place is observed, and from this the completely unseen movement of the luminaries to another place is inferred — so too, because activity is determined by power, and because the manifest is characterized by activity, a completely unseen power must necessarily be accepted. Thus it is established that from power and activity, the unmanifest exists.
  Moreover:
[The unmanifest exists] because of the distinction of cause and effect (<s>kāraṇakāryavibhāga</s>).

) has been explained. Likewise, the mutual dependence and single substratum of sound and the other [subtle elements] in earth and the other [gross elements]; the mutual acquisition, protection, and refinement of the ear and the other [sense faculties]; the effects of the instrument upon the product — namely, sustenance, means, manifestation, and so forth — and the effects of the product upon the instrument — namely, the healing, mending, regeneration, drying, and maintenance of function; the role of earth and the other elements in sustaining, gathering, providing paths, arranging, and giving space, whereby cattle and the like serve as the basis for divine, human, and animal [beings] through seasonal rites, worship, nourishment, consumption, and transactions; the mutual instruction of the <s>varṇas</s> (social classes) in their respective duties and spheres of activity. And other [examples] should be understood from the world as far as possible.
  [Objection:] That is untenable — because [mutual assistance] is impossible either sequentially or simultaneously.
  The mutual assistance of the <s>guṇas</s> through illumination, activity, and restraint that is accepted here — does it occur sequentially or simultaneously? What follows from this? First, it cannot occur sequentially. Why? Because if one [<s>guṇa</s>] acts independently, the same would follow for the other two. If <s>sattva</s> first illuminates by its own power, independent of the other <s>guṇas</s>, and is [then] relied upon as their helper, then just as <s>sattva</s> [acts independently], the other two would also accomplish their own functions without needing assistance — thus mutual assistance becomes purposeless. If, to avoid this defect, simultaneity is adopted — that too is untenable. Why? Because things existing simultaneously cannot assist each other, like the two horns of a cow. Furthermore, because the alternatives of existent and non-existent are both untenable. Here, does <s>sattva</s>, when illuminating, manifest the illumination of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s> when it exists, or when it does not exist? What follows? If it manifests what already exists, then since all would have the same nature, the consequence would be that all are [merely] <s>guṇas</s> [without distinction]. Moreover, like <s>sattva</s>, the other two would also have independence. Just as <s>sattva</s> has the power of illumination and therefore illuminates independently of the other <s>guṇas</s>, so too the other two — this is the defect. But if the power of illumination, being non-existent [in <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>], arises from connection with <s>sattva</s>, then what was said earlier — that the powers exist prior to their operation — is undermined. And from that follows the contradiction of the <s>satkāryavāda</s> (doctrine of pre-existent effect). Furthermore, because [the reason] is inconclusive. For it is not invariably the case that things which mutually assist each other must be preceded by an established state. Thus, <s>sattva</s> and the others mutually assist each other, yet they are not preceded by an established state. Therefore, what was stated — that the unmanifest exists because of the distinction between cause and effect — that is untenable.
  [Reply:] As for what was said — that there is no mutual assistance because it is impossible either sequentially or simultaneously — let the assistance be simultaneous. As for the objection that things existing simultaneously cannot assist each other, like the horns of a cow — to this we say: No, because otherwise [the observed facts] would be inexplicable. For it is not the case that the cow's horns cannot assist each other because they coexist. Rather, it is because they have no common function. But for things that do have a common function, mutual assistance in coexistence is not precluded — for example, earth and the other [elements] through sustaining, gathering, providing paths, arranging, and giving space. Even the hooves and horns, which exist simultaneously in the body without sequential order, do not mutually assist each other. Therefore, coexistence and non-coexistence are not the causes of assistance and non-assistance. Moreover, because it is observed. For indeed, the simultaneous assistance of wind, chariot-components, and so forth in rapid upward motion is observed — there is no defect. So too it should be for the <s>guṇas</s>. If one says the conjunction is the cause — [we ask:] is what is to be proved something different, or is the conjunction merely an attainment? As for the objection regarding the impossibility of the existent-nonexistent alternatives — to this we say: that is untenable. Why? Because, as in the case of the lame and the blind, no defect arises in their mutual assistance. Just as for the lame and the blind, through their mutual connection, the powers of seeing and walking, which [each] does not possess, are manifested in the other — yet they are neither non-existent nor [newly produced] — and [thus] a common purpose is accomplished; and just as the mutual assistance of earth and the other elements manifests [their respective] powers without [producing] the other's power — so too for the <s>guṇas</s>. As for the objection of inconclusiveness — that is untenable. Why? Because of failure to understand the doctrine. Here, since we do not accept a real difference between cause and effect, it is merely a different state of the <s>guṇas</s> that, independently of other states, receives the designation of 'cause' and 'effect.' Among these, the <s>guṇas</s> in the state of <s>pradhāna</s>, having the form of mere potency and possessing an indefinable nature of illumination and the rest, do not have mutual assistance based on that. But when they enter into disequilibrium, then, with their natures of illumination and the rest unrestricted, they engage in mutual assistance based on that. Therefore, the acceptance of mutual assistance among the manifest does not contradict the precedence of the established state — it is only by failing to understand the doctrine that one says 'this reason is inconclusive.' If it is thought that since mutual assistance is not accepted in the state of <s>pradhāna</s>, the same consequence applies later too — [we reply:] if the <s>guṇas</s> were first disturbed from their prior state by their own power alone, then indeed the same would follow later. But since mutual assistance is accepted even in the state of <s>pradhāna</s>, the reason is not inconclusive. And that is not so.
  Why? Because, like fire, it is caused by one's own power. Just as a subtle fire produces a subtle illumination by itself, but for illuminating pots and the like it requires oil-wicks and such — so too, the initial disturbance of the <s>guṇas</s> is by their own power, but [further transformation] requiring <s>mahat</s> and the rest is through mutual assistance. Therefore, it is proper that 'from the distinction between cause and effect, the unmanifest exists.'
  What else?

Cause and effect — [these constitute] the cause-effect [pair]. Their distinction is the cause-effect distinction. The determination by the intellect in two ways — 'this is the cause, this is the effect' — that distinction is the cause-effect distinction. This is observed to be preceded by an abiding entity. For example, beds, seats, chariots, wheels, and the like. And this cause-effect distinction exists for the manifest (<s>vyakta</s>); therefore, this too is preceded by an abiding entity. That which is the abiding entity — that is the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>).
  [The objector] says: This is improper, because it [i.e., the cause-effect distinction in the intended sense] is not observed. For no cause-effect distinction of beds and the like is observed. Therefore this is improper.
  It is replied: No, because 'cause' and 'effect' are synonymous with 'helper' and 'helped.' The cause-effect [relation] does not mean the relation of producer and produced. Rather, it means the relation of helper and helped. And this exists for beds and the like, and for the manifest. Therefore, this is not stated through carelessness.
  [The objector] asks: What, then, is the cause-effect relation of the manifest with respect to what is higher and what is lower?
  It is replied: First, as for the <s>guṇa</s>s — <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> — the manner in which activity occurs through their mutual assistance by means of the properties characterized as illumination, activation, and restraint, and [that they are] of the nature of pleasure, displeasure, and delusion — this [will be discussed] in the [relevant] <s>sūtra</s>.
Because of the non-differentiation of the multiform. // <s>Sāṃkhyakārikā</s> 15 //
